paragraphs: The paper offers a statistical interpretation of Kanerva's sparse distributed memory. Ordinarily, this model is understood as an associative memory that retrieves stored information. Near or beyond its capacity, that behavior breaks down. The authors argue that the computation in this regime can instead be understood as statistical prediction.

Mathematical results establish a broader framework in which the standard sparse distributed memory formulation becomes a special case. This changes how one interprets overloaded operation: failure to behave as an associative store does not by itself describe everything the system is computing. The statistical view supplies another account of its output and another objective against which it can be assessed.

The framework suggests ways to improve the model. One proposed procedure draws on genetic algorithms to increase predictive usefulness. Another aims to improve capacity when the model is used as an associative memory. These are presented as enhancements suggested by the new viewpoint, connecting a reinterpretation of existing behavior with possible changes to both prediction and storage.
summary.tldr: Sparse distributed memory can be interpreted as a statistical predictor near or beyond capacity, suggesting improvements to prediction and associative storage.

title: Statistical Prediction with Kanerva's Sparse Distributed Memory

abstract: The subject of this paper is the integration of multi-layered Artificial Neu(cid:173) ral Networks (ANN) with probability density functions such as Gaussian mixtures found in continuous density Hidden Markov Models (HMM). In the first part of this paper we present an ANN/HMM hybrid in which all the parameters of the the system are simultaneously optimized with respect to a single criterion. In the second part of this paper, we study the relationship between the density of the inputs of the network and the density of the outputs of the networks. A few experiments are presented to explore how to perform density estimation with ANNs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how multilayer neural networks can be combined with probability-density models, especially Gaussian mixtures used in continuous-density hidden Markov models. The aim is to connect neural computation with a probabilistic representation useful for speech recognition. It also examines what such a connection means for estimating distributions more generally.

The first part presents a neural-network and hidden-Markov-model hybrid whose parameters are all optimized simultaneously using one criterion. This gives the combined system a shared training objective. The contribution is therefore not only placing two model types together, but arranging learning so that their adjustable parts are optimized as components of the same system.

The second part studies the relationship between the probability density of network inputs and the density of its outputs. That relationship matters when interpreting a network's transformation as part of density estimation. A few experiments explore how neural networks can perform this task. Together, the two parts investigate both joint training for a speech-oriented hybrid and the distributional questions underlying neural density modeling.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly trains a neural-network/HMM hybrid and explores how network transformations can support probability-density estimation.

title: Neural Network - Gaussian Mixture Hybrid for Speech Recognition or Density Estimation

abstract: Existing metrics for the learning performance of feed-forward neural networks do not provide a satisfactory basis for comparison because the choice of the training epoch limit can determine the results of the comparison. I propose new metrics which have the desirable property of being independent of the training epoch limit. The efficiency measures the yield of correct networks in proportion to the training effort expended. The optimal epoch limit provides the greatest efficiency. The learning performance is modelled statistically, and asymptotic performance is estimated. Implementation details may be found in (Harney, 1992).
originalAbstract: Existing metrics for the learning performance of feed-forward neural networks do not provide a satisfactory basis for comparison because the choice of the training epoch limit can determine the results of the comparison. I propose new metrics which have the desirable property of being independent of the training epoch limit. The efficiency measures the yield of correct networks in proportion to the training effort expended. The optimal epoch limit provides the greatest efficiency. The learning performance is modelled statistically, and asymptotic performance is estimated. Implementation details may be found in (Harney, 1992).

paragraphs: Comparing neural-network training methods can depend heavily on how long each run is allowed to continue. This paper identifies the training epoch limit as a problem for existing performance measures: choosing a different stopping limit can change the result of a comparison. It proposes measures intended to avoid that arbitrary dependence.

The central efficiency measure relates the number of successfully trained networks to the training effort spent obtaining them. This frames learning performance as a balance between successful outcomes and computational effort. Within that framework, the optimal epoch limit is the stopping point that achieves the highest efficiency, making the limit something to determine systematically.

The paper also models learning performance statistically and estimates its asymptotic behavior, meaning its behavior as training extends further. These ideas connect practical decisions about when to stop training with a broader account of learning success. The contribution is a framework for comparing training performance and choosing useful stopping limits, rather than treating a manually selected training budget as an unquestioned benchmark.
summary.tldr: New benchmarking measures compare successful training against effort and identify an efficiency-maximizing training limit.

title: Benchmarking Feed-Forward Neural Networks: Models and Measures

abstract: In a Bayesian framework, we give a principled account of how domain(cid:173) specific prior knowledge such as imperfect analytic domain theories can be optimally incorporated into networks of locally-tuned units: by choosing a specific architecture and by applying a specific training regimen. Our method proved successful in overcoming the data deficiency problem in a large-scale application to devise a neural control for a hot line rolling mill. It achieves in this application significantly higher accuracy than optimally-tuned standard algorithms such as sigmoidal backpropagation, and outperforms the state-of-the-art solution.

Our method proved successful in overcoming the data deficiency problem in a large-scale application to devise a neural control for a hot line rolling mill. It achieves in this application significantly higher accuracy than optimally-tuned standard algorithms such as sigmoidal backpropagation, and outperforms the state-of-the-art solution.

paragraphs: This paper addresses neural control when available data are insufficient but useful domain knowledge already exists. The motivating application is a hot-line rolling mill. The authors consider analytical theories that describe the application imperfectly and ask how those theories can still contribute systematically to learning an accurate control model.

Their answer uses a Bayesian framework to incorporate prior knowledge into networks of locally tuned units. The knowledge influences both the choice of network architecture and the training regimen. This makes domain theory part of how the model is constructed and learned, allowing imperfect analytical information to contribute alongside the available observations.

In the large-scale rolling-mill application, the method successfully addresses data deficiency and achieves substantially higher accuracy than optimally tuned standard algorithms, including sigmoidal backpropagation. It also outperforms the existing state-of-the-art solution. The stated result supports the value of using application knowledge to shape learning when data alone are inadequate, with the evidence coming from this industrial control setting.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian method embeds imperfect domain theory into neural architecture and training to improve rolling-mill control with limited data.

title: Neural Control for Rolling Mills: Incorporating Domain Theories to Overcome Data Deficiency

paragraphs: The paper asks when gradient-descent training should stop if the goal is good generalization. It studies a particular class of feedforward networks with fixed input weights and linear output neurons, trained on finitely many examples. The distinction between performance on those examples and performance beyond them is central to the analysis.

Under general regularity conditions, the authors identify three distinct phases in generalization performance during learning. They show that stopping at a suitable time before reaching the global minimum of empirical error can produce better generalization. Consequently, the point that best fits the available training examples need not be the point with the best predictive behavior.

The work also introduces a notion of effective machine size, connecting its stopping-time question to model complexity. The supported practical implication is that training duration itself matters when selecting a predictor from the learning trajectory. Within the network class studied, deciding when to stop is part of controlling generalization, even while further optimization could still reduce training error.
summary.tldr: For networks with fixed input weights and linear outputs, stopping gradient descent before minimum training error can improve generalization.

title: Optimal Stopping and Effective Machine Complexity in Learning
Functional Models of Selective Attention and Context Dependency

abstract: We present an analog VLSI chip for parallel analog vector quantiza(cid:173) tion. The MOSIS 2.0 J..Lm double-poly CMOS Tiny chip contains an array of 16 x 16 charge-based distance estimation cells, implementing a mean absolute difference (MAD) metric operating on a 16-input analog vector field and 16 analog template vectors. The distance cell includ(cid:173) ing dynamic template storage measures 60 x 78 J..Lm2 • Additionally, the chip features a winner-take-all (WTA) output circuit of linear com(cid:173) plexity, with global positive feedback for fast and decisive settling of a single winner output. Experimental results on the complete 16 x 16 VQ system demonstrate correct operation with 34 dB analog input dynamic range and 3 J..Lsec cycle time at 0.7 mW power dissipation.

The distance cell includ(cid:173) ing dynamic template storage measures 60 x 78 J..Lm2 • Additionally, the chip features a winner-take-all (WTA) output circuit of linear com(cid:173) plexity, with global positive feedback for fast and decisive settling of a single winner output. paragraphs: The paper presents a chip that assigns an incoming analog vector to one of several stored templates. This operation, called vector quantization, requires comparing the input with candidate representatives and choosing the closest one. The design performs these comparisons in parallel, making the selection process a direct operation of the analog circuitry.

Its core is a 16-by-16 array of charge-based distance cells that compares a 16-component input against 16 template vectors. Similarity is measured through mean absolute difference: the average magnitude of the componentwise discrepancies. Each cell includes dynamic template storage. A winner-take-all circuit then selects a single output, using global positive feedback to make that decision settle quickly and decisively.

Tests of the complete chip demonstrate correct operation with a 34-decibel analog input dynamic range, a 3-microsecond cycle time, and power consumption of 0.7 milliwatts. These measurements establish that the distance computation, template storage, and final selection work together in hardware. The contribution is a demonstrated parallel analog implementation of the full quantization operation.
summary.tldr: A charge-based analog chip compares 16-component inputs with 16 templates in parallel and selects the closest match.

title: A Charge-Based CMOS Parallel Analog Vector Quantizer

paragraphs: The paper models head-direction cells, neurons whose activity indicates the direction a rat faces within its surroundings. Their directional preference is independent of the animal's location. The quantity being represented is heading relative to the environment, rather than simply the position of the head relative to the body.

The authors propose a biophysical model in which a circuit involving the thalamus and cortex computes heading by integrating the head's angular velocity over time. In plain terms, the circuit accumulates turning information to update direction. This provides a proposed mechanism connecting a changing movement signal with an ongoing representation of orientation.

The model is implemented in the NEURON simulator and produces testable predictions about the structure and function of the head-direction circuit. The contribution is thus a simulated biological mechanism for a navigational computation, together with predictions that could be examined experimentally. The results suggest how such a circuit might work; the claim presented is a mechanistic proposal supported through modeling.
summary.tldr: A biophysical simulation proposes that a thalamocortical circuit computes heading by accumulating head-turning velocity over time.

title: Simulation of a Thalamocortical Circuit for Computing Directional Heading in the Rat

abstract: The Support Vector (SV) method was recently proposed for estimating regressions, constructing multidimensional splines, and solving linear operator equations [Vapnik, 1995]. In this presentation we report results of applying the SV method to these problems.
originalAbstract: The Support Vector (SV) method was recently proposed for estimating regressions, constructing multidimensional splines, and solving linear operator equations [Vapnik, 1995]. In this presentation we report results of applying the SV method to these problems.
title: Support Vector Method for Function Approximation, Regression Estimation and Signal Processing

abstract: I describe a framework for interpreting Support Vector Machines (SVMs) as maximum a posteriori (MAP) solutions to inference problems with Gaussian Process priors. This can provide intuitive guidelines for choosing a 'good' SVM kernel. It can also assign (by evidence maximization) optimal values to parameters such as the noise level C which cannot be determined unambiguously from properties of the MAP solution alone (such as cross-validation er(cid:173) ror) . I illustrate this using a simple approximate expression for the SVM evidence. Once C has been determined, error bars on SVM predictions can also be obtained. 1 Support Vector Machines: A probabilistic framework Support Vector Machines (SVMs) have recently been the subject of intense re(cid:173) search activity within the neural networks community; for tutorial introductions and overviews of recent developments see [1, 2, 3]. One of the open questions that remains is how to set the 'tunable' parameters of an SVM algorithm: While meth(cid:173) ods for choosing the width of the kernel function and the noise parameter C (which controls how closely the training data are fitted) have been proposed [4, 5] (see also, very recently, [6]), the effect of the overall shape of the kernel function remains imperfectly understood [1]. Error bars (class probabilities) for SVM predictions - important for safety-critical applications, for example - are also difficult to obtain. In this paper I suggest that a probabilistic interpretation of SVMs could be used to tackle these problems. It shows that the SVM kernel defines a prior over functions on the input space, avoiding the need to think in terms of high-dimensional feature spaces. It also allows one to define quantities such as the evidence (likelihood) for a set of hyperparameters (C, kernel amplitude Ko etc). I give a simple approximation to the evidence which can then be maximized to set such hyperparameters. The evidence is sensitive to the values of C and Ko individually, in contrast to properties (such as cross-validation error) of the deterministic solution, which only depends on the product CKo. It can thfrefore be used to assign an unambiguous value to C, from which error bars can be derived. 350

paragraphs: This paper interprets support vector machines as maximum a posteriori solutions under Gaussian process priors. Under this view, an SVM kernel defines prior beliefs over functions on the input space. That interpretation offers intuitive guidance for kernel choice without requiring the explanation to center on a high-dimensional feature representation.

The framework also defines evidence for hyperparameters, including the noise parameter C and kernel amplitude. The author introduces a simple approximation to that evidence and uses its maximization to set parameters. This addresses an ambiguity of the deterministic solution: its properties depend on the product of C and kernel amplitude, whereas the evidence is sensitive to their separate values.

Once C has been determined, the framework can also provide error bars on predictions. Thus, the probabilistic treatment connects kernel interpretation, parameter selection, and predictive uncertainty. The demonstrated parameter-selection procedure uses an approximate evidence expression, so its contribution is a workable probabilistic route to these questions rather than a claim of exact evidence computation.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process interpretation of SVMs supports kernel reasoning, evidence-based hyperparameter selection, and prediction error bars.

title: Probabilistic Methods for Support Vector Machines

abstract: The support vector machine (SVM) is a state-of-the-art technique for regression and classification, combining excellent generalisation properties with a sparse kernel representation. However, it does suffer from a number of disadvantages, notably the absence of prob(cid:173) abilistic outputs, the requirement to estimate a trade-off parameter and the need to utilise 'Mercer' kernel functions. In this paper we introduce the Relevance Vector Machine (RVM), a Bayesian treat(cid:173) ment of a generalised linear model of identical functional form to the SVM. The RVM suffers from none of the above disadvantages, and examples demonstrate that for comparable generalisation per(cid:173) formance, the RVM requires dramatically fewer kernel functions. 1

However, it does suffer from a number of disadvantages, notably the absence of prob(cid:173) abilistic outputs, the requirement to estimate a trade-off parameter and the need to utilise 'Mercer' kernel functions. In this paper we introduce the Relevance Vector Machine (RVM), a Bayesian treat(cid:173) ment of a generalised linear model of identical functional form to the SVM. The RVM suffers from none of the above disadvantages, and examples demonstrate that for comparable generalisation per(cid:173) formance, the RVM requires dramatically fewer kernel functions. 1

paragraphs: Support vector machines combine strong generalization with predictions expressed through a sparse set of kernel functions. The paper identifies three disadvantages of the standard approach: it does not provide probabilistic outputs, requires estimation of a trade-off parameter, and restricts the choice of kernels through the Mercer condition.

The relevance vector machine applies a Bayesian treatment to a generalized linear model with the same functional form as an SVM. This preserves a familiar form for the predictor while changing how the model is inferred. The authors state that the RVM avoids all three disadvantages, providing probabilistic outputs and greater flexibility in the functions used.

The examples also show a substantial sparsity benefit. For comparable generalization performance, the RVM uses dramatically fewer kernel functions. This means the demonstrated predictors achieve similar predictive quality with a smaller collection of contributing kernel terms. The result supports the Bayesian formulation as a way to combine probability-based predictions with compact representations, with the comparative performance claim grounded in the examples presented.
summary.tldr: The relevance vector machine provides Bayesian probabilistic predictions and uses far fewer kernel functions than SVMs in examples with comparable generalization.

title: The Relevance Vector Machine

abstract: We consider an online learning scenario in which the learner can make predictions on the basis of a ﬁxed set of experts. We derive upper and lower relative loss bounds for a class of universal learning algorithms in- volving a switching dynamics over the choice of the experts. On the basis of the performance bounds we provide the optimal a priori discretiza- tion for learning the parameter that governs the switching dynamics. We demonstrate the new algorithm in the context of wireless networks.

We derive upper and lower relative loss bounds for a class of universal learning algorithms in- volving a switching dynamics over the choice of the experts. On the basis of the performance bounds we provide the optimal a priori discretiza- tion for learning the parameter that governs the switching dynamics. We demonstrate the new algorithm in the context of wireless networks.

paragraphs: This paper considers an online learner that predicts using a fixed collection of experts. The sequence being predicted can be non-stationary, so the learner’s choice of expert can change over time. The proposed class of universal learning algorithms represents those changes through switching dynamics over the available experts.

The authors derive upper and lower bounds on relative loss for this class of algorithms. These bounds characterize performance in comparative terms and provide the basis for choosing how to learn the parameter controlling the switching dynamics. That parameter is important because it governs how the algorithm moves among expert choices.

Using the bounds, the paper gives an optimal advance discretization of the switching parameter: a choice of candidate parameter values to use during learning. This turns the theoretical analysis into guidance for constructing the algorithm. A wireless-network application demonstrates the resulting method, connecting expert switching and parameter selection to prediction in a setting where the sequence can change.
summary.tldr: Relative-loss bounds guide optimal discretization of a switching parameter for online prediction with a fixed set of experts.

title: Online Learning of Non-stationary Sequences

paragraphs: Online linear optimization requires choosing a decision each round while facing an unknown, changing linear cost. This paper compares two feedback settings. Full information reveals the cost function after the decision, while bandit feedback reveals only the cost actually incurred. The price of bandit information measures the gap between the best achievable regrets under these settings.

The authors present convergence rates and a bandit algorithm whose regret has square-root dependence on the time horizon. This improves the time dependence over previous nontrivial bounds, which had a two-thirds power or worse. Comparing the presented upper bounds gives a factor of the ambient dimension between bandit and full-information regret, quantifying the cost of reduced feedback.

The paper also establishes lower bounds on the information gap and conjectures its correct dimensional order. These distinguish the performance achieved by the algorithm from the remaining question of the exact gap. Efficient implementation is shown for particular settings of interest, including path planning and Markov decision problems, connecting the regret analysis to structured decision tasks.
summary.tldr: A new bandit optimization algorithm improves regret’s time dependence and bounds the cost of observing only incurred losses.

title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization

abstract: The control of high-dimensional, continuous, non-linear systems is a key problem in reinforcement learning and control. Local, trajectory-based methods, using techniques such as Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) are not directly subject to the curse of dimensionality, but generate only local controllers. In this paper, we introduce Receding Horizon DDP (RH-DDP), an extension to the classic DDP algorithm, which allows us to construct stable and robust controllers based on a library of local-control trajectories. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a series of high-dimensional control problems using a simulated multi-link swimming robot. These experiments show that our approach effectively circumvents dimensionality issues, and is capable of dealing effectively with problems with (at least) 34 state and 14 action dimensions.

Local, trajectory-based methods, using techniques such as Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) are not directly subject to the curse of dimensionality, but generate only local controllers. In this paper, we introduce Receding Horizon DDP (RH-DDP), an extension to the classic DDP algorithm, which allows us to construct stable and robust controllers based on a library of local-control trajectories. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a series of high-dimensional control problems using a simulated multi-link swimming robot. These experiments show that our approach effectively circumvents dimensionality issues, and is capable of dealing effectively with problems with (at least) 34 state and 14 action dimensions.

paragraphs: Controlling a system with many continuous variables and nonlinear dynamics can be computationally difficult. Differential Dynamic Programming approaches the task through local trajectories, avoiding direct exposure to the usual curse of dimensionality. Its drawback in the setting described here is that the resulting controllers are local, leaving a need for a broader control strategy.

The paper introduces Receding Horizon Differential Dynamic Programming, an extension that uses a library of local-control trajectories. The authors describe this extension as enabling stable and robust controllers. The library gives the method a collection of local control behavior to work with, connecting the computational appeal of trajectory-based methods to the construction of more capable controllers.

The approach is evaluated on high-dimensional control tasks involving a simulated swimming robot with multiple links. The experiments show effective handling of problems with at least 34 state dimensions and 14 action dimensions. These results support the method’s ability to circumvent dimensionality difficulties in the tested problems, with the demonstration specifically grounded in simulated robot control.
summary.tldr: Receding Horizon DDP builds stable, robust controllers from local trajectory libraries and handles high-dimensional simulated swimming-robot tasks.

title: Receding Horizon Differential Dynamic Programming

abstract: Dynamic Bayesian networks have been applied widely to reconstruct the structure of regulatory processes from time series data. The standard approach is based on the assumption of a homogeneous Markov chain, which is not valid in many real-world scenarios. Recent research efforts addressing this shortcoming have considered undirected graphs, directed graphs for discretized data, or over-flexible models that lack any information sharing between time series segments. In the present article, we propose a non-stationary dynamic Bayesian network for continuous data, in which parameters are allowed to vary between segments, and in which a common network structure provides essential information sharing across segments. Our model is based on a Bayesian change-point process, and we apply a variant of the allocation sampler of Nobile and Fearnside to infer the number and location of the change-points.

paragraphs: Dynamic Bayesian networks are used to infer regulatory relationships from time series. Standard versions assume that the process follows the same transition rules throughout the observations. This paper addresses situations where that assumption fails by developing a model for continuous data whose parameters can change between time segments.

The model retains a common network structure across segments while allowing segment-specific parameters. This distinction lets the strength or form of modeled relationships vary over time while preserving a shared account of which variables are connected. The shared structure provides information sharing that would be absent if every segment were modeled independently.

A Bayesian change-point process represents the divisions between segments. The authors use a variant of an allocation sampler to infer both how many change points exist and where they occur. The contribution is a structured approach to non-stationary time series: changes are estimated from data, but segments remain linked through a common network. That common structure is a substantive modeling assumption, defining the balance between temporal flexibility and shared information.
summary.tldr: A dynamic Bayesian network models changing continuous time-series parameters while sharing network structure across inferred segments.

title: Non-stationary continuous dynamic Bayesian networks

abstract: We describe probability distributions, dubbed compressible priors, whose independent and identically distributed (iid) realizations result in compressible signals. A signal is compressible when sorted magnitudes of its coefficients exhibit a power-law decay so that the signal can be well-approximated by a sparse signal. Since compressible signals live close to sparse signals, their intrinsic information can be stably embedded via simple non-adaptive linear projections into a much lower dimensional space whose dimension grows logarithmically with the ambient signal dimension. By using order statistics, we show that N-sample iid realizations of generalized Pareto, Student’s t, log-normal, Frechet, and log-logistic distributions are compressible, i.e., they have a constant expected decay rate, which is independent of N. In contrast, we show that generalized Gaussian distribution with shape parameter q is compressible only in restricted cases since the expected decay rate of its N-sample iid realizations decreases with N as 1/[q log(N/q)]. We use compressible priors as a scaffold to build new iterative sparse signal recovery algorithms based on Bayesian inference arguments. We show how tuning of these algorithms explicitly depends on the parameters of the compressible prior of the signal, and how to learn the parameters of the signal’s compressible prior on the fly during recovery.

Algorithm tuning depends explicitly on the prior's parameters, and the parameters can be learned during recovery. The contribution connects a statistical description of coefficient decay with both the design and adaptation of reconstruction procedures.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies priors that generate compressible signals and uses their parameters to design and adapt Bayesian sparse-recovery algorithms.

title: Learning with Compressible Priors

abstract: Typical object detectors trained on images perform poorly on video, as there is a clear distinction in domain between the two types of data. In this paper, we tackle the problem of adapting object detectors learned from images to work well on videos. We treat the problem as one of unsupervised domain adaptation, in which we are given labeled data from the source domain (image), but only unlabeled data from the target domain (video). Our approach, self-paced domain adaptation, seeks to iteratively adapt the detector by re-training the detector with automatically discovered target domain examples, starting with the easiest first. At each iteration, the algorithm adapts by considering an increased number of target domain examples, and a decreased number of source domain examples. To discover target domain examples from the vast amount of video data, we introduce a simple, robust approach that scores trajectory tracks instead of bounding boxes. We also show how rich and expressive features specific to the target domain can be incorporated under the same framework. We show promising results on the 2011 TRECVID Multimedia Event Detection and LabelMe Video datasets that illustrate the benefit of our approach to adapt object detectors to video.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the drop in performance that occurs when an object detector trained on still images is applied to video. Its setup provides labeled images but only unlabeled target videos. The task is therefore to adapt across domains without requiring manually labeled examples from the video domain.

The proposed self-paced procedure repeatedly retrains the detector using automatically discovered video examples, beginning with the easiest ones. As adaptation progresses, it increases the number of target examples and reduces the number from the image source. To find useful examples in large video collections, it scores trajectory tracks rather than individual bounding boxes.

The framework can also incorporate expressive features specific to video, giving adaptation access to information suited to the target domain. Evaluations on the 2011 TRECVID Multimedia Event Detection and LabelMe Video datasets produce promising results. The stated benefit is supported by those experiments: progressively shifting training toward selected video examples can help transfer image detectors to video.
summary.tldr: Self-paced domain adaptation improves image-to-video detector transfer by progressively training on automatically selected video tracks.

title: Shifting Weights: Adapting Object Detectors from Image to Video

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new and computationally efficient framework for learning sparse models. We formulate a unified approach that contains as particular cases models promoting sparse synthesis and analysis type of priors, and mixtures thereof. The supervised training of the proposed model is formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, in which the operators are optimized to achieve the best possible performance on a specific task, e.g., reconstruction or classification. By restricting the operators to be shift invariant, our approach can be thought as a way of learning analysis+synthesis sparsity-promoting convolutional operators. Leveraging recent ideas on fast trainable regressors designed to approximate exact sparse codes, we propose a way of constructing feed-forward neural networks capable of approximating the learned models at a fraction of the computational cost of exact solvers. In the shift-invariant case, this leads to a principled way of constructing task-specific convolutional networks. We illustrate the proposed models on several experiments in music analysis and image processing applications.

paragraphs: Sparse models encourage representations in which relatively few components are active. This paper introduces a unified framework covering synthesis models, analysis models, and combinations of the two. Rather than choosing the operators independently of their eventual use, it learns them under supervision for a specified task, such as reconstruction or classification.

Training is formulated as bilevel optimization: the operators are adjusted according to how well the resulting sparse model performs on the task. When the operators are constrained to be shift invariant, the framework learns convolutional analysis and synthesis operators. This connects task-specific sparse modeling with a structure suitable for processing translated patterns.

Exact sparse-code solvers can be computationally expensive, so the authors also construct feed-forward neural networks that approximate the learned models at a fraction of that cost. Under shift invariance, this yields a principled route to task-specific convolutional networks. Experiments in music analysis and image processing illustrate the framework. The speed claim concerns approximating the learned models, rather than asserting that the feed-forward networks exactly reproduce their solvers.
summary.tldr: A unified supervised sparse-model framework learns task-specific operators and builds efficient neural-network approximations of them.

title: Supervised Sparse Analysis and Synthesis Operators

abstract: Small-variance asymptotics provide an emerging technique for obtaining scalable combinatorial algorithms from rich probabilistic models. We present a small-variance asymptotic analysis of the Hidden Markov Model and its infinite-state Bayesian nonparametric extension. Starting with the standard HMM, we first derive a “hard” inference algorithm analogous to k-means that arises when particular variances in the model tend to zero. This analysis is then extended to the Bayesian nonparametric case, yielding a simple, scalable, and flexible algorithm for discrete-state sequence data with a non-fixed number of states. We also derive the corresponding combinatorial objective functions arising from our analysis, which involve a k-means-like term along with penalties based on state transitions and the number of states. A key property of such algorithms is that — particularly in the nonparametric setting — standard probabilistic inference algorithms lack scalability and are heavily dependent on good initialization. A number of results on synthetic and real data sets demonstrate the advantages of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models describe sequences using unobserved states, but inference can be computationally demanding. This paper uses small-variance asymptotics to derive simpler combinatorial algorithms from these probabilistic models. The approach studies what happens as particular model variances tend to zero, translating a probabilistic formulation into a hard-assignment inference problem.

For the standard hidden Markov model, the resulting algorithm resembles k-means. The authors extend the analysis to an infinite-state Bayesian nonparametric model, producing an algorithm whose number of states is not fixed in advance. They also derive explicit objectives containing a k-means-like fit term and penalties involving state transitions and the number of states.

These objectives preserve sequence-related structure while providing a simple and scalable computational approach. The motivation is especially relevant to the nonparametric setting, where standard probabilistic inference can scale poorly and depend heavily on initialization. Results on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate advantages of the proposed framework, supporting the usefulness of the derived algorithms for discrete-state sequence modeling.
summary.tldr: Small-variance limits yield scalable, k-means-like hidden Markov model algorithms, including a version with a flexible number of states.

title: Small-Variance Asymptotics for Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Our focus is on approximate nearest neighbor retrieval in metric and non-metric spaces. We employ a VP-tree and explore two simple yet effective learning-to prune approaches: density estimation through sampling and “stretching” of the triangle inequality. Both methods are evaluated using data sets with metric (Euclidean) and non-metric (KL-divergence and Itakura-Saito) distance functions. Conditions on spaces where the VP-tree is applicable are discussed. The VP-tree with a learned pruner is compared against the recently proposed state-of-the-art approaches: the bbtree, the multi-probe locality sensitive hashing (LSH), and permutation methods. Our method was competitive against state-of-the-art methods and, in most cases, was more efficient for the same rank approximation quality.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval searches for items close to a query while allowing some loss in result quality to save computation. This paper studies retrieval with both metric and non-metric distance functions. It uses a vantage-point tree, or VP-tree, and learns how to prune portions of the search.

The authors investigate two simple pruning approaches. One estimates density through sampling; the other adjusts the use of the triangle inequality through a procedure described as stretching. Evaluations cover Euclidean distance as well as KL divergence and Itakura-Saito distance. The paper also discusses conditions on the underlying space that determine whether the VP-tree is applicable.

The learned-pruning tree is compared with bbtree, multi-probe locality-sensitive hashing, and permutation methods. It is competitive with these approaches and, in most tested cases, more efficient at the same rank approximation quality. Holding that quality comparable is important to interpreting the result: the reported advantage concerns search efficiency for similarly approximate rankings across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Learning VP-tree pruning rules makes approximate nearest-neighbor search competitive across metric and non-metric distances, often improving efficiency at matched ranking quality.

title: Learning to Prune in Metric and Non-Metric Spaces

abstract: The l1-regularized logistic regression (or sparse logistic regression) is a widely used method for simultaneous classification and feature selection. Although many recent efforts have been devoted to its efficient implementation, its application to high dimensional data still poses significant challenges. In this paper, we present a fast and effective sparse logistic regression screening rule (Slores) to identify the zero components in the solution vector, which may lead to a substantial reduction in the number of features to be entered to the optimization. An appealing feature of Slores is that the data set needs to be scanned only once to run the screening and its computational cost is negligible compared to that of solving the sparse logistic regression problem. Moreover, Slores is independent of solvers for sparse logistic regression, thus Slores can be integrated with any existing solver to improve the efficiency. We have evaluated Slores using high-dimensional data sets from different applications. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Slores outperforms the existing state-of-the-art screening rules and the efficiency of solving sparse logistic regression is improved by one magnitude in general.

paragraphs: Sparse logistic regression combines classification with feature selection by using an l1 penalty that makes some fitted coefficients zero. With very many candidate features, solving the optimization problem can still be expensive. This paper introduces Slores, a screening rule that identifies coefficients that will be zero so their corresponding features can be excluded from the optimization.

The practical value is in reducing the problem before the main solver does its work. Screening requires only one scan of the dataset, and the authors describe its cost as negligible compared with solving sparse logistic regression. Because the rule is independent of the optimization solver, it can be combined with existing solvers rather than requiring a replacement.

Experiments use high-dimensional datasets from several applications. The authors report better screening performance than existing state-of-the-art rules and roughly an order-of-magnitude improvement in solving efficiency in general. These are empirical results; the potential reduction in feature count depends on how many zero coefficients the rule can identify in a given problem.
summary.tldr: Slores speeds up sparse logistic regression by screening out features whose fitted coefficients will be zero.

title: A Safe Screening Rule for Sparse Logistic Regression

abstract: In this paper, we prove that every multivariate polynomial with even degree can be decomposed into a sum of convex and concave polynomials. Motivated by this property, we exploit the concave-convex procedure to perform inference on continuous Markov random fields with polynomial potentials. In particular, we show that the concave-convex decomposition of polynomials can be expressed as a sum-of-squares optimization, which can be efficiently solved via semidefinite programming. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in the context of 3D reconstruction, shape from shading and image denoising, and show that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches in terms of efficiency as well as the quality of the retrieved solution.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we prove that every multivariate polynomial with even degree can be decomposed into a sum of convex and concave polynomials. Motivated by this property, we exploit the concave-convex procedure to perform inference on continuous Markov random fields with polynomial potentials. In particular, we show that the concave-convex decomposition of polynomials can be expressed as a sum-of-squares optimization, which can be efficiently solved via semidefinite programming. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in the context of 3D reconstruction, shape from shading and image denoising, and show that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches in terms of efficiency as well as the quality of the retrieved solution.

paragraphs: The paper begins with a mathematical result: every multivariate polynomial of even degree can be written as a sum of convex and concave polynomials. This gives a useful structure to expressions that may otherwise be difficult to optimize directly. The authors use the decomposition to develop inference methods for continuous Markov random fields whose potentials are polynomials.

Their inference approach applies the concave-convex procedure to the resulting components. A key computational step is obtaining the decomposition itself. The authors show that this can be expressed as a sum-of-squares optimization problem and solved efficiently through semidefinite programming. The mathematical result thus leads to a concrete route for constructing the optimization problem used during inference.

The method is evaluated on 3D reconstruction, shape from shading, and image denoising. In these applications, the authors report significant improvements over existing approaches in both computational efficiency and the quality of the recovered solution. The paper's contribution connects a general polynomial decomposition result with practical inference, showing that the resulting formulation can improve both speed and solution quality in the tested vision problems.
summary.tldr: A convex-concave decomposition of even-degree polynomials enables efficient continuous graphical-model inference with strong results on three vision applications.

title: Efficient Inference of Continuous Markov Random Fields with Polynomial Potentials

abstract: State of the art statistical estimators for high-dimensional problems take the form of regularized, and hence non-smooth, convex programs. A key facet of thesestatistical estimation problems is that these are typically not strongly convex under a high-dimensional sampling regime when the Hessian matrix becomes rank-deficient. Under vanilla convexity however, proximal optimization methods attain only a sublinear rate. In this paper, we investigate a novel variant of strong convexity, which we call Constant Nullspace Strong Convexity (CNSC), where we require that the objective function be strongly convex only over a constant subspace. As we show, the CNSC condition is naturally satisfied by high-dimensional statistical estimators. We then analyze the behavior of proximal methods under this CNSC condition: we show global linear convergence of Proximal Gradient and local quadratic convergence of Proximal Newton Method, when the regularization function comprising the statistical estimator is decomposable. We corroborate our theory via numerical experiments, and show a qualitative difference in the convergence rates of the proximal algorithms when the loss function does satisfy the CNSC condition.

paragraphs: High-dimensional statistical estimation often combines a convex loss with a nonsmooth regularizer. Standard strong convexity can fail because the Hessian is rank-deficient, leaving some directions without curvature. Under ordinary convexity alone, proximal methods have only sublinear convergence guarantees, which do not explain faster behavior available in more structured problems.

The paper introduces Constant Nullspace Strong Convexity, or CNSC. This condition requires strong convexity only on a fixed subspace, allowing the full problem to lack curvature in other directions. The authors show that this weaker form of curvature naturally occurs in high-dimensional statistical estimators and use it to analyze proximal optimization.

Under CNSC and a decomposable regularization function, they establish global linear convergence for Proximal Gradient and local quadratic convergence for Proximal Newton. Linear convergence describes geometric error reduction, while quadratic convergence describes a faster regime near a solution. Numerical experiments corroborate the theory and show a qualitative difference when the loss satisfies CNSC. The result identifies specific structure that can support fast optimization even when full strong convexity is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Strong convexity on a fixed subspace yields fast proximal convergence under the paper's decomposable-regularization condition.

title: Constant Nullspace Strong Convexity and Fast Convergence of Proximal Methods under High-Dimensional Settings

abstract: The framework of online learning with memory naturally captures learning problems with temporal effects, and was previously studied for the experts setting. In this work we extend the notion of learning with memory to the general Online Convex Optimization (OCO) framework, and present two algorithms that attain low regret. The first algorithm applies to Lipschitz continuous loss functions, obtaining optimal regret bounds for both convex and strongly convex losses. The second algorithm attains the optimal regret bounds and applies more broadly to convex losses without requiring Lipschitz continuity, yet is more complicated to implement. We complement the theoretic results with two applications: statistical arbitrage in finance, and multi-step ahead prediction in statistics.
originalAbstract: The framework of online learning with memory naturally captures learning problems with temporal effects, and was previously studied for the experts setting. In this work we extend the notion of learning with memory to the general Online Convex Optimization (OCO) framework, and present two algorithms that attain low regret. The first algorithm applies to Lipschitz continuous loss functions, obtaining optimal regret bounds for both convex and strongly convex losses. The second algorithm attains the optimal regret bounds and applies more broadly to convex losses without requiring Lipschitz continuity, yet is more complicated to implement. We complement the theoretic results with two applications: statistical arbitrage in finance, and multi-step ahead prediction in statistics.

paragraphs: In online learning with memory, the consequences of a decision can extend into later rounds. This captures temporal effects that are absent when each loss depends only on the current action. The paper extends this perspective from the previously studied experts setting to the more general framework of online convex optimization.

The authors present two algorithms with low-regret guarantees. The first assumes Lipschitz-continuous losses and achieves optimal regret bounds for both convex and strongly convex losses. This assumption controls how sharply a loss can change as the decision changes. The second algorithm also achieves optimal bounds and covers convex losses without requiring Lipschitz continuity, but is more complicated to implement.

These results offer a tradeoff between the scope of the loss functions handled and the complexity of the algorithm. The paper also gives applications to statistical arbitrage and prediction several steps ahead. Both applications connect the theory to settings where decisions have temporal consequences, showing why explicitly accounting for memory is relevant beyond an abstract learning model.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms extend online convex optimization to losses with memory, achieving optimal regret bounds under different regularity assumptions.

title: Online Learning for Adversaries with Memory: Price of Past Mistakes

abstract: Generative neural networks are probabilistic models that implement sampling using feedforward neural networks: they take a random input vector and produce a sample from a probability distribution defined by the network weights. These models are expressive and allow efficient computation of samples and derivatives, but cannot be used for computing likelihoods or for marginalization. The generative-adversarial training method allows to train such models through the use of an auxiliary discriminative neural network. We show that the generative-adversarial approach is a special case of an existing more general variational divergence estimation approach. We show that any $f$-divergence can be used for training generative neural networks. We discuss the benefits of various choices of divergence functions on training complexity and the quality of the obtained generative models.
originalAbstract: Generative neural networks are probabilistic models that implement sampling using feedforward neural networks: they take a random input vector and produce a sample from a probability distribution defined by the network weights. These models are expressive and allow efficient computation of samples and derivatives, but cannot be used for computing likelihoods or for marginalization. The generative-adversarial training method allows to train such models through the use of an auxiliary discriminative neural network. We show that the generative-adversarial approach is a special case of an existing more general variational divergence estimation approach. We show that any $f$-divergence can be used for training generative neural networks. We discuss the benefits of various choices of divergence functions on training complexity and the quality of the obtained generative models.

paragraphs: A generative neural sampler turns a random input vector into a sample from a distribution determined by its weights. Such networks can generate samples and compute derivatives efficiently, but the models considered here do not support likelihood computation or marginalization. Adversarial training addresses training through an auxiliary discriminative neural network.

This paper places that training method within a broader mathematical framework. The authors show that generative-adversarial training is a special case of an existing approach to variational divergence estimation. A divergence measures disagreement between distributions, so the connection gives a general way to express the training objective in terms of the difference between generated and target distributions.

The central result is that any f-divergence can be used to train these generative networks. This opens a family of training objectives within the same overarching framework. The paper discusses how different divergence choices affect training complexity and the quality of the resulting models. Its contribution is this generalization and analysis of choices, without asserting that one divergence is universally best.
summary.tldr: f-GAN generalizes adversarial training by showing that any f-divergence can serve as an objective for training generative neural samplers.

title: f-GAN: Training Generative Neural Samplers using Variational Divergence Minimization

abstract: This paper proposes the novel Pose Guided Person Generation Network (PG$^2$) that allows to synthesize person images in arbitrary poses, based on an image of that person and a novel pose. Our generation framework PG$^2$ utilizes the pose information explicitly and consists of two key stages: pose integration and image refinement. In the first stage the condition image and the target pose are fed into a U-Net-like network to generate an initial but coarse image of the person with the target pose. The second stage then refines the initial and blurry result by training a U-Net-like generator in an adversarial way. Extensive experimental results on both 128$\times$64 re-identification images and 256$\times$256 fashion photos show that our model generates high-quality person images with convincing details.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes the novel Pose Guided Person Generation Network (PG$^2$) that allows to synthesize person images in arbitrary poses, based on an image of that person and a novel pose. Our generation framework PG$^2$ utilizes the pose information explicitly and consists of two key stages: pose integration and image refinement. In the first stage the condition image and the target pose are fed into a U-Net-like network to generate an initial but coarse image of the person with the target pose. The second stage then refines the initial and blurry result by training a U-Net-like generator in an adversarial way. Extensive experimental results on both 128$\times$64 re-identification images and 256$\times$256 fashion photos show that our model generates high-quality person images with convincing details.

paragraphs: This paper studies generating an image of a person in a requested pose using an existing image of that person. Its Pose Guided Person Generation Network, called PG2, takes the target pose as explicit input. The task combines information about the person's appearance with a new arrangement of their body.

The framework divides generation into two stages. First, a U-Net-like network receives the source image and desired pose and produces a coarse image showing the target arrangement. Second, another U-Net-like generator refines that initially blurry result through adversarial training. The stages assign pose integration and visual refinement distinct roles within the overall generation process.

Experiments cover both person re-identification images at 128 by 64 resolution and fashion photographs at 256 by 256 resolution. The authors report high-quality generated person images with convincing details in these settings. These results support the two-stage design as a way to combine explicit pose control with appearance refinement across the two evaluated kinds of imagery.
summary.tldr: PG2 generates person images in requested poses through a coarse pose-integration stage followed by adversarial image refinement.

title: Pose Guided Person Image Generation

abstract: Recently, a new class of machine learning algorithms has emerged, where models and discriminators are generated in a competitive setting. The most prominent example is Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). In this paper we examine how these algorithms relate to the Turing test, and derive what - from a Turing perspective - can be considered their defining features. Based on these features, we outline directions for generalizing GANs - resulting in the family of algorithms referred to as Turing Learning. One such direction is to allow the discriminators to interact with the processes from which the data samples are obtained, making them "interrogators", as in the Turing test. We validate this idea using two case studies. In the first case study, a computer infers the behavior of an agent while controlling its environment. In the second case study, a robot infers its own sensor configuration while controlling its movements. The results confirm that by allowing discriminators to interrogate, the accuracy of models is improved.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks train models and discriminators through competition. This paper examines that arrangement through the Turing test, identifying features that define such learning from that perspective. It uses those features to outline a broader family of methods called Turing Learning, extending the possibilities for how models and discriminators interact.

The central extension explored here gives discriminators an active role in obtaining evidence. Instead of only judging supplied samples, they can interact with the processes producing them. The discriminator becomes an interrogator that influences the conditions under which observations arise, bringing the learning setup closer to the interactive character of the Turing test.

Two case studies test the idea. A computer learns an agent's behavior while controlling its environment, and a robot learns its own sensor configuration while controlling its movements. Allowing interrogation improves model accuracy in these studies. The results support active interaction as a useful generalization of adversarial learning in the examined behavior and sensor-learning settings.
summary.tldr: Turing Learning extends adversarial learning by letting discriminators actively interrogate data-producing processes, improving accuracy in two case studies.

title: Generalizing GANs: A Turing Perspective

abstract: Learning meaningful representations that maintain the content necessary for a particular task while filtering away detrimental variations is a problem of great interest in machine learning. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning representations invariant to a specific factor or trait of data. The representation learning process is formulated as an adversarial minimax game. We analyze the optimal equilibrium of such a game and find that it amounts to maximizing the uncertainty of inferring the detrimental factor given the representation while maximizing the certainty of making task-specific predictions. On three benchmark tasks, namely fair and bias-free classification, language-independent generation, and lighting-independent image classification, we show that the proposed framework induces an invariant representation, and leads to better generalization evidenced by the improved performance.

paragraphs: A useful representation should preserve information needed for its task while filtering out a specified source of unwanted variation. This paper studies how to learn that selective invariance. The aim is to make a particular factor difficult to infer from the representation while keeping the representation informative for the intended prediction.

The authors formulate training as an adversarial minimax game. Their analysis of its optimal equilibrium gives the objective a precise interpretation: increase uncertainty about the unwanted factor and increase certainty about task-specific predictions. These two requirements define what the representation should retain and what it should suppress.

The framework is evaluated on three benchmark tasks involving fair and bias-free classification, language-independent generation, and image classification independent of lighting. The reported results show that it induces invariant representations and improves performance, providing evidence of better generalization in these evaluations. The work connects an explicit target for removing information with a training framework that simultaneously protects the information needed for the task.
summary.tldr: Adversarial training learns representations that suppress a chosen unwanted factor while retaining information for the target task.

title: Controllable Invariance through Adversarial Feature Learning

abstract: We present a new algorithmic approach for the task of finding a chordal Markov network structure that maximizes a given scoring function. The algorithm is based on branch and bound and integrates dynamic programming for both domain pruning and for obtaining strong bounds for search-space pruning. Empirically, we show that the approach dominates in terms of running times a recent integer programming approach (and thereby also a recent constraint optimization approach) for the problem. Furthermore, our algorithm scales at times further with respect to the number of variables than a state-of-the-art dynamic programming algorithm for the problem, with the potential of reaching 20 variables and at the same time circumventing the tight exponential lower bounds on memory consumption of the pure dynamic programming approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find the chordal Markov network structure with the highest score under a given scoring function. This is a search problem over possible network structures. The central challenge is to eliminate unpromising possibilities efficiently while retaining the ability to find the best-scoring structure.

The proposed algorithm combines branch and bound with dynamic programming. Dynamic programming contributes both domain pruning and strong bounds that help prune the search space. These components support the same goal at different levels: reducing the choices under consideration and ruling out regions of the search that cannot improve the solution.

Empirical comparisons show faster runtimes than a recent integer-programming approach, and consequently the constraint-optimization approach discussed in the paper. The method also sometimes handles more variables than a leading pure dynamic-programming algorithm, with potential to reach 20 variables. Its hybrid design avoids the tight exponential memory lower bounds affecting that pure approach. The reported scaling advantage is qualified: it occurs in some cases rather than uniformly across all problems.
summary.tldr: Combining branch and bound with dynamic-programming pruning improves search for optimal chordal Markov networks and can reduce memory-related scaling barriers.

title: Learning Chordal Markov Networks via Branch and Bound

abstract: The iterations of many first-order algorithms, when applied to minimizing common regularized regression functions, often resemble neural network layers with pre-specified weights. This observation has prompted the development of learning-based approaches that purport to replace these iterations with enhanced surrogates forged as DNN models from available training data. For example, important NP-hard sparse estimation problems have recently benefitted from this genre of upgrade, with simple feedforward or recurrent networks ousting proximal gradient-based iterations. Analogously, this paper demonstrates that more powerful Bayesian algorithms for promoting sparsity, which rely on complex multi-loop majorization-minimization techniques, mirror the structure of more sophisticated long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, or alternative gated feedback networks previously designed for sequence prediction. As part of this development, we examine the parallels between latent variable trajectories operating across multiple time-scales during optimization, and the activations within deep network structures designed to adaptively model such characteristic sequences. The resulting insights lead to a novel sparse estimation system that, when granted training data, can estimate optimal solutions efficiently in regimes where other algorithms fail, including practical direction-of-arrival (DOA) and 3D geometry recovery problems. The underlying principles we expose are also suggestive of a learning process for a richer class of multi-loop algorithms in other domains.

paragraphs: Iterations of optimization algorithms can resemble neural network layers, suggesting that training data might be used to learn more effective replacements for those iterations. This paper develops that connection for Bayesian sparse estimation algorithms. These algorithms promote solutions with few active components and can involve several nested optimization loops.

The authors show parallels between those multi-loop procedures and gated networks such as LSTMs. In particular, they examine how latent variables evolve across different time scales during optimization and how those trajectories correspond to activations in networks designed to model sequences adaptively. This gives a structural reason to use more sophisticated recurrent architectures for the estimation problem.

summary.tldr: Connections between Bayesian sparse estimation and gated recurrent networks lead to a learned estimator that succeeds in challenging sparse recovery regimes.

title: From Bayesian Sparsity to Gated Recurrent Nets

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a powerful tool for global optimization of expensive functions. One of its key components is the underlying probabilistic model used for the objective function f. In practice, however, it is often unclear how one should appropriately choose a model, especially when gathering data is expensive. In this work, we introduce a novel automated Bayesian optimization approach that dynamically selects promising models for explaining the observed data using Bayesian Optimization in the model space. Crucially, we account for the uncertainty in the choice of model; our method is capable of using multiple models to represent its current belief about f and subsequently using this information for decision making. We argue, and demonstrate empirically, that our approach automatically finds suitable models for the objective function, which ultimately results in more-efficient optimization.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good solutions when evaluating the objective function is expensive. Its decisions depend on a probabilistic model of that function, but choosing an appropriate model can itself be difficult. Limited observations make this choice especially consequential because gathering more evidence carries the same expense as the original optimization problem.

The paper introduces an automated approach that applies Bayesian optimization within the space of possible models. As observations arrive, it searches for promising explanations of the objective function. It also represents uncertainty about model selection: multiple models can contribute to the method's current beliefs and therefore influence subsequent decisions about where to evaluate the objective.

This connects model selection directly to the ongoing optimization process instead of treating it as a settled preliminary choice. The authors argue, and demonstrate empirically, that the approach finds suitable models and improves optimization efficiency. The stated finding concerns the benefit of adapting and combining models under uncertainty; it does not establish that one model is always best.
summary.tldr: Bayesian optimization over model choices adapts the optimizer's beliefs and empirically improves the efficiency of optimizing expensive functions.

title: Automating Bayesian optimization with Bayesian optimization

abstract: We study gradient-based optimization methods obtained by directly discretizing a second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) related to the continuous limit of Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. When the function is smooth enough, we show that acceleration can be achieved by a stable discretization of this ODE using standard Runge-Kutta integrators. Specifically, we prove that under Lipschitz-gradient, convexity and order-$(s+2)$ differentiability assumptions, the sequence of iterates generated by discretizing the proposed second-order ODE converges to the optimal solution at a rate of $\mathcal{O}({N^{-2\frac{s}{s+1}}})$, where $s$ is the order of the Runge-Kutta numerical integrator. Furthermore, we introduce a new local flatness condition on the objective, under which rates even faster than $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2})$ can be achieved with low-order integrators and only gradient information. Notably, this flatness condition is satisfied by several standard loss functions used in machine learning. We provide numerical experiments that verify the theoretical rates predicted by our results.

paragraphs: The paper connects accelerated optimization to the numerical solution of differential equations. It starts from a second-order equation related to the continuous-time limit of Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. The central question is whether directly converting this equation into discrete steps with standard Runge-Kutta integrators can preserve accelerated progress toward an optimum.

The authors prove that stable discretization achieves acceleration when the objective satisfies the required smoothness conditions. Specifically, convexity, a Lipschitz gradient, and differentiability through order s+2 give a convergence rate of O(N^(-2s/(s+1))), where s is the integrator order. This makes the role of the numerical method explicit: its order affects the guaranteed rate.

A further result introduces a local flatness condition under which even low-order integrators can achieve rates faster than O(N^-2), using only gradient information. Several standard machine-learning loss functions satisfy that condition. Numerical experiments verify the predicted theoretical rates, supporting the connection between properties of the objective, the discretization scheme, and accelerated optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: Standard Runge-Kutta discretization can yield accelerated gradient optimization under smoothness assumptions, with faster rates under an additional flatness condition.

title: Direct Runge-Kutta Discretization Achieves Acceleration

abstract: Spectral estimation (SE) aims to identify how the energy of a signal (e.g., a time series) is distributed across different frequencies. This can become particularly challenging when only partial and noisy observations of the signal are available, where current methods fail to handle uncertainty appropriately. In this context, we propose a joint probabilistic model for signals, observations and spectra, where SE is addressed as an inference problem. Assuming a Gaussian process prior over the signal, we apply Bayes' rule to find the analytic posterior distribution of the spectrum given a set of observations. Besides its expressiveness and natural account of spectral uncertainty, the proposed model also provides a functional-form representation of the power spectral density, which can be optimised efficiently. Comparison with previous approaches is addressed theoretically, showing that the proposed method is an infinite-dimensional variant of the Lomb-Scargle approach, and also empirically through three experiments.

paragraphs: Spectral estimation asks how a signal's energy is distributed across frequencies. With incomplete or noisy observations, the task involves uncertainty about the spectrum as well as estimating its shape. This paper treats that uncertainty as part of the estimation problem by building a joint probabilistic model of the signal, its observations, and its spectrum.

The approach assumes a Gaussian process prior over the signal. Under that assumption, the authors use Bayes' rule to derive an analytic posterior distribution for the spectrum given the observations. The result describes uncertainty about spectral content rather than reducing the output to a single estimate. The model also supplies a functional representation of the power spectral density that can be optimized efficiently.

The authors connect their method theoretically to Lomb-Scargle estimation, showing that it is an infinite-dimensional variant of that approach. They also compare it with previous methods through three experiments. The contribution combines this connection to an existing estimator with a probabilistic treatment designed for partial, noisy signal measurements.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process model yields an analytic posterior over a signal's spectrum, explicitly representing uncertainty from partial and noisy observations.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Spectral Estimation

abstract: The development of a metric for structural data is a long-term problem in pattern recognition and machine learning. In this paper, we develop a general metric for comparing nonlinear dynamical systems that is defined with Perron-Frobenius operators in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Our metric includes the existing fundamental metrics for dynamical systems, which are basically defined with principal angles between some appropriately-chosen subspaces, as its special cases. We also describe the estimation of our metric from finite data. We empirically illustrate our metric with an example of rotation dynamics in a unit disk in a complex plane, and evaluate the performance with real-world time-series data.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to measure differences between nonlinear dynamical systems. Here, the objects being compared are systems that evolve over time, making their dynamic structure central to the comparison. Defining a useful metric for such structured objects is the broader pattern-recognition and machine-learning problem motivating the work.

The proposed metric uses Perron-Frobenius operators represented in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. This operator-based formulation supplies a common mathematical framework for the comparison. It includes established dynamical-system metrics as special cases, specifically ones based on principal angles between appropriately selected subspaces. Thus, the construction generalizes existing geometric comparisons rather than standing apart from them.

The authors also describe how to estimate the metric from finite data, connecting the mathematical definition to observations available in practice. They illustrate its behavior using rotation dynamics within a unit disk in the complex plane and evaluate it on real time-series data. These studies provide examples of the metric in use, while the main contribution is a general comparison framework with both connections to prior metrics and a data-based estimation procedure.
summary.tldr: An operator-based metric compares nonlinear dynamical systems, generalizes existing geometric metrics, and can be estimated from finite data.

title: Metric on Nonlinear Dynamical Systems with Perron-Frobenius Operators

abstract: A great challenge in cooperative decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is generating diversified behaviors for each individual agent when receiving only a team reward. Prior studies have paid much effort on reward shaping or designing a centralized critic that can discriminatively credit the agents. In this paper, we propose to merge the two directions and learn each agent an intrinsic reward function which diversely stimulates the agents at each time step. Specifically, the intrinsic reward for a specific agent will be involved in computing a distinct proxy critic for the agent to direct the updating of its individual policy. Meanwhile, the parameterized intrinsic reward function will be updated towards maximizing the expected accumulated team reward from the environment so that the objective is consistent with the original MARL problem. The proposed method is referred to as learning individual intrinsic reward (LIIR) in MARL. We compare LIIR with a number of state-of-the-art MARL methods on battle games in StarCraft II. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of LIIR, and we show LIIR can assign each individual agent an insightful intrinsic reward per time step.
