paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers learning from labeled source data to unlabeled target data. A major obstacle is that source labels may correlate with environmental features that do not remain reliable in the target domain. The paper argues that using target samples mainly as auxiliary training data can overlook distributional clues that expose those misleading relationships.

Invariant Consistency Learning, or ICON, gives source and target domains equal status in learning a classifier. Predictions must agree with source labels and with clusters in the target data. This joint requirement uses the target distribution's own structure to rule out spurious correlations that are inconsistent there, rather than relying solely on supervision inherited from the source.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on Office-Home and VisDA-2017, along with performance exceeding all conventional methods on WILDS 2.0. These findings support treating unlabeled target structure as a direct learning constraint. The central contribution is the consistency requirement linking labeled source examples and target clusters within one invariant classifier.
summary.tldr: ICON aligns predictions with source labels and target clusters to counter spurious correlations and improve unsupervised domain adaptation.

title: Make the U in UDA Matter: Invariant Consistency Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is usually performed on resource-constrained edge devices, e.g., with limited memory for the computation. If the required memory to train a model exceeds this limit, the device will be excluded from the training. This can lead to a lower accuracy as valuable data and computation resources are excluded from training, also causing bias and unfairness. The FL training process should be adjusted to such constraints. The state-of-the-art techniques propose training subsets of the FL model at constrained devices, reducing their resource requirements for training. However, these techniques largely limit the co-adaptation among parameters of the model and are highly inefficient, as we show: it is actually better to train a smaller (less accurate) model by the system where all the devices can train the model end-to-end than applying such techniques. We propose a new method that enables successive freezing and training of the parameters of the FL model at devices, reducing the training’s resource requirements at the devices while still allowing enough co-adaptation between parameters. We show through extensive experimental evaluation that our technique greatly improves the accuracy of the trained model (by 52.4 p.p. ) compared with the state of the art, efficiently aggregating the computation capacity available on distributed devices.

paragraphs: Federated learning can lose useful participants when their devices lack enough memory to train the shared model. Excluding those devices also excludes their data and computation, potentially reducing accuracy and introducing bias or unfairness. Training only selected model parameters reduces memory requirements, but it can restrict how different parameters learn to work together.

The paper argues that this restriction makes existing subset-training techniques inefficient. In the authors' evaluation, training a smaller model that every device can update end to end is better than applying those techniques. Their proposed method instead successively freezes and trains model parameters, reducing the resources needed at each device while preserving enough interaction between the parameters being learned.

Extensive experiments report an accuracy improvement of 52.4 percentage points over the state of the art. This is an experimental result, rather than a guarantee for every device population. Its significance is that accommodating constrained devices need not simply mean shrinking the shared model: changing the training schedule can help combine the capacity available across participating devices.
summary.tldr: Successively freezing and training model parameters helps memory-constrained federated devices participate while substantially improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Aggregating Capacity in FL through Successive Layer Training for Computationally-Constrained Devices

abstract: The training process of ReLU neural networks often exhibits complicated nonlinear phenomena. The nonlinearity of models and non-convexity of loss pose significant challenges for theoretical analysis. Therefore, most previous theoretical works on the optimization dynamics of neural networks focus either on local analysis (like the end of training) or approximate linear models (like Neural Tangent Kernel). In this work, we conduct a complete theoretical characterization of the training process of a two-layer ReLU network trained by Gradient Flow on a linearly separable data. In this specific setting, our analysis captures the whole optimization process starting from random initialization to final convergence. Despite the relatively simple model and data that we studied, we reveal four different phases from the whole training process showing a general simplifying-to-complicating learning trend.Specific nonlinear behaviors can also be precisely identified and captured theoretically, such asinitial condensation, saddle-to-plateau dynamics, plateau escape, changes of activation patterns, learning with increasing complexity, etc.

paragraphs: Training a ReLU network can involve changing activation patterns, plateaus, and other nonlinear behavior. These dynamics are difficult to analyze because both the model and its optimization landscape are complex. Much previous theory therefore examines only a local part of training or replaces the network with an approximately linear model.

This paper characterizes the full training trajectory in a specific setting: a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient flow on linearly separable data. Its analysis begins at random initialization and continues through convergence. Even with this relatively simple network and dataset structure, the authors identify four distinct phases of learning.

The phases reveal an overall progression in which learning first simplifies and then becomes more complex. The theory captures initial condensation, movement from saddles to plateaus, escape from plateaus, and changes in activation patterns. These results show how several nonlinear phenomena can arise within one complete account of training. Their scope remains the stated two-layer, gradient-flow, linearly separable setting.
summary.tldr: A full analysis of two-layer ReLU training under gradient flow reveals four phases and captures nonlinear behavior from initialization to convergence.

title: Understanding Multi-phase Optimization Dynamics and Rich Nonlinear Behaviors of ReLU Networks

abstract: With the increased deployment of machine learning models in various real-world applications, researchers and practitioners alike have emphasized the need for explanations of model behaviour. To this end, two broad strategies have been outlined in prior literature to explain models. Post hoc explanation methods explain the behaviour of complex black-box models by identifying features critical to model predictions; however, prior work has shown that these explanations may not be faithful, in that they incorrectly attribute high importance to features that are unimportant or non-discriminative for the underlying task. Inherently interpretable models, on the other hand, circumvent these issues by explicitly encoding explanations into model architecture, meaning their explanations are naturally faithful, but they often exhibit poor predictive performance due to their limited expressive power. In this work, we identify a key reason for the lack of faithfulness of feature attributions: the lack of robustness of the underlying black-box models, especially the erasure of unimportant distractor features in the input. To address this issue, we propose Distractor Erasure Tuning (DiET), a method that adapts black-box models to be robust to distractor erasure, thus providing discriminative and faithful attributions. This strategy naturally combines the ease-of-use of post hoc explanations with the faithfulness of inherently interpretable models. We perform extensive experiments on semi-synthetic and real-world datasets, and show that DiET produces models that (1) closely approximate the original black-box models they are intended to explain, and (2) yield explanations that match approximate ground truths available by construction.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods explain predictions by assigning importance to parts of an input. However, an explanation may highlight features that do not help distinguish the underlying task's outcomes. This paper identifies a reason for that failure: a black-box model may react unreliably when unimportant distractor features are removed.

Distractor Erasure Tuning, or DiET, adapts the model to become robust to that removal. The approach therefore changes the behavior being explained so that erasing irrelevant information is less disruptive. It aims to combine the convenience of post hoc explanations with faithful, discriminative attributions, while retaining a close approximation to the original model.

The authors evaluate DiET on semi-synthetic and real-world datasets. They report that tuned models closely approximate their original black-box counterparts and produce explanations matching approximate ground truths available by construction. These findings connect explanation quality to model robustness: improving how a model handles distractor removal can also improve the relevance of the features its explanations identify.
summary.tldr: DiET tunes models to tolerate removal of irrelevant features, producing more faithful attributions while closely preserving original model behavior.

title: Discriminative Feature Attributions: Bridging Post Hoc Explainability and Inherent Interpretability

abstract: We provide the first convergence guarantee for black-box variational inference (BBVI) with the reparameterization gradient. While preliminary investigations worked on simplified versions of BBVI (e.g., bounded domain, bounded support, only optimizing for the scale, and such), our setup does not need any such algorithmic modifications. Our results hold for log-smooth posterior densities with and without strong log-concavity and the location-scale variational family. Notably, our analysis reveals that certain algorithm design choices commonly employed in practice, such as nonlinear parameterizations of the scale matrix, can result in suboptimal convergence rates. Fortunately, running BBVI with proximal stochastic gradient descent fixes these limitations and thus achieves the strongest known convergence guarantees. We evaluate this theoretical insight by comparing proximal SGD against other standard implementations of BBVI on large-scale Bayesian inference problems.

paragraphs: Black-box variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior through optimization. This paper gives a convergence guarantee for BBVI using the reparameterization gradient without the algorithmic simplifications used in earlier analyses. Those simplifications included bounded domains or support and restricting optimization to the scale alone.

The results apply to log-smooth posterior densities and location-scale variational families, considering cases both with and without strong log-concavity. Within this setting, the analysis shows that implementation choices can affect convergence rates. In particular, nonlinear parameterizations of the scale matrix, despite their use in practice, can lead to suboptimal rates.

The authors show that proximal stochastic gradient descent resolves these limitations and achieves the strongest known convergence guarantees described in the paper. They investigate this theoretical insight by comparing proximal SGD with standard BBVI implementations on large-scale Bayesian inference problems. The contribution links assumptions about the posterior and variational family to concrete optimizer choices, giving a theoretical reason to reconsider how BBVI handles scale optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes BBVI convergence guarantees and shows how proximal SGD avoids rate limitations caused by certain scale parameterizations.

title: On the Convergence of Black-Box Variational Inference

abstract: Independent component analysis (ICA) is a fundamental statistical tool used to reveal hidden generative processes from observed data. However, traditional ICA approaches struggle with the rotational invariance inherent in Gaussian distributions, often necessitating the assumption of non-Gaussianity in the underlying sources. This may limit their applicability in broader contexts. To accommodate Gaussian sources, we develop an identifiability theory that relies on second-order statistics without imposing further preconditions on the distribution of sources, by introducing novel assumptions on the connective structure from sources to observed variables. Different from recent work that focuses on potentially restrictive connective structures, our proposed assumption of structural variability is both considerably less restrictive and provably necessary. Furthermore, we propose two estimation methods based on second-order statistics and sparsity constraint. Experimental results are provided to validate our identifiability theory and estimation methods.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks hidden sources that generate observed data. Traditional approaches often assume non-Gaussian sources because Gaussian distributions have rotational symmetries that make source recovery ambiguous. This paper develops an identifiability theory that accommodates Gaussian sources, asking when the hidden generative structure can be determined from second-order statistics.

The theory shifts the relevant restrictions toward the connections between sources and observed variables. It introduces a structural-variability assumption that the authors show is necessary and considerably less restrictive than connective assumptions in recent work. The result does not eliminate structural requirements; it offers a route to identifiability without imposing additional distributional preconditions on the sources.

The authors also propose two estimation methods that combine second-order statistics with a sparsity constraint. Experiments validate the theoretical account and the proposed estimators. The significance is that information about sparse source-to-observation connections can support recovery in settings where a non-Gaussianity assumption would exclude the source distributions of interest.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes sparse ICA identifiability using structural assumptions and second-order statistics without requiring non-Gaussian sources.

title: On the Identifiability of Sparse ICA without Assuming Non-Gaussianity

abstract: Automated auction design aims to find empirically high-revenue mechanisms through machine learning. Existing works on multi item auction scenarios can be roughly divided into RegretNet-like and affine maximizer auctions (AMAs) approaches. However, the former cannot strictly ensure dominant strategy incentive compatibility (DSIC), while the latter faces scalability issue due to the large number of allocation candidates. To address these limitations, we propose AMenuNet, a scalable neural network that constructs the AMA parameters (even including the allocation menu) from bidder and item representations. AMenuNet is always DSIC and individually rational (IR) due to the properties of AMAs, and it enhances scalability by generating candidate allocations through a neural network. Additionally, AMenuNet is permutation equivariant, and its number of parameters is independent of auction scale. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that AMenuNet outperforms strong baselines in both contextual and non-contextual multi-item auctions, scales well to larger auctions, generalizes well to different settings, and identifies useful deterministic allocations. Overall, our proposed approach offers an effective solution to automated DSIC auction design, with improved scalability and strong revenue performance in various settings.

paragraphs: Automated auction design uses learning to search for mechanisms that earn high revenue. In auctions with multiple items, two obstacles arise: some learned mechanisms cannot strictly guarantee truthful bidding, while mechanisms with that guarantee can become difficult to scale because they consider too many possible allocations. AMenuNet addresses these issues within the affine maximizer auction family.

The network constructs auction parameters from representations of bidders and items, including a menu of candidate allocations. Generating that menu through a neural network improves scalability. The resulting auction inherits dominant strategy incentive compatibility and individual rationality from its underlying mechanism family. These properties support truthful participation, while the learned parameters determine the auction's revenue behavior.

AMenuNet also respects permutations of bidders and items, and its parameter count does not depend on auction size. Experiments report stronger performance than competitive baselines in contextual and non-contextual auctions, successful scaling to larger auctions, and generalization across settings. The network also identifies useful deterministic allocations, showing that its learned menus can contain effective concrete assignment choices.
summary.tldr: AMenuNet learns scalable allocation menus for high-revenue auctions while preserving the truthfulness and participation guarantees of affine maximizers.

title: A Scalable Neural Network for DSIC Affine Maximizer Auction Design

abstract: In this work, we deepen on the use of normalizing flows for causal reasoning. Specifically, we first leverage recent results on non-linear ICA to show that causal models are identifiable from observational data given a causal ordering, and thus can be recovered using autoregressive normalizing flows (NFs). Second, we analyze different design and learning choices for *causal normalizing flows* to capture the underlying causal data-generating process. Third, we describe how to implement the *do-operator* in causal NFs, and thus, how to answer interventional and counterfactual questions. Finally, in our experiments, we validate our design and training choices through a comprehensive ablation study; compare causal NFs to other approaches for approximating causal models; and empirically demonstrate that causal NFs can be used to address real-world problems—where the presence of mixed discrete-continuous data and partial knowledge on the causal graph is the norm. The code for this work can be found at https://github.com/psanch21/causal-flows.

paragraphs: Learning a data distribution and answering causal questions require connecting observations to the process that produced them. This paper studies how normalizing flows can represent that causal process. Using recent results on nonlinear independent component analysis, it establishes identifiability from observational data given a causal ordering, and shows how autoregressive flows can recover the corresponding models.

The causal ordering is a central condition of that theoretical result. The paper then examines architectural and learning choices that help causal normalizing flows capture the underlying data-generating process. It also explains how to implement the do-operator within these models, enabling questions about interventions and counterfactual alternatives through an explicit causal representation.

Experiments assess design and training choices through an ablation study and compare causal flows with other causal-model approximation approaches. They also demonstrate applications involving mixed discrete and continuous data and only partial knowledge of the causal graph. The contribution connects a conditional identification result with practical modeling choices and causal-query procedures, while empirically exploring settings that complicate real-world use.
summary.tldr: The paper connects causal identification given an ordering with normalizing-flow designs for intervention and counterfactual reasoning.

title: Causal normalizing flows: from theory to practice

abstract: Graphs are ubiquitous in various domains, such as social networks and biological systems. Despite the great successes of graph neural networks (GNNs) in modeling and analyzing complex graph data, the inductive bias of locality assumption, which involves exchanging information only within neighboring connected nodes, restricts GNNs in capturing long-range dependencies and global patterns in graphs. Inspired by the classic Brachistochrone problem, we seek how to devise a new inductive bias for cutting-edge graph application and present a general framework through the lens of variational analysis. The backbone of our framework is a two-way mapping between the discrete GNN model and continuous diffusion functional, which allows us to design application-specific objective function in the continuous domain and engineer discrete deep model with mathematical guarantees. First, we address over-smoothing in current GNNs. Specifically, our inference reveals that the existing layer-by-layer models of graph embedding learning are equivalent to a ${\ell _2}$-norm integral functional of graph gradients, which is the underlying cause of the over-smoothing problem. Similar to edge-preserving filters in image denoising, we introduce the total variation (TV) to promote alignment of the graph diffusion pattern with the global information present in community topologies. On top of this, we devise a new selective mechanism for inductive bias that can be easily integrated into existing GNNs and effectively address the trade-off between model depth and over-smoothing. Second, we devise a novel generative adversarial network (GAN) to predict the spreading flows in the graph through a neural transport equation. To avoid the potential issue of vanishing flows, we tailor the objective function to minimize the transportation within each community while maximizing the inter-community flows. Our new GNN models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on graph learning benchmarks such as Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed.

The two-way mapping allows the authors to design objectives in the continuous setting and derive discrete models with mathematical guarantees.

The authors link existing layer-by-layer embedding models to an integral involving squared graph gradients. They introduce total variation and a selective mechanism to align diffusion with community structure and improve the trade-off between network depth and over-smoothing.

A second application builds a generative adversarial model for predicting spreading flows through a neural transport equation. Its objective minimizes transportation within communities while maximizing flows between communities to address potentially vanishing flows. The resulting models report state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks including Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed. The broader contribution is a principled connection between continuous objectives and graph-network design, demonstrated through two distinct learning problems.
summary.tldr: A continuous-diffusion framework guides the design of graph networks that address over-smoothing and model spreading flows.

title: Re-Think and Re-Design Graph Neural Networks in Spaces of Continuous Graph Diffusion Functionals

abstract: The analogy between Gaussian processes (GPs) and deep artificial neural networks (ANNs) has received a lot of interest, and has shown promise to unbox the blackbox of deep ANNs. Existing theoretical works put strict assumptions on the ANN (e.g. requiring all intermediate layers to be wide, or using specific activation functions). Accommodating those theoretical assumptions is hard in recent deep architectures, and those theoretical conditions need refinement as new deep architectures emerge. In this paper we derive an evidence lower-bound that encourages the GP's posterior to match the ANN's output without any requirement on the ANN. Using our method we find out that on 5 datasets, only a subset of those theoretical assumptions are sufficient. Indeed, in our experiments we used a normal ResNet-18 or feed-forward backbone with a single wide layer in the end. One limitation of training GPs is the lack of scalability with respect to the number of inducing points. We use novel computational techniques that allow us to train GPs with hundreds of thousands of inducing points and with GPU acceleration. As shown in our experiments, doing so has been essential to get a close match between the GPs and the ANNs on 5 datasets. We implement our method as a publicly available tool called GPEX: https://github.com/amirakbarnejad/gpex. On 5 datasets (4 image datasets, and 1 biological dataset) and ANNs with 2 types of functionality (classifier or attention-mechanism) we were able to find GPs whose outputs closely match those of the corresponding ANNs. After matching the GPs to the ANNs, we used the GPs' kernel functions to explain the ANNs' decisions. We provide more than 200 explanations (around 30 in the paper and the rest in the supplementary) which are highly interpretable by humans and show the ability of the obtained GPs to unbox the ANNs' decisions.

The paper derives an evidence lower bound that encourages this match without imposing requirements on the neural network architecture.

They use ordinary ResNet-18 or feed-forward backbones with a single wide final layer, finding that only a subset of earlier theoretical assumptions was sufficient in these tests.

The authors then use the processes’ kernel functions to explain network decisions, providing more than 200 explanations described as highly interpretable by humans. The evidence connects output matching with a practical route to explanations through the fitted Gaussian-process model.
summary.tldr: GPEX fits scalable Gaussian processes to neural-network outputs and uses their kernel functions to explain the networks’ decisions.

title: GPEX, A Framework For Interpreting Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: One of the most common problems studied in the context of differential privacy for graph data is counting the number of non-induced embeddings of a subgraph in a given graph. These counts have very high global sensitivity. Therefore, adding noise based on powerful alternative techniques, such as smooth sensitivity and higher-order local sensitivity have been shown to give significantly better accuracy. However, all these alternatives to global sensitivity become computationally very expensive, and to date efficient polynomial time algorithms are known only for few selected subgraphs, such as triangles, $k$-triangles, and $k$-stars.In this paper, we show that good approximations to these sensitivity metrics can be still used to get private algorithms.Using this approach, we much faster algorithms for privately counting the number of triangles in real-world social networks, which can be easily parallelized.We also give a private polynomial time algorithm for counting any constant size subgraph using less noise than the global sensitivity; we show this can be improved significantly for counting paths in special classes of graphs.

paragraphs: Counting patterns inside a graph is a common privacy-sensitive analysis task. A difficulty is that these counts can have high global sensitivity, forcing methods based on that sensitivity to add substantial noise. More adaptive measures, including smooth sensitivity and higher-order local sensitivity, can improve accuracy but are often expensive to compute.

This paper shows that suitably good approximations to those sensitivity measures can still support private algorithms. The contribution concerns the computation needed to determine privacy-preserving noise, making more accurate approaches practical for a broader range of graph patterns. Previously, efficient polynomial-time methods were known only for a limited selection of subgraphs.

Using this idea, the authors develop faster private triangle-counting algorithms for real social networks that are also easy to parallelize. They provide a polynomial-time private algorithm for any constant-size subgraph using less noise than a global-sensitivity approach. For paths in special graph classes, they obtain further improvements. The result expands the available accuracy–computation tradeoffs while retaining the stated restrictions on pattern size and graph structure.
summary.tldr: Approximating sensitivity measures enables faster private subgraph counting with less noise than global-sensitivity methods.

title: Faster approximate subgraph counts with privacy

abstract: Video salient object ranking aims to simulate the human attention mechanism by dynamically prioritizing the visual attraction of objects in a scene over time. Despite its numerous practical applications, this area remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a graph model for video salient object ranking. This graph simultaneously explores multi-scale spatial contrasts and intra-/inter-instance temporal correlations across frames to extract diverse spatio-temporal saliency cues. It has two advantages: 1. Unlike previous methods that only perform global inter-frame contrast or compare all proposals across frames globally, we explicitly model the motion of each instance by comparing its features with those in the same spatial region in adjacent frames, thus obtaining more accurate motion saliency cues. 2. We synchronize the spatio-temporal saliency cues in a single graph for joint optimization, which exhibits better dynamics compared to the previous stage-wise methods that prioritize spatial cues followed by temporal cues. Additionally, we propose a simple yet effective video retargeting method based on video saliency ranking. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our model in video salient object ranking and the effectiveness of the video retargeting method. Our codes/models are released at [https://github.com/zyf-815/VSOR/tree/main](https://github.com/zyf-815/VSOR/tree/main).

paragraphs: Video salient object ranking asks which objects attract attention most strongly as a scene changes. The paper approaches this as a graph problem, combining spatial contrasts at multiple scales with temporal relationships within individual objects and between different objects. This gives the model several kinds of evidence for deciding how an object's visual priority should change across frames.

Its motion analysis focuses on each object individually. The model compares an object's features with features from the same spatial region in neighboring frames, rather than relying only on global comparisons between frames or proposals. The authors report that this produces more accurate motion-related saliency cues. Spatial and temporal signals are then optimized together within one graph.

That joint treatment matters because the attention ranking depends on both appearance and movement. The paper reports better dynamics than methods that process spatial cues before temporal ones, along with superior ranking results in extensive experiments. It also introduces and evaluates a video retargeting method driven by these rankings, demonstrating a practical use for the resulting attention priorities.
summary.tldr: A unified graph combines object-specific motion with spatial contrast to improve video attention ranking and support video retargeting.

title: A Motion-aware Spatio-temporal Graph for Video Salient Object Ranking

abstract: Jailbreak attacks cause large language models (LLMs) to generate harmful, unethical, or otherwise objectionable content. Evaluating these attacks presents a number of challenges, which the current collection of benchmarks and evaluation techniques do not adequately address. First, there is no clear standard of practice regarding jailbreaking evaluation. Second, existing works compute costs and success rates in incomparable ways. And third, numerous works are not reproducible, as they withhold adversarial prompts, involve closed-source code, or rely on evolving proprietary APIs. To address these challenges, we introduce JailbreakBench, an open-sourced benchmark with the following components: (1) an evolving repository of state-of-the-art adversarial prompts, which we refer to as *jailbreak artifacts*; (2) a jailbreaking dataset comprising 100 behaviors---both original and sourced from prior work---which align with OpenAI's usage policies; (3) a standardized evaluation framework at https://github.com/JailbreakBench/jailbreakbench that includes a clearly defined threat model, system prompts, chat templates, and scoring functions; and (4) a leaderboard at https://jailbreakbench.github.io/ that tracks the performance of attacks and defenses for various LLMs. We have carefully considered the potential ethical implications of releasing this benchmark, and believe that it will be a net positive for the community.

Comparing attacks is difficult when studies use different definitions of success, count costs differently, or withhold the prompts and code needed to reproduce results. JailbreakBench provides shared evaluation infrastructure to address these problems.

The benchmark combines an evolving collection of adversarial prompts with a dataset of 100 behaviors drawn from both new material and prior work. These details establish a common procedure for testing attacks rather than leaving important experimental choices implicit.

The contribution is a reproducible basis for comparison, rather than a claim that a particular defense solves jailbreaking. The authors also acknowledge ethical considerations surrounding release and judge the benchmark's expected community impact to be positive.
summary.tldr: JailbreakBench standardizes jailbreak evaluation through open prompts, a 100-behavior dataset, shared scoring procedures, and a leaderboard.

title: JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models

abstract: Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) enables the prediction of scene depths from a single RGB image, having been widely integrated into production-grade autonomous driving systems, e.g., Tesla Autopilot. Current adversarial attacks to MDE models focus on attaching an optimized adversarial patch to a designated obstacle. Although effective, this approach presents two inherent limitations: its reliance on specific obstacles and its limited malicious impact. In contrast, we propose a pioneering attack to MDE models that \textit{decouples obstacles from patches physically and deploys optimized patches on roads}, thereby extending the attack scope to arbitrary traffic participants. This approach is inspired by our groundbreaking discovery: \textit{various MDE models with different architectures, trained for autonomous driving, heavily rely on road regions} when predicting depths for different obstacles. Based on this discovery, we design the Adversarial Road Marking (AdvRM) attack, which camouflages patches as ordinary road markings and deploys them on roads, thereby posing a continuous threat within the environment. Experimental results from both dataset simulations and real-world scenarios demonstrate that AdvRM is effective, stealthy, and robust against various MDE models, achieving about 1.507 of Mean Relative Shift Ratio (MRSR) over 8 MDE models. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/a-c-a-c/AdvRM.git}

paragraphs: Monocular depth estimation predicts distances from a single color image. This paper investigates a weakness in models trained for autonomous driving: their estimates of obstacle depth can depend heavily on the surrounding road region. The authors observe this dependence across models with different architectures, suggesting that image context can influence depth predictions for multiple traffic participants.

Their Adversarial Road Marking attack places an optimized visual patch on the road and disguises it as an ordinary marking. Earlier patch attacks attached the pattern to a particular obstacle. Separating the patch from the obstacle changes the attack's reach: a road patch can affect depth predictions for participants other than an object carrying the patch, creating a continuing threat in that environment.

Experiments using dataset simulations and real-world scenarios report effectiveness, stealthiness, and robustness across various depth models. The reported Mean Relative Shift Ratio is about 1.507 over eight models. These findings identify road context as a consequential vulnerability in the evaluated systems and show why testing only patches attached to obstacles can miss a broader attack mechanism.
summary.tldr: Adversarial patches disguised as road markings exploit depth models' reliance on road context to affect predictions for traffic participants.

title: Beware of Road Markings: A New Adversarial Patch Attack to Monocular Depth Estimation

abstract: Long-tailed data distributions pose challenges for a variety of domains like e-commerce, finance, biomedical science, and cyber security, where the performance of machine learning models is often dominated by head categories while tail categories are inadequately learned. This work aims to provide a systematic view of long-tailed learning with regard to three pivotal angles: (A1) the characterization of data long-tailedness, (A2) the data complexity of various domains, and (A3) the heterogeneity of emerging tasks. We develop HeroLT, a comprehensive long-tailed learning benchmark integrating 18 state-of-the-art algorithms, 10 evaluation metrics, and 17 real-world datasets across 6 tasks and 4 data modalities. HeroLT with novel angles and extensive experiments (315 in total) enables effective and fair evaluation of newly proposed methods compared with existing baselines on varying dataset types. Finally, we conclude by highlighting the significant applications of long-tailed learning and identifying several promising future directions. For accessibility and reproducibility, we open-source our benchmark HeroLT and corresponding results at https://github.com/SSSKJ/HeroLT.

paragraphs: Long-tailed datasets contain common categories with many examples and rare categories with comparatively few. A model's overall behavior can be dominated by the common categories while rare ones remain poorly learned. This paper aims to make evaluation of that problem more systematic across domains, data types, and tasks.

The authors organize the study around three aspects: how long-tailedness is characterized, how data complexity varies between domains, and how emerging tasks differ from one another. They introduce HeroLT, a benchmark integrating 18 algorithms, 10 evaluation metrics, and 17 real-world datasets spanning six tasks and four data modalities. This provides a shared basis for comparisons across heterogeneous settings.

The work includes 315 experiments intended to support effective and fair evaluation of new methods against existing approaches. Its main contribution is the benchmark, metrics, toolbox, and corresponding results, rather than a single new prediction algorithm. By covering varied dataset types, HeroLT enables researchers to examine long-tailed learning across the multiple dimensions emphasized by the paper.
summary.tldr: HeroLT provides a broad benchmark and toolbox for comparing long-tailed learning methods across tasks, modalities, and dataset types.

title: Towards Heterogeneous Long-tailed Learning: Benchmarking, Metrics, and Toolbox

abstract: Many reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are too costly to use in practice due to the large sizes $S,A$ of the problem's state and action space. To resolve this issue, we study transfer RL with latent low rank structure. We consider the problem of transferring a latent low rank representation when the source and target MDPs have transition kernels with Tucker rank $(S, d, A)$, $(S ,S , d), (d, S , A )$, or $(d , d , d )$. In each setting, we introduce the transfer-ability coefficient $\alpha$ that measures the difficulty of representational transfer. Our algorithm learns latent representations in each source MDP and then exploits the linear structure to remove the dependence on $S , A $, or $SA $ in the target MDP regret bound. We complement our positive results with information theoretic lower bounds that show our algorithms (excluding the ($d, d, d$) setting) are minimax-optimal with respect to $\alpha$.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can become expensive when an environment has many states or actions. This paper studies whether representations learned in source environments can reduce that dependence when learning in a target environment. It assumes particular latent low-rank structures in the transition kernels of the source and target Markov decision processes.

The analysis covers Tucker ranks (S, d, A), (S, S, d), (d, S, A), and (d, d, d), where S and A describe state and action space sizes. For each setting, the authors introduce a transfer-ability coefficient, alpha, that measures how difficult representation transfer is. Their algorithm learns source representations and exploits the resulting linear structure in the target task.

Depending on the setting, the target regret bound removes dependence on S, A, or their product. Information-theoretic lower bounds also establish minimax optimality with respect to alpha for the algorithms outside the fully low-rank (d, d, d) case. The results specify both benefits of structural transfer and limits on how favorably its difficulty can enter the guarantees.
summary.tldr: Under specified low-rank transition structures, transferred representations reduce target-learning complexity, with matching transfer-difficulty lower bounds in three settings.

title: The Limits of Transfer Reinforcement Learning with Latent Low-rank Structure

abstract: Despite recent popularity of attention-based neural architectures in core AI fields like natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV), their potential in modeling complex physical systems remains under-explored. Learning problems in physical systems are often characterized as discovering operators that map between function spaces based on a few instances of function pairs. This task frequently presents a severely ill-posed PDE inverse problem. In this work, we propose a novel neural operator architecture based on the attention mechanism, which we coin Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), and explore its capability towards developing a foundation physical model. In particular, we show that the attention mechanism is equivalent to a double integral operator that enables nonlocal interactions among spatial tokens, with a data-dependent kernel characterizing the inverse mapping from data to the hidden parameter field of the underlying operator. As such, the attention mechanism extracts global prior information from training data generated by multiple systems, and suggests the exploratory space in the form of a nonlinear kernel map. Consequently, NAO can address ill-posedness and rank deficiency in inverse PDE problems by encoding regularization and achieving generalizability. Lastly, we empirically demonstrate the advantages of NAO over baseline neural models in terms of the generalizability to unseen data resolutions and system states. Our work not only suggests a novel neural operator architecture for learning an interpretable foundation model of physical systems, but also offers a new perspective towards understanding the attention mechanism.

paragraphs: Learning a physical system can require recovering an operator that maps one function to another from only a few observed pairs. Such inverse problems can be severely ill-posed. The Nonlocal Attention Operator, or NAO, uses attention to bring information learned across multiple systems into this difficult reconstruction process.

The paper interprets attention as a double integral operator that connects spatial tokens through nonlocal interactions. Its data-dependent kernel describes an inverse mapping from observations to the hidden parameter field of the underlying operator. This interpretation gives the architecture a mathematical connection to the physical inference problem, rather than treating attention only as a generic processing component.

Through training across systems, attention extracts global prior information and represents the space to explore through a nonlinear kernel map. The authors explain how this encodes regularization to address ill-posedness and rank deficiency. Experiments show better generalization than baseline neural models to unseen resolutions and system states. These results support NAO as a step toward interpretable foundation models for physical systems, alongside a new interpretation of attention.
summary.tldr: NAO interprets attention as a nonlocal integral operator that learns cross-system priors and improves tested generalization in inverse physical problems.

title: Nonlocal Attention Operator: Materializing Hidden Knowledge Towards Interpretable Physics Discovery

abstract: Temporal link prediction, aiming at predicting future interactions among entities based on historical interactions, is crucial for a series of real-world applications. Although previous methods have demonstrated the importance of relative encodings for effective temporal link prediction, computational efficiency remains a major concern in constructing these encodings. Moreover, existing relative encodings are usually constructed based on structural connectivity, where temporal information is seldom considered. To address the aforementioned issues, we first analyze existing relative encodings and unify them as a function of temporal walk matrices. This unification establishes a connection between relative encodings and temporal walk matrices, providing a more principled way for analyzing and designing relative encodings. Based on this analysis, we propose a new temporal graph neural network called TPNet, which introduces a temporal walk matrix that incorporates the time decay effect to simultaneously consider both temporal and structural information. Moreover, TPNet designs a random feature propagation mechanism with theoretical guarantees to implicitly maintain the temporal walk matrices, which improves the computation and storage efficiency. Experimental results on 13 benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness and efficiency of TPNet, where TPNet outperforms other baselines on most datasets and achieves a maximum speedup of $33.3 \times$ compared to the SOTA baseline.

paragraphs: Temporal link prediction uses past interactions to predict future connections between entities. Relative encodings help models describe relationships between entities, but constructing them can be expensive, and existing approaches often emphasize connectivity while making limited use of time. This paper develops a unified way to understand these encodings through temporal walk matrices.

Building on that analysis, the authors introduce TPNet, a temporal graph neural network. Its temporal walk matrix includes time decay, allowing the representation to account for both graph structure and when interactions occurred. A random-feature propagation mechanism maintains the relevant matrix information implicitly, with theoretical guarantees, improving computational and storage efficiency.

Experiments on 13 benchmark datasets evaluate both predictive effectiveness and efficiency. TPNet outperforms the compared baselines on most datasets and reaches a maximum speedup of 33.3 times against the leading baseline. The reported speedup is a maximum observed result, while the accuracy gains hold across most of the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: TPNet combines time-aware graph encodings with efficient random-feature propagation, improving most benchmark results and achieving up to 33.3 times speedup.

title: Improving Temporal Link Prediction via Temporal Walk Matrix Projection

abstract: We propose a novel regularization loss that enforces standard Gaussianity, encouraging samples to align with a standard Gaussian distribution. This facilitates a range of downstream tasks involving optimization in the latent space of text-to-image models. We treat elements of a high-dimensional sample as one-dimensional standard Gaussian variables and define a composite loss that combines moment-based regularization in the spatial domain with power spectrum-based regularization in the spectral domain. Since the expected values of moments and power spectrum distributions are analytically known, the loss promotes conformity to these properties. To ensure permutation invariance, the losses are applied to randomly permuted inputs. Notably, existing Gaussianity-based regularizations fall within our unified framework: some correspond to moment losses of specific orders, while the previous covariance-matching loss is equivalent to our spectral loss but incurs higher time complexity due to its spatial-domain computation. We showcase the application of our regularization in generative modeling for test-time reward alignment with a text-to-image model, specifically to enhance aesthetics and text alignment. Our regularization outperforms previous Gaussianity regularization, effectively prevents reward hacking and accelerates convergence.

paragraphs: Optimizing the latent inputs of a text-to-image model can benefit from keeping those inputs consistent with a standard Gaussian distribution. This paper introduces a regularization loss that encourages that consistency. It treats the entries of a high-dimensional sample as one-dimensional Gaussian variables and checks their statistical properties in two complementary ways.

Their expected Gaussian values are known analytically, providing targets for the loss. Applying the losses to randomly permuted inputs provides permutation invariance. The results connect the statistical construction to a practical objective: improving rewarded image properties while controlling departures from the intended latent distribution.
summary.tldr: A combined moment and power-spectrum loss improves Gaussianity regularization, preventing reward hacking and accelerating convergence in demonstrated image-alignment tasks.

title: Moment- and Power-Spectrum-Based Gaussianity Regularization for Text-to-Image Models

abstract: With the exponential growth of data, traditional object detection methods are increasingly struggling to handle vast vocabulary object detection tasks effectively. We analyze two key limitations of classification-based detectors: positive gradient dilution, where rare positive categories receive insufficient learning signals, and hard negative gradient dilution, where discriminative gradients are overwhelmed by numerous easy negatives. To address these challenges, we propose CQ-DINO, a category query-based object detection framework that reformulates classification as a contrastive task between object queries and learnable category queries. Our method introduces image-guided query selection, which reduces the negative space by adaptively retrieving top-K relevant categories per image via cross-attention, thereby rebalancing gradient distributions and facilitating implicit hard example mining. Furthermore, CQ-DINO flexibly integrates explicit hierarchical category relationships in structured datasets (e.g., V3Det) or learns implicit category correlations via self-attention in generic datasets (e.g., COCO). Experiments demonstrate that CQ-DINO achieves superior performance on the challenging V3Det benchmark (surpassing previous methods by 2.1% AP) while maintaining competitiveness in COCO. Our work provides a scalable solution for real-world detection systems requiring wide category coverage.

paragraphs: Object detectors with very large category vocabularies face an imbalance in their learning signals. Rare positive categories may receive too little emphasis, while numerous easy negatives can overwhelm the difficult distinctions the model needs to learn. CQ-DINO identifies these as two forms of gradient dilution and changes how category recognition is organized.

The framework replaces conventional classification with contrastive matching between object queries and learnable category queries. An image-guided selection mechanism uses cross-attention to retrieve the top-K relevant categories for each image. Reducing the negative candidate space rebalances training gradients and implicitly concentrates learning on harder examples. Category relationships are incorporated through explicit hierarchies or learned through self-attention.

On V3Det, CQ-DINO exceeds previous methods by a reported 2.1% AP while remaining competitive on COCO. The results support selecting relevant category comparisons as a way to improve detection with broad vocabularies. Its ability to use either supplied category structure or learned correlations also makes the approach applicable to the different dataset organizations examined in the paper.
summary.tldr: CQ-DINO improves large-vocabulary detection by matching objects to category queries and selecting image-relevant categories to reduce gradient dilution.

title: CQ-DINO: Mitigating Gradient Dilution via Category Queries for Vast Vocabulary Object Detection

abstract: The "black-box service model" enables ML service providers to serve clients while keeping their intellectual property and client data confidential. Confidentiality is critical for delivering ML services legally and responsibly, but makes it difficult for outside parties to verify important model properties such as fairness. Existing methods that assess model fairness confidentially lack either (i) *reliability* because they certify fairness with respect to a static set of data, and therefore fail to guarantee fairness in the presence of distribution shift or service provider malfeasance; and/or (ii) *scalability* due to the computational overhead of confidentiality-preserving cryptographic primitives. We address these problems by introducing *online fairness certificates*, which verify that a model is fair with respect to data received by the service provider *online* during deployment. We then present OATH, a deployably efficient and scalable zero-knowledge proof protocol for confidential online group fairness certification. OATH exploits statistical properties of group fairness via a "cut-and-choose" style protocol, enabling scalability improvements over baselines.

We address these problems by introducing *online fairness certificates*, which verify that a model is fair with respect to data received by the service provider *online* during deployment. We then present OATH, a deployably efficient and scalable zero-knowledge proof protocol for confidential online group fairness certification. paragraphs: Machine learning services often keep their models and clients’ data confidential. That confidentiality makes outside verification of fairness difficult. Existing confidential assessments can also rely on a fixed dataset, leaving them unable to guarantee fairness when deployment data change or a provider behaves improperly. Cryptographic verification can introduce a separate obstacle through computational expense.

The paper introduces online fairness certificates that assess fairness with respect to data actually received during deployment. This shifts the subject of certification from a static evaluation collection to the service’s ongoing inputs. The distinction matters because a certificate about earlier data need not establish the same property for the data a service encounters later.

OATH implements confidential online group fairness certification using a zero-knowledge proof protocol. It exploits statistical properties of group fairness through a cut-and-choose-style construction to improve scalability over baselines. The authors present the protocol as efficient enough for deployment. Its contribution joins operationally relevant fairness verification with confidentiality, addressing both the relevance of the certified data and the cost of certification.
summary.tldr: OATH provides scalable, confidential group fairness certificates for data received during actual model deployment.

title: Secure and Confidential Certificates of Online Fairness

abstract: In this paper we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Language Models (HDLM) -- a novel family of discrete diffusion models for language modeling. HDLM builds on a hierarchical vocabulary where low-level tokens with detailed semantics are surjectively mapped to high-level tokens with coarse-grained meanings. In the forward process, each token is independently perturbed to its higher-level ancestor with more abstract semantics according to the scheduler, while in the reverse process the model progressively predicts the next, more detailed semantics. Taken together, HDLM provides a general time-varying next semantic scale prediction process for language modeling. We derive closed-form expressions for the diffusion Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and show that HDLM can be implemented in a flexible manner while including the existing MDLM as a special case. We also propose practical training techniques based on the insights. Extensive text generation experiments validate the effectiveness of HDLM, which demonstrates consistently lower validation and generative perplexity than baselines.

In the forward process, each token is independently perturbed to its higher-level ancestor with more abstract semantics according to the scheduler, while in the reverse process the model progressively predicts the next, more detailed semantics. Taken together, HDLM provides a general time-varying next semantic scale prediction process for language modeling. We derive closed-form expressions for the diffusion Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and show that HDLM can be implemented in a flexible manner while including the existing MDLM as a special case. We also propose practical training techniques based on the insights. Extensive text generation experiments validate the effectiveness of HDLM, which demonstrates consistently lower validation and generative perplexity than baselines.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Diffusion Language Models generate language by progressively refining semantic detail. Their vocabulary has multiple levels: detailed tokens map to higher-level tokens with broader meanings. Multiple detailed tokens can therefore share a coarser ancestor, giving the diffusion process an explicit structure for moving between levels of abstraction.

During the forward process, each token is independently replaced by a higher-level ancestor according to a schedule. The reverse process learns to predict the next, more detailed semantic level. This makes generation a changing sequence of refinement tasks, with the model recovering increasingly specific meaning as it proceeds through the hierarchy.

The paper derives closed-form expressions for the diffusion evidence lower bound, providing a mathematical foundation for training. The framework allows flexible implementations and includes the existing MDLM approach as a special case. The authors also derive practical training techniques from their analysis. Text-generation experiments consistently show lower validation and generative perplexity than the evaluated baselines, supporting semantic hierarchies as a useful organizing principle for discrete language diffusion.
summary.tldr: HDLM generates text by progressively refining coarse semantic tokens into detailed ones, achieving lower perplexity than evaluated baselines.

title: Next Semantic Scale Prediction via Hierarchical Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Scaling limits, such as infinite-width limits, serve as promising theoretical tools to study large-scale models. However, it is widely believed that existing infinite-width theory does not faithfully explain the behavior of practical networks, especially those trained in *standard parameterization* (SP) meaning He initialization with a global learning rate. For instance, existing theory for SP predicts instability at large learning rates and vanishing feature learning at stable ones. In practice, however, optimal learning rates decay slower than theoretically predicted and networks exhibit both stable training and non-trivial feature learning, even at very large widths. Here, we show that this discrepancy is not fully explained by finite-width phenomena. Instead, we find a resolution through a finer-grained analysis of the regime previously considered unstable and therefore uninteresting. In particular, we show that, under the cross-entropy (CE) loss, the unstable regime comprises two distinct sub-regimes: a catastrophically unstable regime and a more benign controlled divergence regime, where logits diverge but gradients and activations remain stable. Moreover, under large learning rates at the edge of the controlled divergence regime, there exists a well-defined infinite width limit where features continue to evolve in all the hidden layers. In experiments across optimizers, architectures, and data modalities, we validate that neural networks operate in this controlled divergence regime under CE loss but not under MSE loss. Our empirical evidence suggests that width-scaling considerations are surprisingly useful for predicting empirically maximal stable learning rate exponents which provide useful guidance on optimal learning rate exponents. Finally, our analysis clarifies the effectiveness and limitations of recently proposed layerwise learning rate scalings for standard initialization.

paragraphs: Existing infinite-width theory predicts a troubling choice for networks with He initialization and a global learning rate: instability at large rates or vanishing feature learning at stable ones. Practical networks can instead train stably and keep learning features. This paper argues that finite width does not fully explain the discrepancy.

Under cross-entropy loss, the authors separate the supposedly unstable region into catastrophic instability and controlled divergence. In the latter, logits diverge while gradients and activations remain stable. At large learning rates near this region’s edge, they establish an infinite-width limit in which features continue evolving throughout all hidden layers.

Experiments across optimizers, architectures, and data modalities support controlled divergence under cross-entropy, but not under mean squared error. Empirical evidence also suggests that width scaling helps predict maximal stable learning-rate exponents, informing choices of optimal exponents. The result refines what instability means in this setting and clarifies both the usefulness and limitations of recently proposed layerwise learning-rate scalings.
summary.tldr: A controlled-divergence regime under cross-entropy explains how wide networks can use large learning rates while continuing to learn features.

title: On the Surprising Effectiveness of Large Learning Rates under Standard Width Scaling

abstract: The generation speed of LLMs are bottlenecked by autoregressive decoding, where tokens are predicted sequentially one by one. Alternatively, diffusion large language models (dLLMs) theoretically allow for parallel token generation, but in practice struggle to achieve the speed of autoregressive models without significantly sacrificing quality. We therefore introduce adaptive parallel decoding (APD), a novel method that dynamically adjusts the number of tokens sampled in parallel. We achieve this by defining a multiplicative mixture between the dLLM marginal probabilities and the joint probability of sequences under a small auxiliary autoregressive model. This inverts the standard setup of speculative decoding, where the goal is to sample from a large autoregressive verifier by drafting from a smaller model. We further optimize APD by enabling KV caching and limiting the size of the masked input. Altogether, our method puts forward three tunable parameters to flexibly tradeoff throughput and quality. We show that APD provides markedly higher throughput with minimal quality degradations on downstream benchmarks.

paragraphs: Generating text one token at a time limits the speed of autoregressive language models. Diffusion language models can, in principle, generate multiple tokens together, but turning that possibility into practical speed has often required sacrificing output quality. This paper introduces adaptive parallel decoding, or APD, to adjust how many tokens are sampled together during generation.

APD combines the diffusion model’s probabilities for individual tokens with a small autoregressive model’s probability for an entire sequence, using a multiplicative mixture. This brings sequence-level information into parallel sampling. The arrangement reverses the usual speculative-decoding setup, where a smaller model proposes text for a larger autoregressive model to verify.

The authors also enable key-value caching and restrict the size of the masked input to improve efficiency. Three adjustable parameters let users choose a throughput–quality balance. On downstream benchmarks, APD produces markedly higher throughput with minimal quality degradation. The reported gain therefore concerns a controllable trade-off, rather than an unconditional removal of the tension between generation speed and quality.
summary.tldr: APD adaptively combines diffusion and autoregressive probabilities to accelerate parallel text generation with minimal benchmark quality loss.

title: Accelerating Diffusion LLMs via Adaptive Parallel Decoding

abstract: Options markets represent one of the most sophisticated segments of the financial ecosystem, with prices that directly reflect market uncertainty. In this paper, we introduce the first reinforcement learning (RL) framework specifically designed for volatility trading through options, focusing on profit from the difference between implied volatility and realized volatility. Our multi-agent architecture consists of an Option Position Agent (OP-Agent) responsible for volatility timing by controlling long/short volatility positions, and a Hedger Routing Agent (HR-Agent) that manages risk and maximizes path-dependent profits by selecting optimal hedging strategies with different risk preferences. Evaluating our approach using cryptocurrency options data from 2021-2024, we demonstrate superior performance on BTC and ETH, significantly outperforming traditional strategies and machine learning baselines across all profit and risk-adjusted metrics while exhibiting sophisticated trading behavior. The code framework and sample data of this paper have been released on https://github.com/Edwicn/OPHR-MasteringVolatilityTradingwithMultiAgentDeepReinforcementLearning

paragraphs: OPHR applies reinforcement learning to options-based volatility trading, targeting differences between implied volatility and realized volatility. The framework separates the decision about taking a volatility position from the decision about how to hedge it. This division gives distinct agents responsibility for trading exposure and its ongoing risk management.

The Option Position Agent controls long and short volatility positions, handling the timing of volatility exposure. The Hedger Routing Agent selects among hedging strategies with different risk preferences. Its role includes managing risk and maximizing profits that depend on the path taken over time, so the framework considers how a position is managed as well as when it is entered.

The authors evaluate the system on cryptocurrency options data from 2021 through 2024, covering BTC and ETH. They report significant outperformance of traditional strategies and machine-learning baselines across all evaluated profit and risk-adjusted metrics, along with sophisticated trading behavior. These findings provide empirical support for dividing volatility trading into coordinated position-selection and hedging decisions in the studied markets.
summary.tldr: OPHR coordinates volatility-position and hedging agents, outperforming evaluated baselines on BTC and ETH options data.

title: OPHR: Mastering Volatility Trading with Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Gradient smoothing is an efficient approach to reducing noise in gradient-based model explanation methods. SmoothGrad adds Gaussian noise to mitigate much of this noise. However, the crucial hyperparameter in this method, the variance $\sigma$ of the Gaussian noise, is often set manually or determined using a heuristic approach. This results in the smoothed gradients containing extra noise introduced by the smoothing process. In this paper, we aim to analyze the noise and its connection to the out-of-range sampling in the smoothing process of SmoothGrad. Based on this insight, we propose AdaptGrad, an adaptive gradient smoothing method that controls out-of-range sampling to minimize noise. Comprehensive experiments, both qualitative and quantitative, demonstrate that AdaptGrad could effectively reduce almost all the noise in vanilla gradients compared to baseline methods. AdaptGrad is simple and universal, making it a practical solution to enhance gradient-based interpretability methods to achieve clearer visualization.

paragraphs: Gradient-based explanations use a model's sensitivity to its input to help show which parts influence its output. These explanations can be noisy and difficult to interpret. SmoothGrad addresses this by adding Gaussian noise during gradient smoothing, but the amount of noise is commonly chosen manually or through a heuristic.

This paper examines how smoothing can itself introduce unwanted noise. It connects that problem to out-of-range samples generated during the smoothing process. AdaptGrad uses this connection to adapt the sampling procedure, controlling out-of-range sampling with the aim of reducing the extra noise. Its central contribution is therefore a way to make the smoothing process more responsive to the source of the artifacts it can produce.

The authors report qualitative and quantitative experiments in which AdaptGrad could remove almost all noise from the original gradients compared with baseline methods. These findings support its use for clearer gradient visualizations. The abstract presents the method as simple and broadly applicable to gradient-based interpretation, with the reported benefit centered on reducing noise in the resulting explanations.
summary.tldr: AdaptGrad adapts gradient smoothing to control out-of-range sampling and reduce noise in model explanation visualizations.

title: AdaptGrad: Adaptive Sampling to Reduce Noise

abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities that benefits from online reinforcement learning (RL). These capabilities have primarily been demonstrated within the left-to-right autoregressive (AR) generation paradigm. In contrast, non-autoregressive paradigms based on diffusion generate text in a coarse-to-fine manner. Although recent diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) have achieved competitive language modeling performance compared to their AR counterparts, it remains unclear if dLLMs can also leverage recent advances in LLM reasoning. To this end, we propose, a framework to adapt pre-trained masked dLLMs into reasoning models via a combination of supervised finetuning (SFT) and RL. Specifically, we develop and extend techniques to improve reasoning in pretrained dLLMs: (a) we utilize a masked SFT technique to distill knowledge and instill self-improvement behavior directly from existing datasets, and (b) we introduce a novel critic-free, policy-gradient based RL algorithm called diffu-GRPO, the first integration of policy gradient methods to masked dLLMs. Through empirical studies, we investigate the performance of different post-training recipes on multiple mathematical and planning benchmarks. We find that d1 yields the best performance and significantly improves performance of a state-of-the-art dLLM.

paragraphs: Recent reasoning improvements from reinforcement learning have largely been demonstrated in language models that generate text from left to right. Diffusion language models instead generate text through coarse-to-fine refinement. This paper asks whether pretrained masked diffusion models can also benefit from the post-training techniques that have strengthened reasoning in autoregressive models.

The proposed d1 framework combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Its masked supervised training transfers knowledge from existing datasets and encourages self-improvement behavior. The authors also introduce diffu-GRPO, a policy-gradient reinforcement-learning algorithm that does not require a critic. This supplies a way to apply policy-gradient training within the masked diffusion generation setting.

Experiments compare different post-training recipes across mathematical and planning benchmarks. Among the recipes studied, d1 performs best and significantly improves the performance of a state-of-the-art diffusion language model. The findings provide empirical support for improving diffusion-model reasoning through combined supervised and reinforcement learning, extending the demonstrated usefulness of these techniques beyond left-to-right text generation.
summary.tldr: d1 combines masked supervised fine-tuning with critic-free reinforcement learning to improve diffusion language models on mathematical and planning tasks.

title: d1: Scaling Reasoning in Diffusion Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The remarkable success of the autoregressive paradigm has made significant advancement in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), with powerful models like Show-o, Transfusion and Emu3 made notable strides in unified image understanding and generation. For the first time, we uncover a common phenomenon: the understanding capability of MLLMs is usually stronger than their generative capability, with a significant gap between them. Building on this insight, we propose HermesFlow, a simple and general framework designed to seamlessly bridge the gap between understanding and generation in MLLMs. Specifically, we take the homologous data as input to curate homologous preference data of both understanding and generation. Through Pair-DPO and self-play iterative optimization, HermesFlow effectively aligns multimodal understanding and generation using homologous preference data. Extensive experiments demonstrate the significant superiority of our approach over prior methods, particularly in narrowing the gap between multimodal understanding and generation. These findings highlight the potential of HermesFlow as a general alignment framework for next-generation multimodal foundation models.

paragraphs: Models that combine image understanding and image generation do not necessarily perform equally well at both. The authors identify a common pattern in multimodal language models: their understanding ability is usually stronger than their ability to generate. HermesFlow is designed to reduce this imbalance within a unified model.

The framework builds related preference data for understanding and generation from corresponding source data. This connects the two learning objectives through a shared basis for judging better and worse responses. HermesFlow then uses Pair-DPO together with iterative self-play optimization to align the two capabilities, making their relationship an explicit part of training.

The reported experiments show substantial improvements over prior methods, particularly in narrowing the gap between understanding and generation. This matters because progress on one capability alone may leave a unified model unevenly capable across its intended uses. The findings support HermesFlow as a possible general alignment framework for multimodal foundation models, with that broader role presented as potential rather than a guarantee across every model.
summary.tldr: HermesFlow uses paired preference learning and iterative self-play to narrow the observed gap between multimodal understanding and generation.

title: HermesFlow: Seamlessly Closing the Gap in Multimodal Understanding and Generation

abstract: Recent advances in graph machine learning have shifted to data-centric paradigms, driven by two emerging research fields: (1) Federated graph learning (FGL) facilitates multi-client collaboration but struggles with data and task heterogeneity, resulting in limited practicality; (2) Graph foundation model (GFM) enables desirable domain generalization but is typically confined to single-machine training, neglecting the potential of cross-silo data and computational resources. It is evident that these two paradigms are complementary, and their integration offers substantial advantages. Motivated by this, we present a pioneering study about the federated graph foundation model (FedGFM), a novel decentralized GFM training paradigm. Despite the promising vision of FedGFM, knowledge entanglement has emerged as a critical challenge, where multi-domain knowledge is encoded into indistinguishable representations, thereby limiting downstream adaptation. To this end, we propose FedGFM+, an effective FedGFM framework with two key modules to mitigate knowledge entanglement in a dual-pronged manner. (1) AncDAI: From a global perspective, we introduce a novel anchor-based domain-aware initialization strategy. Before pre-training, each client encodes its local graph into a domain-specific prototypes, which serve as semantic anchors in the representation space. Around each anchor, we construct synthetic embeddings to initialize the global model. We theoretically show that these prototypes are distinguishable across domains, and the initialization provides a strong inductive bias that facilitates disentanglement of domain-specific knowledge. (2) AdaDPP: From a local perspective, during pre-training, each client independently learns a lightweight graph prompt that captures domain semantic preferences. During fine-tuning, prompts from all clients are aggregated into an adaptive domain-sensitive prompt pool, from which the GFM selects relevant prompts to augment the target graph’s attributes, thereby improving the downstream adaptation. FedGFM+ is extensively evaluated on 8 diverse benchmarks spanning multiple domains and tasks, outperforming 20 baselines from isolated supervised learning, FGL, and federated variants of centralized GFM paradigms.
