paragraphs: Federated graph learning combines contributions from multiple clients, while graph foundation models aim to transfer across domains. Combining them creates an opportunity to use distributed data and computation, but can entangle domain-specific knowledge in representations that are difficult to distinguish. FedGFM+ addresses this problem during initialization and downstream adaptation.

Before pretraining, each client summarizes its graph with domain-specific prototypes. These become semantic anchors around which synthetic embeddings are constructed to initialize the global model. The authors theoretically establish that the prototypes are distinguishable across domains and that this initialization encourages separation of domain knowledge.

During local pretraining, clients also learn lightweight graph prompts capturing their domain preferences. Fine-tuning combines these into an adaptive pool, from which relevant prompts augment the target graph's attributes. Evaluations on eight benchmarks spanning multiple domains and tasks outperform twenty baselines. The results support preserving domain distinctions at both the shared representation level and the later adaptation stage.
summary.tldr: FedGFM+ uses domain-specific initialization anchors and adaptive prompts to reduce knowledge entanglement in federated graph foundation models.

title: Towards Effective Federated Graph Foundation Model via Mitigating Knowledge Entanglement

abstract: Using pre-trained models has been found to reduce the effect of data heterogeneity and speed up federated learning algorithms. Recent works have explored training-free methods using first- and second-order statistics to aggregate local client data distributions at the server and achieve high performance without any training. In this work, we propose a training-free method based on an unbiased estimator of class covariance matrices which only uses first-order statistics in the form of class means communicated by clients to the server. We show how these estimated class covariances can be used to initialize the global classifier, thus exploiting the covariances without actually sharing them. We also show that using only within-class covariances results in a better classifier initialization. Our approach improves performance in the range of 4-26% with exactly the same communication cost when compared to methods sharing only class means and achieves performance competitive or superior to methods sharing second-order statistics with dramatically less communication overhead. The proposed method is much more communication-efficient than federated prompt-tuning methods and still outperforms them. Finally, using our method to initialize classifiers and then performing federated fine-tuning or linear probing again yields better performance. Code is available at https://github.com/dipamgoswami/FedCOF.

paragraphs: Training-free federated learning can combine summaries of client data to construct a global classifier without training it. Class means provide a compact summary, while covariance matrices describe additional variation within classes but require more communication. This paper asks whether the server can benefit from that richer information when clients send only their class means.

The authors propose an unbiased estimator of class covariance matrices based on the communicated means. The server uses these estimates to initialize the global classifier, gaining access to covariance information without receiving covariance matrices directly. They also find that restricting initialization to within-class covariances produces a better classifier. The method makes the distribution of client means useful beyond simply supplying average class representations.

The reported performance improvement over methods that share only means is 4–26%, at the same communication cost. Results are competitive with or better than approaches transmitting second-order statistics, with much less communication, and also exceed the compared federated prompt-tuning methods. The initialization remains useful when followed by federated fine-tuning or linear probing, showing benefits beyond the training-free configuration.
summary.tldr: Estimating class covariances from client class means improves federated classifier initialization without increasing the communication required by mean-only methods.

title: Covariances for Free: Exploiting Mean Distributions for Training-free Federated Learning

abstract: Collaborative visual perception methods have gained widespread attention in the autonomous driving community in recent years due to their ability to address sensor limitation problems. However, the absence of explicit depth information often makes it difficult for camera-based perception systems, e.g., 3D object detection, to generate accurate predictions. To alleviate the ambiguity in depth estimation, we propose RayFusion, a ray-based fusion method for collaborative visual perception. Using ray occupancy information from collaborators, RayFusion reduces redundancy and false positive predictions along camera rays, enhancing the detection performance of purely camera-based collaborative perception systems. Comprehensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, substantially advancing the performance of collaborative visual perception. Our code will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Camera-based perception systems can struggle to place objects accurately in three dimensions because images do not provide explicit depth. This ambiguity also affects collaborative perception, where multiple participants contribute visual information. RayFusion focuses on using information from collaborators to reduce uncertainty about where objects lie along camera viewing rays.

The method fuses ray occupancy information supplied by collaborators. This information helps reduce redundant predictions and false positives along a ray, addressing the depth ambiguity that can otherwise weaken three-dimensional object detection. Its design targets the geometric uncertainty underlying those predictions while operating within a purely camera-based collaborative perception system.

Comprehensive experiments report consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art models. Those findings support ray-based fusion as an effective way to improve detection in the evaluated collaborative setting. The paper’s contribution is a particular use of shared visual evidence: collaborators provide occupancy information that helps resolve ambiguous predictions along viewing directions, linking collaboration directly to the depth-estimation problem.
summary.tldr: RayFusion uses collaborators’ ray occupancy information to reduce depth ambiguity, redundant detections, and false positives in camera-based perception.

title: RayFusion: Ray Fusion Enhanced Collaborative Visual Perception

abstract: Human–AI conversation frequently relies on quoting earlier text—“check it with the formula I just highlighted”—yet today’s large language models (LLMs) lack an explicit mechanism for locating and exploiting such spans. We formalize the challenge as span-conditioned generation, decomposing each turn into the dialogue history, a set of token-offset quotation spans, and an intent utterance. Building on this abstraction, we introduce a quotation-centric data pipeline that automatically synthesizes task-specific dialogues, verifies answer correctness through multi-stage consistency checks, and yields both a heterogeneous training corpus and the first benchmark covering five representative scenarios. To meet the benchmark’s zero-overhead and parameter-efficiency requirements, we propose QuAda, a lightweight training-based method that attaches two bottleneck projections to every attention head, dynamically amplifying or suppressing attention to quoted spans at inference time while leaving the prompt unchanged and updating < 2.8% of backbone weights. Experiments across models show that QuAda is suitable for all scenarios and generalizes to unseen topics, offering an effective, plug-and-play solution for quotation-aware dialogue.

paragraphs: Conversation often depends on referring to a specific piece of earlier text. This paper makes that reference explicit by treating each turn as dialogue history, quoted spans identified by token offsets, and an utterance expressing the user’s intent. This formulation gives the model a defined target for interpreting requests about highlighted or quoted material.

The authors build an automated data pipeline that synthesizes task-specific dialogues and checks answer correctness through multiple consistency stages. It produces a varied training corpus and a benchmark spanning five scenarios. This supplies both training material and a structured way to evaluate whether models can use quotations appropriately.

Their method, QuAda, adds two small bottleneck projections to each attention head. These modules increase or decrease attention to quoted spans during inference while leaving the prompt unchanged and updating less than 2.8% of backbone weights during training. Experiments across models report suitability for all benchmark scenarios and generalization to unseen topics. The results support explicit quotation handling as a capability that can be added through lightweight attention adaptation.
summary.tldr: QuAda adds lightweight attention modules that help language models use explicitly marked quotations without changing the prompt.

title: Mind the Quote: Enabling Quotation-Aware Dialogue in LLMs via Plug-and-Play Modules

abstract: Language and vision-language models have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, but their internal mechanisms remain only partly understood. In this work, we study how individual attention heads in text-generative models specialize in specific semantic or visual attributes. Building on an established interpretability method, we reinterpret the practice of probing intermediate activations with the final decoding layer through the lens of signal processing. This lets us analyze multiple samples in a principled way and rank attention heads based on their relevance to target concepts. Our results show consistent patterns of specialization at the head level across both unimodal and multimodal transformers. Remarkably, we find that editing as few as 1% of the heads, selected using our method, can reliably suppress or enhance targeted concepts in the model output. We validate our approach on language tasks such as question answering and toxicity mitigation, as well as vision-language tasks including image classification and captioning. Our findings highlight an interpretable and controllable structure within attention layers, offering simple tools for understanding and editing large-scale generative models.

abstract: Neural processes (NPs) are a class of models that learn stochastic processes directly from data and can be used for inference, sampling and conditional sampling. We introduce a new NP model based on flow matching, a generative modeling paradigm that has demonstrated strong performance on various data modalities. Following the NP training framework, the model provides amortized predictions of conditional distributions over any arbitrary points in the data. Compared to previous NP models, our model is simple to implement and can be used to sample from conditional distributions using an ODE solver, without requiring auxiliary conditioning methods.In addition, the model provides a controllable tradeoff between accuracy and running time via the number of steps in the ODE solver. We show that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art neural process methods on various benchmarks including synthetic 1D Gaussian processes data, 2D images, and real-world weather data.

paragraphs: Neural processes learn distributions over data-dependent functions, supporting prediction and sampling conditioned on observations. This paper introduces a neural process built using flow matching, a generative modeling approach. The objective is to predict conditional distributions at arbitrary requested points while retaining a straightforward procedure for drawing samples from those distributions.

The model follows the neural process training framework, so a trained model provides amortized conditional predictions across different sets of points. Sampling uses an ordinary differential equation solver without an additional conditioning method. This makes conditional generation part of the model's sampling procedure. The solver's number of steps also gives users a way to control the balance between prediction accuracy and running time.

The authors evaluate the method on synthetic one-dimensional Gaussian process data, two-dimensional images, and real weather data. They report better performance than previous state-of-the-art neural process methods across these benchmarks. Together, the results support flow matching as a useful foundation for neural processes, combining conditional sampling with an adjustable computational budget across several kinds of data.
summary.tldr: Flow Matching Neural Processes provide conditional sampling through an ODE solver with an adjustable accuracy–runtime tradeoff.

title: Flow Matching Neural Processes

abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion (MCTD) integrates diffusion models with structured tree search to enable effective trajectory exploration through stepwise reasoning. However, MCTD remains fundamentally limited by training trajectory lengths. While periodic replanning allows plan concatenation for longer plan generation, the planning process remains locally confined, as MCTD searches within individual trajectories without access to global context. We propose Compositional Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion (C-MCTD), a framework that elevates planning from individual trajectory optimization to reasoning over complete plan compositions. C-MCTD introduces three complementary components: (1) Online Composer, which performs globally-aware planning by searching across entire plan compositions; (2) Distributed Composer, which reduces search complexity through parallel exploration from multiple starting points; and (3) Preplan Composer, which accelerates inference by leveraging cached plan graphs.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion combines diffusion models with tree search to explore possible trajectories. Its planning range is constrained by the trajectory lengths used during training. Replanning can join shorter plans into a longer sequence, but the underlying search still operates inside individual trajectories and lacks a view of the overall composition.

C-MCTD changes the unit of planning from one trajectory to a composition of trajectories. Its Online Composer searches over complete plan compositions, giving the planning process access to global context. This addresses the distinction between simply concatenating locally chosen segments and reasoning about those segments together as parts of one plan.

Two additional components address the cost of that broader search. The Distributed Composer explores from multiple starting points in parallel to reduce search complexity. The Preplan Composer reuses cached plan graphs to accelerate inference. Together, the components target global coordination, search cost, and reuse of prior planning work. The abstract presents this framework and its intended computational benefits without reporting numerical planning results.
summary.tldr: C-MCTD extends diffusion-based planning by searching over complete plan compositions, using parallel exploration and cached plan graphs to manage computation.

title: Compositional Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion for Extendable Planning

abstract: Modern single-image super-resolution (SISR) models deliver photo-realistic results at the scale factors on which they are trained, but collapse when asked to magnify far beyond that regime. We address this scalability bottleneck with Chain-of-Zoom (CoZ), a model-agnostic framework that factorizes SISR into an autoregressive chain of intermediate scale-states with multi-scale-aware prompts. CoZ repeatedly re-uses a backbone SR model, decomposing the conditional probability into tractable sub-problems to achieve extreme resolutions without additional training. Because visual cues diminish at high magnifications, we augment each zoom step with multi-scale-aware text prompts generated by a vision-language model (VLM). The prompt extractor itself is fine-tuned using Generalized Reward Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a critic VLM, aligning text guidance towards human preference. Experiments show that a standard $4\times$ diffusion SR model wrapped in CoZ attains beyond $256\times$ enlargement with high perceptual quality and fidelity.

paragraphs: An image enlargement model can produce convincing results at its training scale yet struggle when asked for much greater magnification. Chain-of-Zoom addresses this by breaking an extreme enlargement into a sequence of intermediate zoom levels. Each step reuses an existing super-resolution model, making the large transformation a chain of smaller conditional generation problems.

As magnification increases, the remaining visual evidence becomes less informative. The framework therefore supplies each step with text guidance produced by a vision-language model and tailored to multiple scales. Its prompt extractor is fine-tuned using Generalized Reward Policy Optimization and a critic vision-language model, with the aim of making the guidance better match human preferences.

The distinction between these components matters: the super-resolution backbone can be reused without additional training, while the prompt extractor receives preference-oriented training. Experiments show that a standard diffusion model designed for 4× super-resolution can, within this framework, produce enlargements beyond 256× with high reported perceptual quality and fidelity. The contribution is a reusable procedure for extending a model’s effective zoom range.
summary.tldr: Chain-of-Zoom repeatedly applies a super-resolution model with scale-aware text guidance to achieve enlargements beyond 256×.

title: Chain-of-Zoom: Extreme Super-Resolution via Scale Autoregression and Preference Alignment

abstract: Generating realistic graphs faces challenges in estimating accurate distribution of graphs in an embedding space while preserving structural characteristics. However, existing graph generation methods primarily focus on approximating the joint distribution of nodes and edges, often overlooking topological properties such as connected components and loops, hindering accurate representation of global structures. To address this issue, we propose a Topology-Aware diffusion-based Graph Generation (TAGG), which aims to sample synthetic graphs that closely resemble the structural characteristics of the original graph based on persistent homology. Specifically, we suggest two core components: 1) Persistence Diagram Matching (PDM) loss which ensures high topological fidelity of generated graphs, and 2) topology-aware attention module (TAM) which induces the denoising network to capture the homological characteristics of the original graphs. Extensive experiments on conventional graph benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach demonstrating high generation performance across various metrics, while achieving closer alignment with the distribution of topological features observed in the original graphs. Furthermore, application to real brain network data showcases its potential for complex and real graph applications.

Connected components and loops are examples of properties that can be overlooked when a model concentrates on the joint distribution of nodes and edges. TAGG brings these topological characteristics into diffusion-based graph generation.

The method uses persistent homology to represent structural information and incorporates it through two components. A Persistence Diagram Matching loss encourages generated graphs to retain the desired topology. A topology-aware attention module guides the denoising network toward the homological characteristics of the original graphs. One component shapes the training objective, while the other influences how the network processes structural information.

Experiments on conventional graph benchmarks report strong generation performance across multiple metrics and closer agreement with the original distribution of topological features. An application to real brain networks further demonstrates potential for complex graph data. The results support explicitly modeling topology when the goal is to reproduce the large-scale organization of graphs as well as their local connections.
summary.tldr: TAGG incorporates persistent-homology losses and attention into graph diffusion to better preserve global topological structure.

title: Topology-aware Graph Diffusion Model with Persistent Homology

abstract: Heavy-tailed noise is pervasive in modern machine learning applications, arising from data heterogeneity, outliers, and non-stationary stochastic environments. While second-order methods can significantly accelerate convergence in light-tailed or bounded-noise settings, such algorithms are often brittle and lack guarantees under heavy-tailed noise—precisely the regimes where robustness is most critical. In this work, we take a first step toward a theoretical understanding of second-order optimization under heavy-tailed noise. We consider a setting where stochastic gradients and Hessians have only bounded $p$-th moments, for some $p\in (1,2]$, and establish tight lower bounds on the sample complexity of any second-order method. We then develop a variant of normalized stochastic gradient descent that leverages second-order information and provably matches these lower bounds. To address the instability caused by large deviations, we introduce a novel algorithm based on gradient and Hessian clipping, and prove high-probability upper bounds that nearly match the fundamental limits. Our results provide the first comprehensive sample complexity characterization for second-order optimization under heavy-tailed noise. This positions Hessian clipping as a robust and theoretically sound strategy for second-order algorithm design in heavy-tailed regimes.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization uses curvature information as well as gradients to guide learning. Although this can accelerate convergence under well-behaved noise, unusually large random deviations can make such methods unstable. This paper develops a theoretical account of second-order optimization when the noise has heavy tails.

The analysis assumes that stochastic gradients and Hessians have bounded p-th moments for some p greater than one and at most two. Under that condition, the authors establish tight lower bounds on how many samples any second-order method needs. They then construct a normalized stochastic gradient method that uses second-order information and matches those bounds, connecting a fundamental limit with an achievable algorithm.

A further algorithm clips both gradients and Hessians to control large deviations. Its high-probability upper bounds nearly match the fundamental limits. These results distinguish exact matching by the normalized method from near-matching guarantees for the clipping-based method. Together, they characterize sample requirements in the studied heavy-tailed setting and give Hessian clipping a theoretical basis as a robustness strategy.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes sample-complexity limits under heavy-tailed noise and develops second-order methods with matching or nearly matching guarantees.

title: Second-order Optimization under Heavy-Tailed Noise: Hessian Clipping and Sample Complexity Limits

abstract: Classical optimisation theory guarantees monotonic objective decrease for gradient descent (GD) when employed in a small step size, or "stable", regime. In contrast, gradient descent on neural networks is frequently performed in a large step size regime called the "edge of stability", in which the objective decreases non-monotonically with an observed implicit bias towards flat minima. In this paper, we take a step toward quantifying this phenomenon by providing convergence rates for gradient descent with large learning rates in an overparametrised least squares setting. The key insight behind our analysis is that, as a consequence of overparametrisation, the set of global minimisers forms a Riemannian manifold $M$, which enables the decomposition of the GD dynamics into components parallel and orthogonal to $M$. The parallel component corresponds to Riemannian gradient descent on the objective sharpness, while the orthogonal component corresponds to a quadratic dynamical system. This insight allows us to derive convergence rates in three regimes characterised by the learning rate size: the subcritical regime, in which transient instability is overcome in finite time before linear convergence to a suboptimally flat global minimum; the critical regime, in which instability persists for all time with a power-law convergence toward the optimally flat global minimum; the supercritical regime, in which instability persists for all time with linear convergence to an oscillation of period two centred on the optimally flat global minimum.

paragraphs: Large learning rates can make gradient descent temporarily increase its objective while still progressing toward flatter solutions. This paper quantifies that behavior in an overparametrised least squares setting. Its analysis uses the fact that global minimizers form a curved geometric set, called a Riemannian manifold, rather than a single isolated solution.

The authors split the updates into motion along this set and motion perpendicular to it. Motion along the set acts like gradient descent on objective sharpness, explaining how training can favor flatter minimizers. The perpendicular motion follows a quadratic dynamical system. Together, these components allow the authors to derive convergence rates for three learning-rate regimes.

In the subcritical regime, instability ends after finite time, followed by linear convergence to a global minimum with suboptimal flatness. At the critical rate, instability persists while convergence toward the optimally flat minimum follows a power law. Above that rate, training converges linearly to a two-step oscillation centered on the optimally flat minimum. These distinct outcomes make the learning rate central to both convergence behavior and the resulting flatness.
summary.tldr: The paper derives three learning-rate-dependent convergence regimes for large-step gradient descent in overparametrised least squares.

title: Convergence Rates for Gradient Descent on the Edge of Stability for Overparametrised Least Squares

abstract: The emergence of agentic recommender systems powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) represents a paradigm shift in personalized recommendations, leveraging LLMs’ advanced reasoning and role-playing capabilities to enable autonomous, adaptive decision-making. Unlike traditional recommendation approaches, agentic recommender systems can dynamically gather and interpret user-item interactions from complex environments, generating robust recommendation strategies that generalize across diverse scenarios. However, the field currently lacks standardized evaluation protocols to systematically assess these methods. To address this critical gap, we propose: (1) an interactive textual recommendation simulator incorporating rich user and item metadata and three typical evaluation scenarios (classic, evolving-interest, and cold-start recommendation tasks); (2) a unified modular framework for developing agentic recommender systems; and (3) the first comprehensive benchmark comparing over 10 classical and agentic recommendation methods. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of agentic systems and establish actionable design guidelines for their core components. The benchmark environment has been rigorously validated through an open challenge and remains publicly available with a maintained leaderboard at https://tsinghua-fib-lab.github.io/AgentSocietyChallenge/pages/overview.html. The benchmark is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/SGJQovo/AgentRecBench.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can gather and interpret information about users and items while deciding what to recommend. Evaluating these systems requires accounting for their interactions with an environment, including how they respond when user interests change or information is scarce. AgentRecBench addresses the lack of a shared evaluation setup for this emerging approach to personalization.

The paper introduces an interactive text-based simulator containing detailed user and item metadata. It covers conventional recommendation, evolving interests, and cold-start tasks. A unified modular framework also supports building agentic recommenders, allowing their components to be studied within a common environment. Together, these resources connect system development with evaluation across distinct recommendation conditions.

The benchmark compares more than ten classical and agentic methods. The authors report superior performance from agentic systems in their evaluation and derive practical guidance for designing their core components. They also report validating the environment through an open challenge. The contribution is both comparative evidence and shared infrastructure for studying adaptive recommendation behavior.
summary.tldr: AgentRecBench provides a shared simulator, development framework, and benchmark for evaluating language-model agents as personalized recommenders.

title: AgentRecBench: Benchmarking LLM Agent-based Personalized Recommender Systems

abstract:
We consider the empirical distribution of the embeddings of a $k$-layer polynomial GNN on a semi-supervised node classification task and prove a central limit theorem for them. Assuming a community based model for the underlying graph, with growing average degree $
u_n	o\infty$, we show that the empirical distribution of the centered features, when scaled by $
u_{n}^{k-1/2}$ converge in 1-Wasserstein distance to a centered stable mixture of multivariate normal distributions. In addition, the joint empirical distribution of uncentered features and labels when normalized by $
u_n^k$ approach that of mixture of multivariate normal distributions, with stable means and covariance matrices vanishing as $
u_n^{-1}$. We explicitly identify the asymptotic means and covariances, showing that the mixture collapses towards a 1-D version as $k$ is increased. Our results provides a precise and nuanced lens on how oversmoothing presents itself in the large graph limit, in the sparse regime. In particular, we show that training with cross-entropy on these embeddings is asymptotically equivalent to training on these nearly collapsed Gaussian mixtures.

paragraphs: This paper studies the distribution of node representations produced by polynomial graph neural networks in semi-supervised classification. Its theoretical setting assumes a graph with community structure whose average degree grows without bound. Within that setting, the authors establish a central limit theorem describing how representations fluctuate around their centers as the graph becomes large.

The result identifies a stable mixture of multivariate Gaussian distributions after centering and applying a depth-dependent scaling. A related result describes normalized representations together with their labels: their community-associated means stabilize, while their covariance matrices shrink inversely with average degree. The authors explicitly calculate these limiting means and covariances, giving a quantitative account of both location and variability.

As network depth increases, the mixture moves toward a one-dimensional form. This characterizes oversmoothing through the geometry of the representation distribution. The paper also proves that cross-entropy training on these embeddings becomes asymptotically equivalent to training on the nearly collapsed Gaussian mixtures, connecting the distributional analysis to the learning objective.
summary.tldr: Under a growing-degree community graph model, polynomial GNN embeddings approach Gaussian mixtures whose collapse with depth precisely characterizes oversmoothing.

title: A CLT for Polynomial GNNs on Community-Based Graphs

abstract: MEMS gyroscopes play a critical role in inertial navigation and motion control applications but typically suffer from a fundamental trade-off between measurement range and noise performance. Existing hardware-based solutions aimed at mitigating this issue introduce additional complexity, cost, and scalability challenges. Deep-learning methods primarily focus on noise reduction and typically require precisely aligned ground-truth signals, making them difficult to deploy in practical scenarios and leaving the fundamental trade-off unresolved. To address these challenges, we introduce Mixture of Experts for MEMS Gyroscopes (MoE-Gyro), a novel self-supervised framework specifically designed for simultaneous over-range signal reconstruction and noise suppression. MoE-Gyro employs two experts: an Over‑Range Reconstruction Expert (ORE), featuring a Gaussian-Decay Attention mechanism for reconstructing saturated segments; and a Denoise Expert (DE), utilizing dual-branch complementary masking combined with FFT-guided augmentation for robust noise reduction. A lightweight gating module dynamically routes input segments to the appropriate expert. Furthermore, existing evaluation lack a comprehensive standard for assessing multi-dimensional signal enhancement. To bridge this gap, we introduce IMU Signal Enhancement Benchmark (ISEBench), an open-source benchmarking platform comprising the GyroPeak-100 dataset and a unified evaluation of IMU signal enhancement methods. We evaluate MoE-Gyro using our proposed ISEBench, demonstrating that our framework significantly extends the measurable range from ±450°/s to ±1500°/s, reduces Bias Instability by 98.4%, and achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively addressing the long-standing trade-off in inertial sensing.Our code is available at: https://github.com/2002-Pan/Moe-Gyro

paragraphs: MEMS gyroscopes face a trade-off between measuring fast rotation and maintaining low noise. Hardware changes can add cost and complexity, while many learning methods focus only on denoising and require precisely aligned reference signals. MoE-Gyro addresses both saturated measurements and noise within a self-supervised framework.

The model divides the work between two experts. An over-range reconstruction expert uses Gaussian-decay attention to recover saturated signal segments. A denoising expert combines complementary masking in two branches with frequency-guided augmentation. A lightweight gating module routes input segments to the appropriate expert, allowing the framework to handle different signal problems through specialized processing.

The authors also introduce ISEBench, a signal-enhancement evaluation platform containing the GyroPeak-100 dataset and a unified benchmarking setup. In this evaluation, MoE-Gyro extends the measurable range from ±450 to ±1500 degrees per second and reduces Bias Instability by 98.4%, achieving state-of-the-art performance. These reported results support jointly reconstructing over-range motion and suppressing noise, rather than evaluating signal enhancement only through its ability to denoise measurements already within range.
summary.tldr: MoE-Gyro uses two self-supervised experts to reconstruct saturated gyroscope signals and reduce noise, improving both range and stability in its benchmark.

title: MoE-Gyro: Self-Supervised Over-Range Reconstruction and Denoising for MEMS Gyroscopes

abstract: Reward shaping is effective in addressing the sparse-reward challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) by providing immediate feedback through auxiliary, informative rewards. Based on the reward shaping strategy, we propose a novel multi-task reinforcement learning framework that integrates a centralized reward agent (CRA) and multiple distributed policy agents. The CRA functions as a knowledge pool, aimed at distilling knowledge from various tasks and distributing it to individual policy agents to improve learning efficiency. Specifically, the shaped rewards serve as a straightforward metric for encoding knowledge. This framework not only enhances knowledge sharing across established tasks but also adapts to new tasks by transferring meaningful reward signals. We validate the proposed method on both discrete and continuous domains, including the representative Meta-World benchmark, demonstrating its robustness in multi-task sparse-reward settings and its effective transferability to unseen tasks.
originalAbstract: Reward shaping is effective in addressing the sparse-reward challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) by providing immediate feedback through auxiliary, informative rewards. Based on the reward shaping strategy, we propose a novel multi-task reinforcement learning framework that integrates a centralized reward agent (CRA) and multiple distributed policy agents. The CRA functions as a knowledge pool, aimed at distilling knowledge from various tasks and distributing it to individual policy agents to improve learning efficiency. Specifically, the shaped rewards serve as a straightforward metric for encoding knowledge. This framework not only enhances knowledge sharing across established tasks but also adapts to new tasks by transferring meaningful reward signals. We validate the proposed method on both discrete and continuous domains, including the representative Meta-World benchmark, demonstrating its robustness in multi-task sparse-reward settings and its effective transferability to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because useful feedback may arrive too infrequently to guide behavior efficiently. Reward shaping addresses this by adding informative intermediate rewards. This paper uses that idea to connect learning across multiple tasks, with a centralized reward agent supporting several distributed policy agents.

The centralized agent acts as a shared store of knowledge distilled from different tasks. It communicates that knowledge through shaped reward signals, which give individual policy agents additional feedback during learning. The key design choice is the form of what gets shared: rewards encode useful knowledge in a signal that each policy agent can use while learning its own task.

The framework also transfers meaningful reward signals to new tasks. Evaluations cover discrete and continuous domains, including Meta-World, and demonstrate robustness in the tested multi-task settings with sparse rewards and effective transfer to unseen tasks. These findings support reward generation as a practical mechanism for both sharing existing task knowledge and helping agents learn beyond the original set of tasks.
summary.tldr: A centralized reward agent shares knowledge through informative reward signals, improving multi-task learning and transfer in sparse-reward experiments.

title: Centralized Reward Agent for Knowledge Sharing and Transfer in Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Efficiently learning accurate models of dynamical systems is of central importance for developing rational agents that can succeed in a wide range of challenging domains. The difficulty of this learning problem is particularly acute in settings with large observation spaces and partial observability. We present a new algorithm, called Compressed Predictive State Representation (CPSR), for learning models of high-dimensional partially observable uncontrolled dynamical systems from small sample sets. The algorithm, which extends previous work on Predictive State Representations, exploits a particular sparse structure present in many domains. This sparse structure is used to compress information during learning, allowing for an increase in both the efficiency and predictive power. The compression technique also relieves the burden of domain specific feature selection and allows for domains with extremely large discrete observation spaces to be efficiently modelled. We present empirical results showing that the algorithm is able to build accurate models more efficiently than its uncompressed counterparts, and provide theoretical results on the accuracy of the learned compressed model.

The compression also reduces the burden of selecting domain-specific features, making the approach relevant when constructing a manageable representation by hand would be difficult.

Together, these contributions support compression as a useful part of learning when the relevant sparse structure is present, with both experimental evidence and mathematical analysis addressing the quality of the resulting predictions.
summary.tldr: CPSR exploits sparse structure to learn accurate compressed models of high-dimensional partially observed systems more efficiently.

title: Modelling Sparse Dynamical Systems with Compressed Predictive State Representations

abstract: The use of topic models to analyze domain-specific texts often requires manual validation of the latent topics to ensure they are meaningful. We introduce a framework to support large-scale assessment of topical relevance. We measure the correspondence between a set of latent topics and a set of reference concepts to quantify four types of topical misalignment: junk, fused, missing, and repeated topics. Our analysis compares 10,000 topic model variants to 200 expert-provided domain concepts, and demonstrates how our framework can inform choices of model parameters, inference algorithms, and intrinsic measures of topical quality.

paragraphs: Topic models discover latent themes in text, but domain-specific applications often require manual checks that those themes correspond to meaningful concepts. This paper introduces a framework for assessing that correspondence at scale. It compares a model's topics with a reference set of domain concepts, making topical relevance something that can be examined systematically.

The framework quantifies four kinds of misalignment: junk, fused, missing, and repeated topics. These categories distinguish irrelevant topics, topics that combine concepts, concepts left uncovered, and redundant topical coverage. Separating these outcomes makes the assessment more informative than treating every failure of correspondence as the same problem.

The analysis compares 10,000 topic model variants against 200 concepts supplied by domain experts. It demonstrates how alignment diagnostics can inform choices of model parameters, inference algorithms, and intrinsic topic-quality measures. The contribution is a structured way to relate model output to domain expectations, allowing large-scale comparisons to reveal how different modeling choices affect conceptual coverage.
summary.tldr: Comparing learned topics with expert reference concepts exposes four kinds of misalignment and helps guide topic-model choices.

title: Topic Model Diagnostics: Assessing Domain Relevance via Topical Alignment

abstract: This paper advocates a new ML-based programming framework, called Programming by Feedback (PF), which involves a sequence of interactions between the active computer and the user. The latter only provides preference judgments on pairs of solutions supplied by the active computer. The active computer involves two components: the learning component estimates the user’s utility function and accounts for the user’s (possibly limited) competence; the optimization component explores the search space and returns the most appropriate candidate solution. A proof of principle of the approach is proposed, showing that PF requires a handful of interactions in order to solve some discrete and continuous benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Programming by Feedback proposes a programming framework built around repeated interactions between a user and an active computer. The user provides preference judgments between pairs of candidate solutions. These comparisons serve as the information the system uses to determine what the user wants, making the interaction itself part of how a solution is developed.

The computer has two cooperating components. A learning component estimates the user's utility function while accounting for the possibility that the user's competence is limited. An optimization component explores the solution space and returns an appropriate candidate. Together, these components connect preference estimation with the search for solutions that fit the inferred preferences.

The paper presents a proof of principle on discrete and continuous benchmark problems. In some of these problems, the framework reaches a solution with only a handful of interactions. This supports the feasibility of the proposed feedback loop in the demonstrated cases: a small number of pairwise judgments can guide both learning what is preferred and searching for an acceptable solution.
summary.tldr: Programming by Feedback combines preference learning and optimization to solve some benchmark problems through only a handful of user comparisons.

title: Programming by Feedback

abstract: We consider the problem of binary class probability estimation (CPE) when one class is rare compared to the other. It is well known that standard algorithms such as logistic regression do not perform well on this task as they tend to under-estimate the probability of the rare class. Common fixes include under-sampling and weighting, together with various correction schemes. Recently, Wang & Dey (2010) suggested the use of a parametrized family of asymmetric link functions based on the generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution, which has been used for modeling rare events in statistics. The approach showed promising initial results, but combined with the logarithmic CPE loss implicitly used in their work, it results in a non-convex composite loss that is difficult to optimize. In this paper, we use tools from the theory of proper composite losses (Buja et al, 2005; Reid & Williamson, 2010) to construct a canonical underlying CPE loss corresponding to the GEV link, which yields a convex proper composite loss that we call the GEV-canonical loss; this loss is tailored for the task of CPE when one class is rare, and is easy to minimize using an IRLS-type algorithm similar to that used for logistic regression. Our experiments on both synthetic and real data demonstrate that the resulting algorithm – which we term GEV-canonical regression – outperforms common approaches such as under-sampling and weights correction for this problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimating class probabilities when one of two classes is rare. The concern is the probability assigned to that rare outcome, not just the final class prediction. The authors identify underestimation by standard methods such as logistic regression as a motivation for developing a probability estimator suited to this imbalance.

Earlier work used asymmetric link functions derived from the generalized extreme value distribution. These functions offered a promising way to model rare outcomes, but pairing them with logarithmic probability-estimation loss produced a non-convex optimization problem. This paper changes the underlying loss to match the link, using the theory of proper composite losses to construct a convex GEV-canonical objective.

That matching is the key contribution: it retains the rare-class-oriented link while making the resulting objective easier to optimize. The authors minimize it with an iteratively reweighted least-squares-type algorithm resembling the one used for logistic regression. Experiments on synthetic and real data show the resulting regression method outperforming common approaches based on undersampling and weight correction for this probability-estimation task.
summary.tldr: GEV-canonical regression pairs an asymmetric rare-event link with a suitable loss to obtain convex, effective rare-class probability estimation.

title: GEV-Canonical Regression for Accurate Binary Class Probability Estimation when One Class is Rare

abstract: We propose a distributed first-order augmented Lagrangian (DFAL) algorithm to minimize the sum of composite convex functions, where each term in the sum is a private cost function belonging to a node, and only nodes connected by an edge can directly communicate with each other. This optimization model abstracts a number of applications in distributed sensing and machine learning. We show that any limit point of DFAL iterates is optimal; and for any eps > 0, an eps-optimal and eps-feasible solution can be computed within O(log(1/eps)) DFAL iterations, which require O(\psi_\textmax^1.5/d_\textmin ⋅1/ε) proximal gradient computations and communications per node in total, where \psi_\textmax denotes the largest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian, and d_\textmin is the minimum degree of the graph. We also propose an asynchronous version of DFAL by incorporating randomized block coordinate descent methods; and demonstrate the efficiency of DFAL on large scale sparse-group LASSO problems.

paragraphs: The paper considers a network of nodes that jointly minimize a sum of convex costs. Each node owns its own private cost function, and direct communication is restricted to connected neighbors. This captures distributed learning and sensing problems in which a collective solution must be reached through local computation and communication.

The proposed distributed first-order augmented Lagrangian algorithm, DFAL, has an optimality guarantee for any limit point of its iterates. For a requested accuracy epsilon, the authors also bound the number of outer iterations needed to obtain an approximately optimal and feasible solution. That count grows logarithmically with inverse accuracy, while the total proximal-gradient computations and communications per node have a separate bound involving inverse accuracy and properties of the communication graph.

The authors additionally construct an asynchronous version using randomized block coordinate descent. Experiments on large sparse-group LASSO problems demonstrate DFAL's efficiency. The contribution combines a distributed optimization procedure with guarantees that explicitly account for network structure, making clear that both numerical accuracy and connectivity affect the required work.
summary.tldr: DFAL solves distributed composite convex problems with optimality and complexity guarantees, plus an asynchronous variant.

title: An Asynchronous Distributed Proximal Gradient Method for Composite Convex Optimization

abstract: The ability to represent complex high dimensional probability distributions in a compact form is one of the key insights in the field of graphical models. Factored representations are ubiquitous in machine learning and lead to major computational advantages. We explore a different type of compact representation based on discrete Fourier representations, complementing the classical approach based on conditional independencies. We show that a large class of probabilistic graphical models have a compact Fourier representation. This theoretical result opens up an entirely new way of approximating a probability distribution. We demonstrate the significance of this approach by applying it to the variable elimination algorithm. Compared with the traditional bucket representation and other approximate inference algorithms, we obtain significant improvements.

paragraphs: The paper explores a different way to represent high-dimensional probability distributions compactly. Graphical models usually gain efficiency by factoring distributions according to conditional independence relationships. The authors investigate discrete Fourier representations as a complementary source of compactness, opening another route to representing and approximating the same kinds of probabilistic objects.

Their theoretical result shows that a large class of probabilistic graphical models admits compact Fourier representations. This matters because the representation used for a distribution influences how inference computations can be performed. The result provides a basis for approximation methods that work with Fourier structure alongside the familiar factor-based view.

To demonstrate the approach, the authors apply it to variable elimination, an algorithm for removing variables while computing probabilistic quantities. They report significant improvements over the traditional bucket representation and other approximate inference algorithms. The contribution combines a representation theorem with an inference application, showing that changing how distributions are stored and manipulated can yield practical benefits in the comparisons studied.
summary.tldr: Compact Fourier representations offer an alternative basis for probabilistic inference and improve variable elimination in the reported comparisons.

title: Variable Elimination in the Fourier Domain

abstract: We provide convergence guarantees in Wasserstein distance for a variety of variance-reduction methods: SAGA Langevin diffusion, SVRG Langevin diffusion and control-variate underdamped Langevin diffusion. We analyze these methods under a uniform set of assumptions on the log-posterior distribution, assuming it to be smooth, strongly convex and Hessian Lipschitz. This is achieved by a new proof technique combining ideas from finite-sum optimization and the analysis of sampling methods. Our sharp theoretical bounds allow us to identify regimes of interest where each method performs better than the others. Our theory is verified with experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient Monte Carlo methods aim to sample from a target distribution while using stochastic gradient information. This paper studies theoretical guarantees for three approaches that incorporate variance reduction: SAGA Langevin diffusion, SVRG Langevin diffusion, and control-variate underdamped Langevin diffusion. The objective is to understand their convergence on a shared analytical basis.

The guarantees use Wasserstein distance to measure distributional approximation. The analysis places all three methods under a uniform set of assumptions on the log-posterior, stated as smoothness, strong convexity, and a Lipschitz Hessian. Using the same assumptions makes the resulting comparisons more directly informative about differences between the methods.

A new proof technique combines ideas from finite-sum optimization with tools for analyzing sampling algorithms. The resulting sharp bounds identify regimes in which each method performs better than the others, rather than declaring one approach uniformly superior. Experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets verify the theory, connecting the mathematical comparisons to observed performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A unified convergence analysis identifies when different variance-reduced Langevin sampling methods have an advantage.

title: On the Theory of Variance Reduction for Stochastic Gradient Monte Carlo

abstract: Gradient-based meta-learning methods leverage gradient descent to learn the commonalities among various tasks. While previous such methods have been successful in meta-learning tasks, they resort to simple gradient descent during meta-testing. Our primary contribution is the MT-net , which enables the meta-learner to learn on each layer’s activation space a subspace that the task-specific learner performs gradient descent on. Additionally, a task-specific learner of an MT-net performs gradient descent with respect to a meta-learned distance metric, which warps the activation space to be more sensitive to task identity. We demonstrate that the dimension of this learned subspace reflects the complexity of the task-specific learner’s adaptation task, and also that our model is less sensitive to the choice of initial learning rates than previous gradient-based meta-learning methods. Our method achieves state-of-the-art or comparable performance on few-shot classification and regression tasks.

paragraphs: Gradient-based meta-learning uses multiple tasks to learn shared structure that can help a model adapt to a new task. The paper observes that earlier methods still use simple gradient descent during that adaptation. MT-net expands what is learned across tasks by shaping both the space available for adaptation and the geometry of the updates.

For each layer's activations, the meta-learner selects a subspace in which the task-specific learner performs gradient descent. It also learns a distance metric that changes how movement through activation space is measured. This reshaping makes the space more sensitive to task identity, so adaptation follows structure learned from the collection of tasks.

The authors demonstrate that the learned subspace's dimension reflects the complexity of the adaptation problem. They also find less sensitivity to initial learning-rate choices than in earlier gradient-based meta-learning methods. On few-shot classification and regression tasks, MT-net achieves leading or comparable performance, supporting the usefulness of learning how adaptation should proceed as well as shared task information.
summary.tldr: MT-net learns layerwise adaptation subspaces and distance metrics, achieving competitive few-shot performance with reduced learning-rate sensitivity.

title: Gradient-Based Meta-Learning with Learned Layerwise Metric and Subspace

abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a prominent role in many disciplines of science and engineering. PDEs are commonly derived based on empirical observations. However, with the rapid development of sensors, computational power, and data storage in the past decade, huge quantities of data can be easily collected and efficiently stored. Such vast quantity of data offers new opportunities for data-driven discovery of physical laws. Inspired by the latest development of neural network designs in deep learning, we propose a new feed-forward deep network, called PDE-Net, to fulfill two objectives at the same time: to accurately predict dynamics of complex systems and to uncover the underlying hidden PDE models. Comparing with existing approaches, our approach has the most flexibility by learning both differential operators and the nonlinear response function of the underlying PDE model. A special feature of the proposed PDE-Net is that all filters are properly constrained, which enables us to easily identify the governing PDE models while still maintaining the expressive and predictive power of the network. These constrains are carefully designed by fully exploiting the relation between the orders of differential operators and the orders of sum rules of filters (an important concept originated from wavelet theory). Numerical experiments show that the PDE-Net has the potential to uncover the hidden PDE of the observed dynamics, and predict the dynamical behavior for a relatively long time, even in a noisy environment.

The stated evidence supports that potential rather than a universal discovery guarantee. The approach matters because its architecture supports interpretation and prediction within the same learned model: the filters help connect what the network computes to the mathematical structure of the system’s dynamics.
summary.tldr: PDE-Net constrains learned filters to jointly predict system dynamics and identify potential governing PDEs, with promising numerical results under noise.

title: PDE-Net: Learning PDEs from Data

abstract: The fundamental task of general density estimation $p(x)$ has been of keen interest to machine learning. In this work, we attempt to systematically characterize methods for density estimation. Broadly speaking, most of the existing methods can be categorized into either using: a ) autoregressive models to estimate the conditional factors of the chain rule, $p(x_{i}\, |\, x_{i-1}, \ldots)$; or b ) non-linear transformations of variables of a simple base distribution. Based on the study of the characteristics of these categories, we propose multiple novel methods for each category. For example we propose RNN based transformations to model non-Markovian dependencies. Further, through a comprehensive study over both real world and synthetic data, we show that jointly leveraging transformations of variables and autoregressive conditional models, results in a considerable improvement in performance. We illustrate the use of our models in outlier detection and image modeling. Finally we introduce a novel data driven framework for learning a family of distributions.

paragraphs: Density estimation learns a probability distribution over data. This paper organizes many existing approaches into two broad groups: autoregressive models, which express a joint distribution through conditional factors, and methods that nonlinearly transform variables from a simple base distribution. The authors study the characteristics of both groups to develop new methods.

Their proposals include recurrent-neural-network transformations for modeling non-Markovian dependencies, allowing dependencies to extend beyond a restricted immediate history. They also investigate combining variable transformations with autoregressive conditional models. This combination brings together two ways of describing a distribution rather than requiring the model to rely on only one of them.

A comprehensive study on real-world and synthetic data reports considerable performance improvements from using the two approaches jointly. The paper illustrates applications to outlier detection and image modeling, connecting density estimation to concrete tasks. It additionally introduces a data-driven framework for learning a family of distributions. Overall, the stated findings support combining transformations and conditional modeling as a productive design choice for density estimators.
summary.tldr: The paper develops density estimators that combine nonlinear transformations with autoregressive models and reports substantial gains on real and synthetic data.

title: Transformation Autoregressive Networks

abstract: Clustering is a fundamental problem in unsupervised learning. Popular methods like K-means, may suffer from instability as they are prone to get stuck in its local minima. Recently, the sumof-norms (SON) model (also known as clustering path), which is a convex relaxation of hierarchical clustering model, has been proposed in (Lindsten et al., 2011) and (Hocking et al., 2011). Although numerical algorithms like alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) and alternating minimization algorithm (AMA) have been proposed to solve convex clustering model (Chi & Lange, 2015), it is known to be very challenging to solve large-scale problems. In this paper, we propose a semismooth Newton based augmented Lagrangian method for large-scale convex clustering problems. Extensive numerical experiments on both simulated and real data demonstrate that our algorithm is highly efficient and robust for solving large-scale problems. Moreover, the numerical results also show the superior performance and scalability of our algorithm comparing to existing first-order methods.

paragraphs: Clustering methods such as K-means can be unstable because optimization can become trapped in local minima. Convex clustering offers a different formulation: the sum-of-norms model is a convex relaxation of hierarchical clustering. However, solving this model becomes computationally challenging as the problem grows, even with existing optimization algorithms.

The paper proposes an augmented Lagrangian method built around a semismooth Newton approach for large-scale convex clustering. Its contribution concerns how to solve the clustering optimization problem efficiently. The motivation is that a useful convex formulation also needs a practical solver if it is to handle large datasets.

Experiments on simulated and real data show that the proposed algorithm is efficient and robust on large problems. The reported numerical comparisons also favor it over existing first-order methods in performance and scalability. These findings support the method as a computational improvement for convex clustering; the abstract’s central result is about solving the model effectively, rather than a new criterion for judging the resulting clusters.
summary.tldr: A semismooth Newton augmented Lagrangian solver makes large-scale convex clustering more efficient in reported experiments.

title: An Efficient Semismooth Newton based Algorithm for Convex Clustering

abstract: Acquiring abilities in the absence of a task-oriented reward function is at the frontier of reinforcement learning research. This problem has been studied through the lens of empowerment, which draws a connection between option discovery and information theory. Information-theoretic skill discovery methods have garnered much interest from the community, but little research has been conducted in understanding their limitations. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, we show that existing algorithms suffer from a common limitation – they discover options that provide a poor coverage of the state space. In light of this, we propose Explore, Discover and Learn (EDL), an alternative approach to information-theoretic skill discovery. Crucially, EDL optimizes the same information-theoretic objective derived from the empowerment literature, but addresses the optimization problem using different machinery. We perform an extensive evaluation of skill discovery methods on controlled environments and show that EDL offers significant advantages, such as overcoming the coverage problem, reducing the dependence of learned skills on the initial state, and allowing the user to define a prior over which behaviors should be learned.

Through theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, we show that existing algorithms suffer from a common limitation – they discover options that provide a poor coverage of the state space. In light of this, we propose Explore, Discover and Learn (EDL), an alternative approach to information-theoretic skill discovery. Crucially, EDL optimizes the same information-theoretic objective derived from the empowerment literature, but addresses the optimization problem using different machinery. We perform an extensive evaluation of skill discovery methods on controlled environments and show that EDL offers significant advantages, such as overcoming the coverage problem, reducing the dependence of learned skills on the initial state, and allowing the user to define a prior over which behaviors should be learned.

paragraphs: This paper studies how reinforcement learning agents can acquire skills without a task-specific reward. Information-theoretic approaches to skill discovery connect this problem to empowerment, but the authors identify a recurring weakness: the learned options cover the state space poorly. Their theoretical analysis and experiments show that existing algorithms can leave much of the available state space outside their discovered behaviors.

Explore, Discover and Learn, or EDL, addresses this problem by changing how the optimization is performed. It retains the same information-theoretic objective used in the empowerment literature. This distinction is central: the paper shows that changing the machinery used to pursue an objective can address a limitation without replacing the objective itself.

In an extensive evaluation on controlled environments, EDL overcomes the observed coverage problem and reduces how strongly learned skills depend on the initial state. It also lets users specify a prior over desired behaviors. These results support a more controllable form of unsupervised skill discovery, where the learned abilities cover states more broadly and can reflect preferences about which behaviors should emerge.
summary.tldr: EDL changes the optimization of an existing information-theoretic skill objective to improve state coverage and control over learned behaviors.

title: Explore, Discover and Learn: Unsupervised Discovery of State-Covering Skills

abstract: Hypothesis testing of random networks is an emerging area of modern research, especially in the high-dimensional regime, where the number of samples is smaller or comparable to the size of the graph. In this paper we consider the goodness-of-fit testing problem for large inhomogeneous random (IER) graphs, where given a (known) reference symmetric matrix $Q \in [0, 1]^{n \times n}$ and $m$ independent samples from an IER graph given by an unknown symmetric matrix $P \in [0, 1]^{n \times n}$, the goal is to test the hypothesis $P=Q$ versus $||P-Q|| \geq \varepsilon$, where $||\cdot||$ is some specified norm on symmetric matrices. Building on recent related work on two-sample testing for IER graphs, we derive the optimal minimax sample complexities for the goodness-of-fit problem in various natural norms, such as the Frobenius norm and the operator norm. We also propose practical implementations of natural test statistics, using their asymptotic distributions and through the parametric bootstrap. We compare the performances of the different tests in simulations, and show that the proposed tests outperform the baseline tests across various natural random graphs models.

The reference is represented by a known symmetric matrix Q, while independent graph samples come from an unknown matrix P. The statistical task is to distinguish equality from a difference of at least a chosen size, measured using a matrix norm.

Simulations compare these procedures and report improvements over baseline tests across several random graph models. The work therefore connects fundamental detection requirements with implementable tests, while keeping the definition of a detectable difference explicit through the selected norm.
summary.tldr: The paper derives optimal sample requirements and practical tests for detecting departures from a known random-graph model.

title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests for Inhomogeneous Random Graphs

abstract: Solving large complex partial differential equations (PDEs), such as those that arise in computational fluid dynamics (CFD), is a computationally expensive process. This has motivated the use of deep learning approaches to approximate the PDE solutions, yet the simulation results predicted from these approaches typically do not generalize well to truly novel scenarios. In this work, we develop a hybrid (graph) neural network that combines a traditional graph convolutional network with an embedded differentiable fluid dynamics simulator inside the network itself. By combining an actual CFD simulator (run on a much coarser resolution representation of the problem) with the graph network, we show that we can both generalize well to new situations and benefit from the substantial speedup of neural network CFD predictions, while also substantially outperforming the coarse CFD simulation alone.

Neural networks offer faster approximations, but their predictions often transfer poorly to genuinely new scenarios. This paper addresses that tension by combining a learned predictor with an actual fluid simulator inside the same network.

To keep the simulation component economical, the simulator operates on a much coarser representation of the problem. The resulting predictor therefore incorporates a numerical simulation while retaining the graph network's role in producing the final fluid-flow prediction.

The authors report that this hybrid approach generalizes well to new situations and preserves substantial speed advantages associated with neural CFD prediction. It also substantially improves on the coarse simulator alone. These findings support the value of combining the two components: a coarse simulation supplies useful physical computation, while the learned component improves the prediction beyond what that inexpensive simulation achieves by itself.
summary.tldr: Embedding a coarse differentiable fluid simulator in a graph network improves prediction and generalization while retaining substantial speed benefits.

title: Combining Differentiable PDE Solvers and Graph Neural Networks for Fluid Flow Prediction

abstract: Posterior distribution approximation is a central task in Bayesian inference. Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) and its extensions have been practically used and theoretically studied. While SGLD updates a single particle at a time, ensemble methods that update multiple particles simultaneously have been recently gathering attention. Compared with the naive parallel-chain SGLD that updates multiple particles independently, ensemble methods update particles with their interactions. Thus, these methods are expected to be more particle-efficient than the naive parallel-chain SGLD because particles can be aware of other particles’ behavior through their interactions. Although ensemble methods numerically demonstrated their superior performance, no theoretical guarantee exists to assure such particle-efficiency and it is unclear whether those ensemble methods are really superior to the naive parallel-chain SGLD in the non-asymptotic settings. To cope with this problem, we propose a novel ensemble method that uses a non-reversible Markov chain for the interaction, and we present a non-asymptotic theoretical analysis for our method. Our analysis shows that, for the first time, the interaction causes a faster convergence rate than the naive parallel-chain SGLD in the non-asymptotic setting if the discretization error is appropriately controlled. Numerical experiments show that we can control the discretization error by tuning the interaction appropriately.

Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics updates a single particle, while ensemble approaches update multiple particles that can interact. Those interactions are intended to make the particles collectively more useful than independent parallel chains. Earlier numerical successes, however, had not established that this advantage holds over a finite run.

The paper proposes an ensemble sampler whose interactions use a non-reversible Markov chain. It then analyzes convergence in a non-asymptotic setting, meaning that the analysis addresses finite progress rather than only eventual behavior. The central result is that interactions can produce faster convergence than independent parallel-chain SGLD if discretization error is appropriately controlled.

That condition is central to the finding: the acceleration depends on managing the error introduced by discrete updates. Numerical experiments show that tuning the interaction can control this error. The paper thus supplies a conditional theoretical explanation for the usefulness of interacting particles, alongside experimental evidence that the required error control can be achieved through interaction tuning.
summary.tldr: Non-reversible particle interactions accelerate ensemble sampling over independent SGLD chains when discretization error is appropriately controlled.

title: Accelerating the diffusion-based ensemble sampling by non-reversible dynamics

abstract: Stochastic neural networks with discrete random variables are an important class of models for their expressiveness and interpretability. Since direct differentiation and backpropagation is not possible, Monte Carlo gradient estimation techniques are a popular alternative. Efficient stochastic gradient estimators, such Straight-Through and Gumbel-Softmax, work well for shallow stochastic models. Their performance, however, suffers with hierarchical, more complex models. We focus on stochastic networks with Boolean latent variables. To analyze such networks, we introduce the framework of harmonic analysis for Boolean functions to derive an analytic formulation for the bias and variance in the Straight-Through estimator. Exploiting these formulations, we propose \emph{FouST}, a low-bias and low-variance gradient estimation algorithm that is just as efficient. Extensive experiments show that FouST performs favorably compared to state-of-the-art biased estimators and is much faster than unbiased ones.

paragraphs: Neural networks with discrete random variables cannot be trained by directly differentiating through those variables in the usual way. Gradient estimators provide a workaround, but their accuracy and variability affect learning. This paper focuses on networks whose latent variables are Boolean, taking one of two possible values.

The authors use harmonic analysis of Boolean functions to derive analytic expressions for the bias and variance of the Straight-Through estimator. Bias concerns systematic error in the estimated gradient, while variance concerns how much estimates fluctuate. These expressions guide the design of FouST, an estimator intended to keep both quantities low while retaining the efficiency of Straight-Through estimation.

The motivation is especially relevant to hierarchical stochastic networks, where efficient estimators such as Straight-Through and Gumbel-Softmax can lose effectiveness. Extensive experiments report that FouST compares favorably with state-of-the-art biased estimators and is much faster than unbiased alternatives. The contribution links a mathematical diagnosis of gradient-estimation error to an efficient algorithm, with experimental support for the resulting trade-off.
summary.tldr: FouST uses an analysis of Boolean functions to build efficient gradient estimates with low bias and variance for stochastic networks.

title: Low Bias Low Variance Gradient Estimates for Boolean Stochastic Networks

abstract: Recovering a signal from its Fourier intensity underlies many important applications, including lensless imaging and imaging through scattering media. Conventional algorithms for retrieving the phase suffer when noise is present but display global convergence when given clean data. Neural networks have been used to improve algorithm robustness, but efforts to date are sensitive to initial conditions and give inconsistent performance. Here, we combine iterative methods from phase retrieval with image statistics from deep denoisers, via regularization-by-denoising. The resulting methods inherit the advantages of each approach and outperform other noise-robust phase retrieval algorithms. Our work paves the way for hybrid imaging methods that integrate machine-learned constraints in conventional algorithms.
