paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a signal from its Fourier intensity, a problem arising in lensless imaging and imaging through scattering media. The paper describes complementary strengths and weaknesses in existing approaches. Conventional iterative methods show global convergence with clean data but struggle with noise, while previous neural approaches improve robustness yet can depend strongly on initialization.

The authors combine iterative phase retrieval with image statistics supplied by deep denoisers. They integrate these components through regularization-by-denoising, allowing learned information about images to influence reconstruction within an iterative algorithm. This design brings a learned image constraint into a conventional reconstruction procedure, rather than treating the two approaches as separate alternatives.

The resulting methods are reported to inherit advantages from both approaches and outperform other noise-robust phase retrieval algorithms. The finding supports hybrid imaging systems that combine established iterative methods with machine-learned constraints. The abstract's clean-data global convergence statement describes conventional methods; its reported result for the hybrid methods emphasizes their combined advantages and improved noise-robust performance.
summary.tldr: Combining iterative phase retrieval with deep denoisers improves reconstruction performance in the presence of noise.

title: When deep denoising meets iterative phase retrieval

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are effective in generating realistic images but the training is often unstable. There are existing efforts that model the training dynamics of GANs in the parameter space but the analysis cannot directly motivate practically effective stabilizing methods. To this end, we present a conceptually novel perspective from control theory to directly model the dynamics of GANs in the frequency domain and provide simple yet effective methods to stabilize GAN’s training. We first analyze the training dynamic of a prototypical Dirac GAN and adopt the widely-used closed-loop control (CLC) to improve its stability. We then extend CLC to stabilize the training dynamic of normal GANs, which can be implemented as an L2 regularizer on the output of the discriminator. Empirical results show that our method can effectively stabilize the training and obtain state-of-the-art performance on data generation tasks.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can produce realistic images, but their training dynamics are often unstable. This paper approaches that instability through control theory. It models the dynamics in the frequency domain, seeking an analysis that directly suggests a practical intervention for stabilizing training.

The resulting intervention can be implemented as an L2 regularizer on the discriminator's output, translating the control-theoretic perspective into a simple change to the training objective.

Experiments show effective stabilization and state-of-the-art performance on the reported data-generation tasks. The contribution is the connection between an analysis of training dynamics and an implementable regularizer. The simplified GAN supplies the starting point for understanding stability, while the extension and experiments establish the method's practical relevance to broader GAN models. The empirical findings support the proposed intervention in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A control-theoretic analysis motivates an L2 penalty on discriminator outputs that stabilizes GAN training and improves reported generation performance.

title: Understanding and Stabilizing GANs’ Training Dynamics Using Control Theory

abstract: Quantifying the value of data is a fundamental problem in machine learning and has multiple important use cases: (1) building insights about the dataset and task, (2) domain adaptation, (3) corrupted sample discovery, and (4) robust learning. We propose Data Valuation using Reinforcement Learning (DVRL), to adaptively learn data values jointly with the predictor model. DVRL uses a data value estimator (DVE) to learn how likely each datum is used in training of the predictor model. DVE is trained using a reinforcement signal that reflects performance on the target task. We demonstrate that DVRL yields superior data value estimates compared to alternative methods across numerous datasets and application scenarios. The corrupted sample discovery performance of DVRL is close to optimal in many regimes (i.e. as if the noisy samples were known apriori), and for domain adaptation and robust learning DVRL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art by 14.6% and 10.8%, respectively.

This paper introduces Data Valuation using Reinforcement Learning, or DVRL, to estimate that usefulness while also training the predictor. The intended applications include understanding datasets, adapting between domains, identifying corrupted examples, and learning robustly from imperfect data.

A data value estimator learns the probability that each example will be used to train the predictor. Its feedback comes from a reinforcement signal reflecting performance on the target task. This ties the assigned values to what helps the prediction problem, and allows the estimator and predictor to develop together rather than treating valuation as a separate fixed preprocessing step.

Across the reported datasets and application settings, DVRL produces better value estimates than the compared alternatives. Corrupted-sample discovery is close to the reference of knowing the noisy samples in advance in many regimes. The abstract also reports improvements of 14.6% for domain adaptation and 10.8% for robust learning over the stated state-of-the-art comparisons.
summary.tldr: DVRL learns which training examples are useful through task-performance feedback, improving data valuation and several learning applications in the reported experiments.

title: Data Valuation using Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modeling distributions on Riemannian manifolds is a crucial component in understanding non-Euclidean data that arises, e.g., in physics and geology. The budding approaches in this space are limited by representational and computational tradeoffs. We propose and study a class of flows that uses convex potentials from Riemannian optimal transport. These are universal and can model distributions on any compact Riemannian manifold without requiring domain knowledge of the manifold to be integrated into the architecture. We demonstrate that these flows can model standard distributions on spheres, and tori, on synthetic and geological data.

paragraphs: Some data naturally live on curved spaces rather than ordinary flat coordinate spaces. Modeling probability distributions on these Riemannian manifolds is relevant to areas such as physics and geology. The paper addresses the representational and computational tradeoffs faced by emerging methods for learning distributions with this kind of geometry.

The authors propose a class of flows built from convex potentials in Riemannian optimal transport. They establish universality for distributions on any compact Riemannian manifold. The construction does not require manifold-specific domain knowledge to be embedded into the architecture, giving the same modeling approach a broad geometric scope. Compactness is part of the stated universality claim.

Demonstrations show that the flows can represent standard distributions on spheres and tori, using synthetic and geological data. These examples connect the general modeling framework to concrete curved spaces. The contribution combines a broad representational result with demonstrations on particular manifolds, offering a way to build distribution models around geometric transport principles.
summary.tldr: Flows built from Riemannian optimal-transport potentials universally model distributions on compact manifolds without manifold-specific architectural knowledge.

title: Riemannian Convex Potential Maps

abstract: Transformer architectures are widely used, but training them is non-trivial, requiring custom learning rate schedules, scaling terms, residual connections, careful placement of submodules such as normalization, and so on. In this paper, we improve upon recent analysis of Transformers and formalize a notion of sensitivity to capture the difficulty of training. Sensitivity characterizes how the variance of activation and gradient norms change in expectation when parameters are randomly perturbed. We analyze the sensitivity of previous Transformer architectures and design a new architecture, the Catformer, which replaces residual connections or RNN-based gating mechanisms with concatenation. We prove that Catformers are less sensitive than other Transformer variants and demonstrate that this leads to more stable training. On DMLab30, a suite of high-dimension reinforcement tasks, Catformer outperforms other transformers, including Gated Transformer-XL—the state-of-the-art architecture designed to address stability—by 13%.

This paper develops a sensitivity measure to make part of that training difficulty mathematically explicit. It examines how random parameter perturbations change the variance of activation and gradient norms in expectation.

The authors analyze existing Transformer architectures through this measure and use the results to design Catformer. Its central architectural change replaces residual connections or recurrent gating mechanisms with concatenation. They prove that Catformers have lower sensitivity than the Transformer variants they analyze, providing a theoretical basis for the design.

The contribution links a defined mathematical property to an architectural modification and an observed training benefit, giving a concrete route from sensitivity analysis to improved performance in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Catformer uses concatenation to reduce Transformer sensitivity, yielding more stable training and improved DMLab30 performance.

title: Catformer: Designing Stable Transformers via Sensitivity Analysis

abstract: We consider training models with differential privacy (DP) using mini-batch gradients. The existing state-of-the-art, Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), requires \emph{privacy amplification by sampling or shuffling} to obtain the best privacy/accuracy/computation trade-offs. Unfortunately, the precise requirements on exact sampling and shuffling can be hard to obtain in important practical scenarios, particularly federated learning (FL). We design and analyze a DP variant of Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (DP-FTRL) that compares favorably (both theoretically and empirically) to amplified DP-SGD, while allowing for much more flexible data access patterns. DP-FTRL does not use any form of privacy amplification.
originalAbstract: We consider training models with differential privacy (DP) using mini-batch gradients. The existing state-of-the-art, Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), requires \emph{privacy amplification by sampling or shuffling} to obtain the best privacy/accuracy/computation trade-offs. Unfortunately, the precise requirements on exact sampling and shuffling can be hard to obtain in important practical scenarios, particularly federated learning (FL). We design and analyze a DP variant of Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (DP-FTRL) that compares favorably (both theoretically and empirically) to amplified DP-SGD, while allowing for much more flexible data access patterns. DP-FTRL does not use any form of privacy amplification.

paragraphs: The paper studies differentially private model training with mini-batch gradients. DP-SGD obtains its strongest privacy, accuracy, and computation trade-offs through privacy amplification from sampling or shuffling. Those benefits rely on precise requirements for data access, which can be difficult to satisfy in practical systems, particularly in federated learning.

The authors design and analyze a private version of Follow-The-Regularized-Leader, called DP-FTRL. Its central distinction is that it uses no privacy amplification. This allows substantially more flexible patterns of access to training data while still providing differential privacy, reducing dependence on exact sampling or shuffling procedures.

The paper reports that DP-FTRL compares favorably with amplified DP-SGD in both theory and experiments. This makes the contribution relevant to the design of the training system as well as the optimizer: privacy guarantees and useful trade-offs can be pursued with fewer restrictions on data access. The stated result is a favorable comparison, rather than a claim that DP-FTRL dominates every possible DP-SGD configuration.
summary.tldr: DP-FTRL provides private training without privacy amplification and compares favorably with amplified DP-SGD while permitting more flexible data access.

title: Practical and Private (Deep) Learning Without Sampling or Shuffling

abstract: We study the stochastic Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem with random delays in the feedback received by the algorithm. We consider two settings: the {\it reward dependent} delay setting, where realized delays may depend on the stochastic rewards, and the {\it reward-independent} delay setting. Our main contribution is algorithms that achieve near-optimal regret in each of the settings, with an additional additive dependence on the quantiles of the delay distribution. Our results do not make any assumptions on the delay distributions: in particular, we do not assume they come from any parametric family of distributions and allow for unbounded support and expectation; we further allow for the case of infinite delays where the algorithm might occasionally not observe any feedback.

We consider two settings: the {\it reward dependent} delay setting, where realized delays may depend on the stochastic rewards, and the {\it reward-independent} delay setting. Our main contribution is algorithms that achieve near-optimal regret in each of the settings, with an additional additive dependence on the quantiles of the delay distribution. Our results do not make any assumptions on the delay distributions: in particular, we do not assume they come from any parametric family of distributions and allow for unbounded support and expectation; we further allow for the case of infinite delays where the algorithm might occasionally not observe any feedback.

paragraphs: In bandit learning, an algorithm chooses actions and uses their rewards to improve future choices. This paper studies the case where feedback arrives after random delays. It separates two settings: delays that may depend on the realized reward, and delays that are independent of rewards. That distinction is part of the problem the algorithms must accommodate.

The authors provide algorithms with near-optimal regret in both settings. Their guarantees include an additional additive dependence on quantiles of the delay distribution. Quantiles describe how long particular fractions of feedback take to arrive, allowing delay effects to be expressed without requiring a finite average waiting time.

The analysis imposes no distributional assumptions on the delays. It permits distributions outside any specified parametric family, unbounded support, and unbounded expectation. It also allows infinite delays, so some feedback may never be observed. The contribution is therefore a regret analysis and algorithmic treatment that accommodates exceptionally broad feedback timing behavior, while still explicitly accounting for its cost.
summary.tldr: These bandit algorithms achieve near-optimal regret with quantile-based delay costs, allowing arbitrary delay distributions and occasionally missing feedback.

title: Stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits with Unrestricted Delay Distributions

abstract: Landmark codes underpin reliable physical layer communication, e.g., Reed-Muller, BCH, Convolution, Turbo, LDPC, and Polar codes: each is a linear code and represents a mathematical breakthrough. The impact on humanity is huge: each of these codes has been used in global wireless communication standards (satellite, WiFi, cellular). Reliability of communication over the classical additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel enables benchmarking and ranking of the different codes. In this paper, we construct KO codes, a computationally efficient family of deep-learning driven (encoder, decoder) pairs that outperform the state-of-the-art reliability performance on the standardized AWGN channel. KO codes beat state-of-the-art Reed-Muller and Polar codes, under the low-complexity successive cancellation decoding, in the challenging short-to-medium block length regime on the AWGN channel. We show that the gains of KO codes are primarily due to the nonlinear mapping of information bits directly to transmit symbols (bypassing modulation) and yet possess an efficient, high-performance decoder. The key technical innovation that renders this possible is design of a novel family of neural architectures inspired by the computation tree of the {\bf K}ronecker {\bf O}peration (KO) central to Reed-Muller and Polar codes. These architectures pave way for the discovery of a much richer class of hitherto unexplored nonlinear algebraic structures.

In this paper, we construct KO codes, a computationally efficient family of deep-learning driven (encoder, decoder) pairs that outperform the state-of-the-art reliability performance on the standardized AWGN channel. We show that the gains of KO codes are primarily due to the nonlinear mapping of information bits directly to transmit symbols (bypassing modulation) and yet possess an efficient, high-performance decoder. The key technical innovation that renders this possible is design of a novel family of neural architectures inspired by the computation tree of the {\bf K}ronecker {\bf O}peration (KO) central to Reed-Muller and Polar codes. These architectures pave way for the discovery of a much richer class of hitherto unexplored nonlinear algebraic structures.

paragraphs: Reliable wireless communication depends on encoding information so that a decoder can recover it after noise corrupts transmission. This paper introduces KO codes, a family of learned encoder and decoder pairs. Their goal is to improve reliability while retaining computational efficiency, with evaluation on the standard additive white Gaussian noise channel.

The neural architectures are inspired by the computation tree of the Kronecker operation used in Reed-Muller and Polar codes. The authors attribute the gains primarily to a nonlinear mapping from information bits directly to transmitted symbols, bypassing a separate modulation step. The architecture also provides an efficient decoder, making decoding performance part of the design.

In the short-to-medium block length regime, KO codes outperform the compared Reed-Muller and Polar codes using low-complexity successive cancellation decoding on that channel. This is a result within the stated channel and decoding comparison. More broadly, the construction points toward exploring richer nonlinear coding structures while preserving an efficient way to recover the transmitted information.
summary.tldr: KO codes learn efficient nonlinear encoders and decoders that improve reliability over the stated Reed-Muller and Polar comparisons on the AWGN channel.

title: KO codes: inventing nonlinear encoding and decoding for reliable wireless communication via deep-learning

abstract: In this work, we propose TimeGrad, an autoregressive model for multivariate probabilistic time series forecasting which samples from the data distribution at each time step by estimating its gradient. To this end, we use diffusion probabilistic models, a class of latent variable models closely connected to score matching and energy-based methods. Our model learns gradients by optimizing a variational bound on the data likelihood and at inference time converts white noise into a sample of the distribution of interest through a Markov chain using Langevin sampling. We demonstrate experimentally that the proposed autoregressive denoising diffusion model is the new state-of-the-art multivariate probabilistic forecasting method on real-world data sets with thousands of correlated dimensions. We hope that this method is a useful tool for practitioners and lays the foundation for future research in this area.

This paper introduces TimeGrad, an autoregressive forecasting model that generates samples at successive time steps. Its target is a distribution of outcomes across multiple variables, allowing forecasts to express more than a single predicted future.

TimeGrad uses diffusion probabilistic models to learn the gradient information needed for sampling. Training optimizes a variational bound on the likelihood of the data. At prediction time, the model starts with white noise and uses a Markov chain with Langevin sampling to transform that noise into a sample from the distribution of interest.

This connects sequential forecasting with a generative procedure that builds samples through repeated updates. The authors report state-of-the-art multivariate probabilistic forecasting results in experiments on real-world datasets containing thousands of correlated dimensions. Those results support the usefulness of the approach for the evaluated high-dimensional forecasting problems, while the proposed combination provides a direction for further research into diffusion-based time series models.
summary.tldr: TimeGrad uses autoregressive diffusion sampling to produce probabilistic forecasts and reports state-of-the-art results on high-dimensional real-world time series.

title: Autoregressive Denoising Diffusion Models for Multivariate Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting

abstract: We study online learning with bandit feedback (i.e. learner has access to only zeroth-order oracle) where cost/reward functions $\f_t$ admit a "pseudo-1d" structure, i.e. $\f_t(\w) = \loss_t(\pred_t(\w))$ where the output of $\pred_t$ is one-dimensional. At each round, the learner observes context $\x_t$, plays prediction $\pred_t(\w_t; \x_t)$ (e.g. $\pred_t(\cdot)=⟨\x_t, \cdot⟩$) for some $\w_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and observes loss $\loss_t(\pred_t(\w_t))$ where $\loss_t$ is a convex Lipschitz-continuous function. The goal is to minimize the standard regret metric. This pseudo-1d bandit convex optimization problem (\SBCO) arises frequently in domains such as online decision-making or parameter-tuning in large systems. For this problem, we first show a regret lower bound of $\min(\sqrt{dT}, T^{3/4})$ for any algorithm, where $T$ is the number of rounds. We propose a new algorithm \sbcalg that combines randomized online gradient descent with a kernelized exponential weights method to exploit the pseudo-1d structure effectively, guaranteeing the {\em optimal} regret bound mentioned above, up to additional logarithmic factors. In contrast, applying state-of-the-art online convex optimization methods leads to $\tilde{O}\left(\min\left(d^{9.5}\sqrt{T},\sqrt{d}T^{3/4}\right)\right)$ regret, that is significantly suboptimal in terms of $d$.

title: Optimal regret algorithm for Pseudo-1d Bandit Convex Optimization

abstract: Investigating active learning, we focus on the relation between the number of labeled examples (budget size), and suitable querying strategies. Our theoretical analysis shows a behavior reminiscent of phase transition: typical examples are best queried when the budget is low, while unrepresentative examples are best queried when the budget is large. Combined evidence shows that a similar phenomenon occurs in common classification models. Accordingly, we propose TypiClust – a deep active learning strategy suited for low budgets. In a comparative empirical investigation of supervised learning, using a variety of architectures and image datasets, TypiClust outperforms all other active learning strategies in the low-budget regime. Using TypiClust in the semi-supervised framework, performance gets an even more significant boost. In particular, state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods trained on CIFAR-10 with 10 labeled examples selected by TypiClust, reach 93.2% accuracy – an improvement of 39.4% over random selection. Code is available at https://github.com/avihu111/TypiClust.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples should receive labels. This paper asks how that choice should change with the labeling budget. Its theoretical analysis identifies a transition: representative examples are preferable when labels are scarce, whereas less representative examples become preferable when the budget is large. Combined evidence suggests a similar pattern in common classification models.

The authors turn this finding into TypiClust, a deep active learning strategy designed for small budgets. The central idea is that selecting useful examples depends on how much labeled information the learner already has. A strategy that works well after many labels have been collected may therefore be poorly suited to the beginning of learning.

In supervised experiments across image datasets and architectures, TypiClust outperforms the other strategies tested in the low-budget setting. Its gains are larger when combined with semi-supervised learning. On CIFAR-10, semi-supervised methods using ten TypiClust-selected labels reach 93.2% accuracy. These findings support choosing an acquisition strategy with the available budget explicitly in mind.
summary.tldr: TypiClust exploits the finding that representative examples are especially valuable when an active learner has very few labels.

title: Active Learning on a Budget: Opposite Strategies Suit High and Low Budgets

abstract: Differentially private (DP) stochastic convex optimization (SCO) is ubiquitous in trustworthy machine learning algorithm design. This paper studies the DP-SCO problem with streaming data sampled from a distribution and arrives sequentially. We also consider the continual release model where parameters related to private information are updated and released upon each new data. Numerous algorithms have been developed to achieve optimal excess risks in different $\ell_p$ norm geometries, but none of the existing ones can be adapted to the streaming and continual release setting. We propose a private variant of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm with recursive gradients for variance reduction to update and reveal the parameters upon each data. Combined with the adaptive DP analysis, our algorithm achieves the first optimal excess risk in linear time in the case $1<p\leq 2$ and the state-of-the-art excess risk meeting the non-private lower ones when $2<p\leq \infty$. Our algorithm can also be extended to the case $p=1$ to achieve nearly dimension-independent excess risk. While previous variance reduction results on recursive gradient have theoretical guarantee only in the i.i.d. setting, we establish such a guarantee in a non-stationary setting. To demonstrate the virtues of our method, we design the first DP algorithm for high-dimensional generalized linear bandits with logarithmic regret.

Repeated release makes privacy part of the ongoing learning process. The authors address different norm geometries, where the geometry affects the achievable excess risk, or gap from the best objective value.

Together, these results connect private continual parameter release with efficient optimization and sequential decision-making.
summary.tldr: A private streaming Frank-Wolfe method provides strong excess-risk guarantees under continual release and supports bandit learning with logarithmic regret.

title: Private Streaming SCO in $\ell_p$ geometry with Applications in High Dimensional Online Decision Making

abstract: Active learning is a label-efficient approach to train highly effective models while interactively selecting only small subsets of unlabelled data for labelling and training. In “open world" settings, the classes of interest can make up a small fraction of the overall dataset – most of the data may be viewed as an out-of-distribution or irrelevant class. This leads to extreme class-imbalance, and our theory and methods focus on this core issue. We propose a new strategy for active learning called GALAXY (Graph-based Active Learning At the eXtrEme), which blends ideas from graph-based active learning and deep learning. GALAXY automatically and adaptively selects more class-balanced examples for labeling than most other methods for active learning. Our theory shows that GALAXY performs a refined form of uncertainty sampling that gathers a much more class-balanced dataset than vanilla uncertainty sampling. Experimentally, we demonstrate GALAXY’s superiority over existing state-of-art deep active learning algorithms in unbalanced vision classification settings generated from popular datasets.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive labels, aiming to train an effective model with limited annotation. This becomes difficult in open-world settings where the classes of interest occupy only a small fraction of the data. Most examples may belong to an irrelevant or out-of-distribution class, creating extreme imbalance in the available pool.

GALAXY combines graph-based active learning with deep learning to address that imbalance. It adaptively selects examples that produce a more balanced labeled collection than most competing active-learning methods. The theoretical analysis describes the approach as a refined form of uncertainty sampling and shows that it gathers a substantially more class-balanced dataset than ordinary uncertainty sampling.

Experiments on imbalanced vision-classification settings constructed from popular datasets show advantages over existing leading deep active-learning algorithms. The practical contribution is a selection strategy that accounts for the difficulty of finding relevant classes within a heavily imbalanced pool. Its theoretical and empirical results connect better selection balance with effective learning in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: GALAXY uses graph-based selection to gather more class-balanced labels and improve active learning under extreme class imbalance.

title: GALAXY: Graph-based Active Learning at the Extreme

abstract: We introduce fast algorithms for correlation clustering with respect to the Min Max objective that provide constant factor approximations on complete graphs. Our algorithms are the first purely combinatorial approximation algorithms for this problem. We construct a novel semi-metric on the set of vertices, which we call the correlation metric, that indicates to our clustering algorithms whether pairs of nodes should be in the same cluster. The paper demonstrates empirically that, compared to prior work, our algorithms sacrifice little in the objective quality to obtain significantly better run-time. Moreover, our algorithms scale to larger networks that are effectively intractable for known algorithms.

The paper demonstrates empirically that, compared to prior work, our algorithms sacrifice little in the objective quality to obtain significantly better run-time. paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups vertices using information about which pairs should belong together. This paper studies its Min Max objective and develops fast algorithms for complete graphs. The goal is to obtain clusterings with a formal quality guarantee while reducing the computational burden that prevents existing approaches from handling larger networks.

The central construction is a new semi-metric called the correlation metric. It assigns pairwise information that guides the clustering algorithms toward deciding whether two vertices should share a cluster. The authors use this construction to obtain constant-factor approximation guarantees and describe their methods as the first purely combinatorial approximation algorithms for this problem.

The empirical results show a favorable tradeoff: relative to prior work, the algorithms give up little objective quality while achieving substantially shorter running times. They also handle larger networks that known algorithms find effectively intractable. The theoretical guarantee is stated for complete graphs, while the experiments establish the practical speed and quality tradeoff. Together, these contributions make approximate solutions more accessible at network sizes that were previously difficult to process.
summary.tldr: A new correlation metric enables fast combinatorial constant-factor approximations for Min Max correlation clustering on complete graphs.

title: Fast Combinatorial Algorithms for Min Max Correlation Clustering

abstract: Random forests and, more generally, (decision-)tree ensembles are widely used methods for classification and regression. Recent algorithmic advances allow to compute decision trees that are optimal for various measures such as their size or depth. We are not aware of such research for tree ensembles and aim to contribute to this area. Mainly, we provide two novel algorithms and corresponding lower bounds. First, we are able to carry over and substantially improve on tractability results for decision trees, obtaining a $(6\delta D S)^S \cdot \mathrm{poly}$-time algorithm, where $S$ is the number of cuts in the tree ensemble, $D$ the largest domain size, and $\delta$ is the largest number of features in which two examples differ. To achieve this, we introduce the witness-tree technique which also seems promising for practice. Second, we show that dynamic programming, which has been successful for decision trees, may also be viable for tree ensembles, providing an $\ell^n \cdot \mathrm{poly}$-time algorithm, where $\ell$ is the number of trees and $n$ the number of examples. Finally, we compare the number of cuts necessary to classify training data sets for decision trees and tree ensembles, showing that ensembles may need exponentially fewer cuts for increasing number of trees.

paragraphs: Decision-tree ensembles are widely used, but finding an ensemble that is optimal for a specified criterion poses an algorithmic challenge. This paper develops exact algorithms and corresponding lower bounds for that problem. It extends work on optimal individual trees to collections of trees, where the interaction among multiple trees changes the search.

The first algorithm uses a new witness-tree technique. Its running time depends exponentially on the total number of cuts, with additional dependence on the largest feature-domain size and the maximum number of features distinguishing two examples. The second algorithm uses dynamic programming, with an exponential term given by the number of trees raised to the number of examples. These dependencies clarify which problem dimensions govern computational difficulty.

The authors also compare the number of cuts required to classify training data using one tree versus an ensemble. They show that ensembles can require exponentially fewer cuts as the number of trees increases. This establishes a possible representational advantage, alongside algorithms for searching for optimal ensembles; it does not imply that every dataset benefits equally.
summary.tldr: Two exact algorithms clarify the complexity of optimal tree ensembles, which can classify some datasets with exponentially fewer cuts than individual trees.

title: On Computing Optimal Tree Ensembles

abstract: We study the SAM (Sharpness-Aware Minimization) optimizer which has recently attracted a lot of interest due to its increased performance over more classical variants of stochastic gradient descent. Our main contribution is the derivation of continuous-time models (in the form of SDEs) for SAM and two of its variants, both for the full-batch and mini-batch settings. We demonstrate that these SDEs are rigorous approximations of the real discrete-time algorithms (in a weak sense, scaling linearly with the learning rate). Using these models, we then offer an explanation of why SAM prefers flat minima over sharp ones – by showing that it minimizes an implicitly regularized loss with a Hessian-dependent noise structure. Finally, we prove that SAM is attracted to saddle points under some realistic conditions. Our theoretical results are supported by detailed experiments.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, has attracted interest because of its performance relative to more conventional stochastic gradient methods. This paper develops continuous-time mathematical models of SAM and two variants. The models take the form of stochastic differential equations and cover both full-batch and mini-batch training.

The authors establish that these models approximate the discrete algorithms rigorously in a weak sense, with approximation error scaling linearly with the learning rate. This supplies a basis for studying the optimizer through continuous dynamics. Using that description, they explain SAM’s preference for flat minima through an implicitly regularized loss together with noise whose structure depends on the Hessian.

The analysis also reveals a less straightforward behavior: SAM can be attracted to saddle points under certain realistic conditions. This is a conditional theoretical finding, not a claim that every SAM run will approach a saddle. Detailed experiments support the theoretical results. Together, the findings clarify both the mechanism behind the optimizer’s preference for flatter solutions and a possible complication in its dynamics.
summary.tldr: Continuous-time models explain SAM’s preference for flat minima and show that it can also be attracted to saddle points under stated conditions.

title: An SDE for Modeling SAM: Theory and Insights

abstract: Representational drift refers to over-time changes in neural activation accompanied by a stable task performance. Despite being observed in the brain and in artificial networks, the mechanisms of drift and its implications are not fully understood. Motivated by recent experimental findings of stimulus-dependent drift in the piriform cortex, we use theory and simulations to study this phenomenon in a two-layer linear feedforward network. Specifically, in a continual online learning scenario, we study the drift induced by the noise inherent in the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). By decomposing the learning dynamics into the normal and tangent spaces of the minimum-loss manifold, we show the former corresponds to a finite variance fluctuation, while the latter could be considered as an effective diffusion process on the manifold. We analytically compute the fluctuation and the diffusion coefficients for the stimuli representations in the hidden layer as functions of network parameters and input distribution. Further, consistent with experiments, we show that the drift rate is slower for a more frequently presented stimulus. Overall, our analysis yields a theoretical framework for better understanding of the drift phenomenon in biological and artificial neural networks.

paragraphs: Representational drift occurs when a network’s internal activations change over time while its task performance remains stable. This paper investigates how noise from stochastic gradient descent can produce that behavior. The authors use theory and simulations in a two-layer linear feedforward network undergoing continual online learning, motivated by experimental observations of stimulus-dependent drift in the brain.

They separate learning dynamics into motion perpendicular to and along the set of minimum-loss solutions. Perpendicular motion produces fluctuations with finite variance. Motion along the set can be viewed as an effective diffusion process, allowing internal representations to move while remaining associated with minimum-loss solutions. This decomposition distinguishes two effects of the same noisy learning dynamics.

The authors analytically calculate fluctuation and diffusion coefficients for hidden-layer stimulus representations as functions of network parameters and the input distribution. They also find slower drift for stimuli presented more frequently, consistent with the motivating experiments. The result provides a theoretical mechanism for stable performance alongside changing representations within the studied linear network.
summary.tldr: In a two-layer linear network, SGD noise produces representational diffusion, with more frequently presented stimuli drifting more slowly.

title: Stochastic Gradient Descent-Induced Drift of Representation in a Two-Layer Neural Network

abstract: Sampling diverse programs from a code language model and reranking with model likelihood is a popular method for code generation but it is prone to preferring degenerate solutions. Inspired by collaborative programming, we propose Coder-Reviewer reranking. We augment Coder language models from past work, which generate programs given language instructions, with Reviewer models, which evaluate the likelihood of the instruction given the generated programs. We perform an extensive study across six datasets with eight models from three model families. Experimental results show that Coder-Reviewer reranking leads to consistent and significant improvement (up to 17% absolute accuracy gain) over reranking with the Coder model only. When combined with executability filtering, Coder-Reviewer reranking can often outperform the minimum Bayes risk method. Coder-Reviewer reranking is easy to implement by prompting, can generalize to different programming languages, and works well with off-the-shelf hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Code generation systems can sample several candidate programs and rank them using the probability assigned by a language model. However, that ranking can favor degenerate solutions. This paper introduces Coder-Reviewer reranking, which evaluates candidates from two directions to improve the choice among programs that have already been generated.

The Coder scores a program given the user’s instruction. The Reviewer evaluates how likely that instruction is given the program. Combining these perspectives adds a check on whether a candidate program supports the requested description. The approach can be implemented through prompting, works across programming languages, and performs well with readily available hyperparameter settings.

The evaluation covers six datasets and eight models from three model families. The authors report consistent, significant improvements over ranking with the Coder alone, reaching an absolute accuracy gain of up to 17%. When paired with filtering for executability, the approach often outperforms minimum Bayes risk reranking. These findings support using the reverse instruction-given-program score as a useful complement to the usual generation score.
summary.tldr: Ranking generated programs with both code-given-instruction and instruction-given-code scores improves code selection in the reported experiments.

title: Coder Reviewer Reranking for Code Generation

abstract: Vision-language representation learning models (e.g., CLIP) have achieved state-of-the-art performance on various downstream tasks, which usually need large-scale training data to learn discriminative representation. Recent progress on generative diffusion models (e.g., DALL-E 2) has demonstrated that diverse high-quality samples can be synthesized by randomly sampling from generative distribution. By virtue of generative capability in this paper, we propose a novel vision-language Representation Learning method with diffusion-based Embedding Generation (RLEG), which exploits diffusion models to generate feature embedding online for learning effective vision-language representation. Specifically, we first adopt image and text encoders to extract the corresponding embeddings. Secondly, pretrained diffusion-based embedding generators are harnessed to transfer the embedding modality online between vision and language domains. The embeddings generated from the generators are then served as augmented embedding-level samples, which are applied to contrastive learning with the variant of the CLIP framework. Experimental results show that the proposed method could learn effective representation and achieve state-of-the-art performance on various tasks including image classification, image-text retrieval, object detection, semantic segmentation, and text-conditional image generation.

By virtue of generative capability in this paper, we propose a novel vision-language Representation Learning method with diffusion-based Embedding Generation (RLEG), which exploits diffusion models to generate feature embedding online for learning effective vision-language representation. Specifically, we first adopt image and text encoders to extract the corresponding embeddings. Experimental results show that the proposed method could learn effective representation and achieve state-of-the-art performance on various tasks including image classification, image-text retrieval, object detection, semantic segmentation, and text-conditional image generation.

paragraphs: Vision-language models learn representations that connect images with text, typically using large training collections. Its augmentation operates on feature embeddings, the numerical representations produced by image and text encoders.

The method first extracts embeddings for both modalities. Pretrained diffusion-based generators then transfer embeddings between the visual and language domains during training. The generated embeddings become additional samples for contrastive learning within a modified CLIP framework. Generation is therefore integrated into representation learning as an ongoing source of augmented feature-level examples.

The breadth of the evaluated tasks suggests that the learned features are useful for several kinds of visual and multimodal prediction. summary.tldr: RLEG generates cross-modal feature embeddings with diffusion models and uses them as training augmentations for vision-language representation learning.

title: RLEG: Vision-Language Representation Learning with Diffusion-based Embedding Generation

abstract: In the field of Structure-based Drug Design (SBDD), deep learning-based generative models have achieved outstanding performance in terms of docking score. However, further study shows that the existing molecular generative methods and docking scores both have lacked consideration in terms of specificity, which means that generated molecules bind to almost every protein pocket with high affinity. To address this, we introduce the Delta Score, a new metric for evaluating the specificity of molecular binding. To further incorporate this insight for generation, we develop an innovative energy-guided approach using contrastive learning, with active compounds as decoys, to direct generative models toward creating molecules with high specificity. Our empirical results show that this method not only enhances the delta score but also maintains or improves traditional docking scores, successfully bridging the gap between SBDD and real-world needs.

paragraphs: A generated molecule can receive a favorable docking score for a protein pocket without being selective about that pocket. The paper identifies this as a weakness in existing structure-based molecular generation: generated molecules may also score well against many other pockets. Strong apparent binding alone therefore does not capture the specificity the authors want to evaluate.

They introduce Delta Score as a metric for molecular binding specificity. To make specificity influence generation as well as evaluation, they develop an energy-guided approach based on contrastive learning, using active compounds as decoys. This guidance directs the generative model toward molecules with stronger specificity.

Empirical results show improvements in Delta Score while traditional docking scores are maintained or improved. The two results together matter because the method improves the proposed specificity measure without requiring a reported sacrifice in the conventional scoring objective. The findings support adding specificity to both the evaluation and generation process, with the stated evidence expressed through these molecular scoring outcomes.
summary.tldr: Delta Score and contrastive energy guidance improve generated molecules’ measured binding specificity while maintaining or improving docking scores.

title: Rethinking Specificity in SBDD: Leveraging Delta Score and Energy-Guided Diffusion

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human intentions has become a critical task for safely deploying models in real-world systems. While existing alignment approaches have seen empirical success, theoretically understanding how these methods affect model behavior remains an open question. Our work provides an initial attempt to theoretically analyze the learning dynamics of human preference alignment. We formally show how the distribution of preference datasets influences the rate of model updates and provide rigorous guarantees on the training accuracy. Our theory also reveals an intricate phenomenon where the optimization is prone to prioritizing certain behaviors with higher preference distinguishability. We empirically validate our findings on contemporary LLMs and alignment tasks, reinforcing our theoretical insights and shedding light on considerations for future alignment approaches. paragraphs: Training language models with human preferences can change their behavior, but understanding how those changes unfold remains a theoretical challenge. This paper offers an initial analysis of alignment learning dynamics. It focuses on how the distribution of examples in a preference dataset affects the model's updates during training.

The authors formally connect that data distribution to the rate of model updates and establish guarantees on training accuracy. Their theory also identifies a tendency for optimization to favor behaviors whose preferences are more distinguishable. This means the ease of distinguishing preferred behavior can influence what training prioritizes, making the composition of preference data relevant to the learning process itself.

Experiments on contemporary language models and alignment tasks support the theoretical findings. The contribution links empirical alignment behavior to a mathematical account of update rates and uneven prioritization. Its accuracy guarantees concern training, while the broader insight is that different behaviors can receive different emphasis during optimization because of how clearly their preferences are expressed in the data.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how preference-data distributions shape alignment updates and can favor behaviors with more distinguishable preferences.

title: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Alignment with Human Feedback

abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) can solve many challenging sequential decision making problems, achieving zero-shot transfer across related tasks remains a challenge. The difficulty lies in finding a good representation for the current task so that the agent understands how it relates to previously seen tasks. To achieve zero-shot transfer, we introduce the function encoder, a representation learning algorithm which represents a function as a weighted combination of learned, non-linear basis functions. By using a function encoder to represent the reward function or the transition function, the agent has information on how the current task relates to previously seen tasks via a coherent vector representation. Thus, the agent is able to achieve transfer between related tasks at run time with no additional training. We demonstrate state-of-the-art data efficiency, asymptotic performance, and training stability in three RL fields by augmenting basic RL algorithms with a function encoder task representation.

That common representation gives the agent information about relationships among tasks, supporting reuse of what it has already learned.

The authors augment basic reinforcement-learning algorithms with these function-encoder task representations. Across three reinforcement-learning fields, they report state-of-the-art data efficiency, asymptotic performance, and training stability. The contribution centers on representing task-defining functions: encoding rewards or dynamics in a shared learned basis enables the reported zero-shot transfer between related tasks without further training at run time.
summary.tldr: Function encoders represent rewards or dynamics in a learned basis to enable transfer between related reinforcement-learning tasks without additional training.

title: Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning via Function Encoders

abstract: Non-convex minimization problems are universally considered hard, and even guaranteeing that a computed solution is locally minimizing is known to be NP-hard. In this general context, our paper focuses on the problem of finding stationary points that satisfy an approximate second-order optimality condition, which serves to exclude strict saddles and other non-minimizing stationary points. Our main result is that the problem of finding approximate second-order stationary points (SOSPs) is PLS-complete, i.e., of the same complexity as the problem of finding first-order stationary points (FOSPs), thus resolving an open question in the field. In particular, our results imply that, under the widely believed complexity conjecture that PLS $\neq$ FNP, finding approximate SOSPs in unconstrained domains is easier than in constrained domains, which is known to be NP-hard. This comes in stark contrast with earlier results which implied that, unless PLS = CLS, finding approximate FOSPs in unconstrained domains is harder than in constrained domains.

paragraphs: For a nonconvex objective, reaching a point with a small gradient does not establish that the point is locally minimizing. Second-order conditions add information about curvature and help rule out strict saddles and other non-minimizing stationary points. This paper asks how computationally difficult it is to find points satisfying approximate second-order conditions.

The main result classifies the problem as PLS-complete, placing it in the same complexity class as finding approximate first-order stationary points. This resolves the question of whether imposing the second-order requirement changes that complexity classification. It does not imply that checking these conditions guarantees a local minimum, a stronger task already known to be NP-hard.

The result also reveals an unusual distinction between constrained and unconstrained domains. Under the conjecture that PLS differs from FNP, finding approximate second-order stationary points is easier in unconstrained domains than in constrained ones. Earlier first-order results give the opposite comparison unless PLS equals CLS. These conditional contrasts show that adding constraints can affect first-order and second-order search problems differently.
summary.tldr: Finding approximate second-order stationary points is PLS-complete, matching first-order search and revealing a conditional complexity contrast between constrained and unconstrained domains.

title: The Computational Complexity of Finding Second-Order Stationary Points

abstract: Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures represent images as collections of high-dimensional vectorized tokens, each corresponding to a rectangular non-overlapping patch. This representation trades spatial granularity for embedding dimensionality, and results in semantically rich but spatially coarsely quantized feature maps. In order to retrieve spatial details beneficial to fine-grained inference tasks we propose a training-free method inspired by "stochastic resonance." Specifically, we perform sub-token spatial transformations to the input data, and aggregate the resulting ViT features after applying the inverse transformation. The resulting "Stochastic Resonance Transformer" (SRT) retains the rich semantic information of the original representation, but grounds it on a finer-scale spatial domain, partly mitigating the coarse effect of spatial tokenization. SRT is applicable across any layer of any ViT architecture, consistently boosting performance on several tasks including segmentation, classification, depth estimation, and others by up to 14.9% without the need for any fine-tuning. Code: https://github.com/donglao/srt.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers represent images using tokens corresponding to nonoverlapping rectangular patches. Those tokens can carry rich semantic information, but the patch grid makes spatial features coarse. The paper targets this loss of detail, which matters when predictions need information at a finer spatial scale.

The proposed Stochastic Resonance Transformer applies spatial transformations smaller than a token to the input. It extracts features from the transformed inputs, applies the inverse transformations to align those features, and aggregates them. The resulting representation preserves semantic information while placing it on a finer spatial domain, partially reducing the coarsening caused by tokenization.

The procedure requires no training or fine-tuning, and the authors state that it can be applied at any layer of any ViT architecture. They report consistent gains across several tasks, including segmentation, classification, and depth estimation, with improvements reaching 14.9%. These findings show that manipulating and combining existing features can recover useful spatial detail without changing the learned model through additional training.
summary.tldr: Small input transformations and aligned feature aggregation recover finer ViT spatial representations without training or fine-tuning.

title: Sub-token ViT Embedding via Stochastic Resonance Transformers

abstract: One of the significant challenges in treatment effect estimation is collider bias, a specific form of sample selection bias induced by the common causes of both the treatment and outcome. Identifying treatment effects under collider bias requires well-defined shadow variables in observational data, which are assumed to be related to the outcome and independent of the sample selection mechanism, conditional on the other observed variables. However, finding a valid shadow variable is not an easy task in real-world scenarios and requires domain-specific knowledge from experts. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel method that can automatically learn shadow-variable representations from observational data without prior knowledge. To ensure the learned representations satisfy the assumptions of the shadow variable, we introduce a tester to perform hypothesis testing in the representation learning process. We iteratively generate representations and test whether they satisfy the shadow-variable assumptions until they pass the test. With the help of the learned shadow-variable representations, we propose a novel treatment effect estimator to address collider bias. Experiments show that the proposed methods outperform existing treatment effect estimation methods under collider bias and prove their potential application value.

paragraphs: Collider bias can make treatment-effect estimation unreliable when the observed sample is selected in a way that distorts the relevant relationships. A shadow variable can help identify treatment effects in this setting. It must relate to the outcome while remaining independent of sample selection after conditioning on the other observed variables.

Finding a variable with those properties ordinarily requires domain expertise. This paper instead proposes learning shadow-variable representations automatically from observational data without prior knowledge. A tester performs hypothesis testing during representation learning. The procedure alternates between generating representations and checking the shadow-variable assumptions, continuing until a representation passes the test.

The learned representations then support a new treatment-effect estimator designed to address collider bias. Experiments report that the proposed methods outperform existing treatment-effect estimation methods in the studied collider-bias settings. The distinctive contribution is the integration of representation learning with explicit checks of the required assumptions. Those assumptions remain central to the approach, with hypothesis testing providing the stated mechanism for assessing candidate representations.
summary.tldr: The paper learns and tests shadow-variable representations from observational data to support treatment-effect estimation under collider bias.

title: Learning Shadow Variable Representation for Treatment Effect Estimation under Collider Bias

abstract: This study introduces a novel transformer model optimized for large-scale point cloud processing in scientific domains such as high-energy physics (HEP) and astrophysics. Addressing the limitations of graph neural networks and standard transformers, our model integrates local inductive bias and achieves near-linear complexity with hardware-friendly regular operations. One contribution of this work is the quantitative analysis of the error-complexity tradeoff of various sparsification techniques for building efficient transformers. Our findings highlight the superiority of using locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), especially OR & AND-construction LSH, in kernel approximation for large-scale point cloud data with local inductive bias. Based on this finding, we propose LSH-based Efficient Point Transformer (HEPT), which combines E$^2$LSH with OR & AND constructions and is built upon regular computations. HEPT demonstrates remarkable performance on two critical yet time-consuming HEP tasks, significantly outperforming existing GNNs and transformers in accuracy and computational speed, marking a significant advancement in geometric deep learning and large-scale scientific data processing. Our code is available at https://github.com/Graph-COM/HEPT.

paragraphs: Scientific point clouds can be large enough to make standard transformer processing expensive. HEPT addresses this problem with a transformer that incorporates local structure, achieves near-linear complexity, and uses regular computations suited to hardware. The intended applications include large point-cloud datasets in high-energy physics and astrophysics.

The paper first analyzes how different sparsification techniques trade approximation error against computational cost. Its findings favor locality-sensitive hashing, particularly combinations using OR and AND constructions, for kernel approximation when the data has useful local structure. This analysis supplies the basis for the architecture rather than introducing an efficiency mechanism without examining its approximation behavior.

HEPT combines E²LSH with those constructions and organizes the resulting operations into regular computations. On two high-energy physics tasks, it substantially outperforms the evaluated graph neural networks and transformers in both accuracy and speed. The result links three design goals: retaining local information, controlling approximation costs, and making the computations efficient to execute. The empirical performance claims concern the two reported physics tasks.
summary.tldr: HEPT uses locality-sensitive hashing to process large point clouds efficiently, improving accuracy and speed on two high-energy physics tasks.

title: Locality-Sensitive Hashing-Based Efficient Point Transformer with Applications in High-Energy Physics

abstract: Deep neural networks come in many sizes and architectures. The choice of architecture, in conjunction with the dataset and learning algorithm, is commonly understood to affect the learned neural representations. Yet, recent results have shown that different architectures learn representations with striking qualitative similarities. Here we derive an effective theory of representation learning under the assumption that the encoding map from input to hidden representation and the decoding map from representation to output are arbitrary smooth functions. This theory schematizes representation learning dynamics in the regime of complex, large architectures, where hidden representations are not strongly constrained by the parametrization. We show through experiments that the effective theory describes aspects of representation learning dynamics across a range of deep networks with different activation functions and architectures, and exhibits phenomena similar to the “rich” and “lazy” regime. While many network behaviors depend quantitatively on architecture, our findings point to certain behaviors that are widely conserved once models are sufficiently flexible.

paragraphs: Neural architectures differ substantially, yet their learned representations can display similar qualitative patterns. This paper asks whether a shared description of representation learning can explain some of those similarities. It develops an effective theory intended for large, flexible architectures whose hidden representations are not strongly restricted by their particular parameterization.

The theory assumes that the map from inputs to hidden representations and the map from representations to outputs are arbitrary smooth functions. This abstraction shifts attention toward how representations evolve when architecture imposes relatively weak constraints. It is an account of a particular flexible-model regime, rather than a claim that architecture has no effect on what networks learn.

Experiments show that the theory captures aspects of learning dynamics across networks with different architectures and activation functions. It also displays phenomena resembling rich and lazy learning regimes. Although quantitative behavior still depends on architecture, the findings suggest that certain qualitative behaviors are widely shared once models have sufficient flexibility. The contribution is a common theoretical description of those conserved aspects.
summary.tldr: An effective theory explains shared aspects of representation learning dynamics when neural architectures are sufficiently flexible.

title: When Representations Align: Universality in Representation Learning Dynamics

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) faces threats from model poisoning attacks. Existing defenses, typically relying on cross-client/global information to mitigate these attacks, fall short when faced with non-IID data distributions and/or a large number of malicious clients. To address these challenges, we present FedREDefense. Unlike existing methods, it doesn’t hinge on similar distributions across clients or a predominant presence of benign clients. Instead, it assesses the likelihood that a client’s model update is a product of genuine training, solely based on the characteristics of the model update itself. Our key finding is that model updates stemming from genuine training can be approximately reconstructed with some distilled local knowledge, while those from deliberate handcrafted model poisoning attacks cannot. Drawing on this distinction, FedREDefense identifies and filters out malicious clients based on the discrepancies in their model update Reconstruction Errors. Empirical tests on three benchmark datasets confirm that FedREDefense successfully filters model poisoning attacks in FL—even in scenarios with high non-IID degrees and large numbers of malicious clients.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines model updates from multiple clients, creating an opportunity for malicious participants to submit poisoned updates. Defenses based on comparisons across clients can struggle when clients have very different data or many clients are malicious. FedREDefense instead assesses whether an update appears to have resulted from genuine training.

Its assessment relies on characteristics of the update itself, rather than requiring similar client distributions or a predominantly benign client population.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets show successful filtering of model poisoning attacks, including settings with strongly non-identical data distributions and large numbers of malicious clients. The result supports reconstruction error as a useful defense signal in these challenging settings. The stated distinction specifically connects genuine training updates with the handcrafted poisoning behavior examined by the method.
summary.tldr: FedREDefense detects poisoned federated-learning updates through reconstruction errors, without relying on similar client data or a benign majority.

title: FedREDefense: Defending against Model Poisoning Attacks for Federated Learning using Model Update Reconstruction Error

abstract: Inferring reward functions from demonstrations is a key challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in multi-agent RL (MARL). The large joint state-action spaces and intricate inter-agent interactions in MARL make inferring the joint reward function especially challenging. While prior studies in single-agent settings have explored ways to recover reward functions and expert policies from human preference feedback, such studies in MARL remain limited. Existing methods typically combine two separate stages, supervised reward learning, and standard MARL algorithms, leading to unstable training processes. In this work, we exploit the inherent connection between reward functions and Q functions in cooperative MARL to introduce a novel end-to-end preference-based learning framework. Our framework is supported by a carefully designed multi-agent value decomposition strategy that enhances training efficiency. Extensive experiments on two state-of-the-art benchmarks, SMAC and MAMuJoCo, using preference data generated by both rule-based and large language model approaches demonstrate that our algorithm consistently outperforms existing methods across various tasks.

paragraphs: Learning rewards from preferences becomes difficult when several agents act together. Their joint state-action space is large, and interactions between agents complicate the interpretation of desirable behavior. Existing approaches commonly learn a reward model first and then run a separate multi-agent reinforcement learning procedure. The paper identifies unstable training as a problem with that separation.

O-MAPL introduces an end-to-end preference-learning framework for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. It uses the inherent relationship between reward functions and Q functions, which represent action values. A specially designed multi-agent value decomposition strategy supports the framework and improves training efficiency, addressing the complexity of learning about coordinated behavior.

The authors evaluate the method on SMAC and MAMuJoCo using preference data produced by both rule-based procedures and large language models. It consistently outperforms existing methods across the tested tasks. These results support connecting preference learning more directly with multi-agent value learning, while the use of two preference-generation approaches broadens the empirical evidence beyond a single feedback source.
summary.tldr: O-MAPL connects preferences and multi-agent value learning in an end-to-end framework that outperforms existing methods on the evaluated cooperative tasks.

title: O-MAPL: Offline Multi-agent Preference Learning

abstract: Patch-based image tokenization ignores the morphology of the visual world, limiting effective and efficient learning of image understanding. Inspired by subword tokenization, we introduce subobject-level adaptive token segmentation and explore several approaches, including superpixel, SAM, and a proposed Efficient and PanOptiC (EPOC) image tokenizer. Our EPOC combines boundary detection–a simple task that can be handled well by a compact model–with watershed segmentation, which inherently guarantees no pixels are left unsegmented. Intrinsic evaluations across 5 datasets demonstrate that EPOC’s segmentation aligns well with human annotations of both object- and part-level visual morphology, producing more monosemantic tokens and offering substantial efficiency advantages. For extrinsic evaluation, we designed a token embedding that handles arbitrary-shaped tokens, and trained VLMs with different tokenizers on 4 datasets of object recognition and detailed captioning. The results reveal that subobject tokenization enables faster convergence and better generalization while using fewer visual tokens.

The results reveal that subobject tokenization enables faster convergence and better generalization while using fewer visual tokens.

paragraphs: Fixed image patches can cut across object boundaries and combine unrelated visual content within a token. This paper explores adaptive tokenization at the level of objects and their parts, drawing inspiration from subword tokenization. It examines several segmentation approaches, including superpixels, SAM, and a new tokenizer called EPOC.

EPOC combines boundary detection with watershed segmentation. A compact model handles boundary detection, while the segmentation procedure ensures that every pixel is assigned to a region. Across five datasets, the resulting regions align well with human annotations of objects and parts. The authors report tokens with more coherent semantic content and substantial efficiency advantages.

To test whether these regions improve learning, the researchers design an embedding method for tokens with arbitrary shapes. They train vision-language models with different tokenizers on four datasets covering object recognition and detailed captioning. The results show faster convergence and better generalization with fewer visual tokens. This connects segmentation quality to downstream usefulness: respecting visual boundaries can improve both the representation of an image and the efficiency with which a model learns from it.
summary.tldr: EPOC creates image tokens aligned with objects and parts, enabling tested vision-language models to learn faster and generalize better with fewer tokens.

title: Subobject-level Image Tokenization

abstract: Sequential recommendation in e-commerce utilizes users’ anonymous browsing histories to personalize product suggestions without relying on private information. Existing item ID-based methods and multimodal models often overlook the temporal alignment of modalities like textual descriptions, visual content, and prices in user browsing sequences. To address this limitation, this paper proposes the Multimodal Time-aligned Shared Token Recommender (MTSTRec), a transformer-based framework with a single time-aligned shared token per product for efficient cross-modality fusion. MTSTRec preserves the distinct contributions of each modality while aligning them temporally to better capture user preferences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MTSTRec achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple sequential recommendation benchmarks, significantly improving upon existing multimodal fusion. Our code is available at https://github.com/idssplab/MTSTRec.

The paper argues that existing approaches often overlook how these modalities should align within the browsing sequence, limiting their ability to capture evolving preferences.

Aligning the information temporally connects the different descriptions of a product to its place in the user's history, giving the model a coordinated representation of the sequence.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across multiple sequential recommendation benchmarks and significant improvements over existing multimodal fusion approaches. The findings support temporal alignment as a useful part of combining product information. The recommendation setting described relies on anonymous browsing histories rather than private personal information, with the model learning preferences from the sequence of product interactions.
summary.tldr: MTSTRec aligns product modalities within browsing sequences using a shared token, improving sequential recommendation benchmarks.

title: MTSTRec: Multimodal Time-Aligned Shared Token Recommender

abstract: Information asymmetry is a pervasive feature of multi-agent systems, especially evident in economics and social sciences. In these settings, agents tailor their actions based on private information to maximize their rewards. These strategic behaviors often introduce complexities due to confounding variables. Simultaneously, knowledge transportability poses another significant challenge, arising from the difficulties of conducting experiments in target environments. It requires transferring knowledge from environments where empirical data is more readily available. Against these backdrops, this paper explores a fundamental question in online learning: Can we employ non-i.i.d. actions to learn about confounders even when requiring knowledge transfer? We present a sample-efficient algorithm designed to accurately identify system dynamics under information asymmetry and to navigate the challenges of knowledge transfer effectively in reinforcement learning, framed within an online strategic interaction model. Our method provably achieves learning of an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with a tight sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$.
