paragraphs: When agents possess private information, their actions reflect both that information and their incentives. This can create confounding, making observed behavior difficult to interpret. The paper also considers knowledge transportability: learning must draw on environments where data is available because experiments in the target environment are difficult to conduct.

The authors ask whether actions that are not independent and identically distributed can still help reveal confounders while knowledge is transferred between environments. They formulate an online strategic interaction model and develop a reinforcement learning algorithm that identifies system dynamics despite information asymmetry. The method addresses strategic behavior and transfer within the same learning problem.

The main result is a tight sample-complexity guarantee of roughly 1/epsilon squared, with logarithmic factors suppressed, for learning an epsilon-optimal policy. Such a policy comes within epsilon of optimal performance in the modeled setting. The result gives a precise account of how data requirements grow with the requested accuracy, establishing sample-efficient learning for a problem that combines hidden information, strategic actions, and knowledge transfer.
summary.tldr: A strategic online learning algorithm handles information asymmetry and knowledge transfer with tight sample complexity proportional to 1/epsilon² up to logarithmic factors.

title: The Sample Complexity of Online Strategic Decision Making with Information Asymmetry and Knowledge Transportability

abstract: Achieving both high safety and high usefulness simultaneously in large language models has become a critical challenge in recent years. Models often exhibit unsafe behavior or adopt an overly cautious approach leading to frequent overrefusal of benign prompts, which reduces their usefulness. A major factor underlying these behaviors is how the models are finetuned and aligned, particularly the nature and extent of the data used. In this work, we examine how overgenerating finetuning data with advanced teacher models (e.g., GPT-4o)—covering both general-purpose and toxic prompts—affects safety and usefulness in instruction-following language models. Additionally, we present POROver, an alignment strategy designed for models that are highly safe but prone to overrefusal. POROver employs preference optimization algorithms and leverages completions from an advanced teacher model to reduce overrefusals while maintaining safety. Our results show that overgenerating completions for general-purpose prompts significantly boosts safety with only a minimal impact on usefulness. Specifically, the F1 score calculated between safety and usefulness increases from 74.4% to 91.8% because of a substantial rise in safety. Moreover, overgeneration for toxic prompts raises usefulness from 11.1% to 57.6% while preserving safety. Finally, applying POROVer increases usefulness further—from 57.6% to 82.1%—while keeping safety at comparable levels.

paragraphs: A language model can become less useful when its safety behavior causes it to reject benign requests. This paper studies how the amount and type of teacher-generated finetuning data affect that balance. It examines generating additional completions for both general-purpose and toxic prompts using an advanced teacher model.

Applying it increases usefulness further, from 57.6% to 82.1%, with comparable safety. The reported results show how data generation and subsequent preference training can improve the safety-usefulness balance in the evaluated models.
summary.tldr: Teacher-generated completions and POROver preference optimization improve reported usefulness while maintaining strong safety and reducing unnecessary refusals.

title: POROver: Improving Safety and Reducing Overrefusal in Large Language Models with Overgeneration and Preference Optimization

abstract: Estimating the unknown reward functions driving agents’ behavior is a central challenge in inverse games and reinforcement learning. This paper introduces a unified framework for reward function recovery in two-player zero-sum matrix games and Markov games with entropy regularization. Given observed player strategies and actions, we aim to reconstruct the underlying reward functions. This task is challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of inverse problems, the non-uniqueness of feasible rewards, and limited observational data coverage. To address these challenges, we establish reward function identifiability using the quantal response equilibrium (QRE) under linear assumptions. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose an algorithm to learn reward from observed actions, designed to capture all plausible reward parameters by constructing confidence sets. Our algorithm works in both static and dynamic settings and is adaptable to incorporate other methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). We provide strong theoretical guarantees for the reliability and sample-efficiency of our algorithm. Empirical results demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in accurately recovering reward functions across various scenarios, offering new insights into decision-making in competitive environments.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer what competing players are trying to achieve from their observed strategies and actions. It considers two-player zero-sum matrix games and Markov games with entropy regularization. Recovering rewards is difficult because different reward functions can explain similar behavior, and observations may cover only part of the relevant decisions.

The authors establish conditions for identifying reward functions using quantal response equilibrium under linear assumptions. These assumptions are central to the theoretical result: the framework provides a structured setting in which behavioral observations can distinguish rewards despite the ambiguity of the inverse problem.

Building on that foundation, the proposed algorithm constructs confidence sets intended to include all plausible reward parameters. It handles static and dynamic games and can incorporate approaches such as maximum likelihood estimation. The authors provide guarantees concerning reliability and sample efficiency, alongside experiments demonstrating accurate reward recovery across several scenarios. Representing a set of plausible rewards also makes uncertainty part of the recovery procedure, rather than reducing the task immediately to a single estimate.
summary.tldr: A framework recovers competitive players’ reward functions under linear assumptions while using confidence sets to represent plausible alternatives.

title: Decoding Rewards in Competitive Games: Inverse Game Theory with Entropy Regularization

abstract: Segment Anything Model (SAM) has demonstrated remarkable zero-shot segmentation capabilities across various visual tasks. However, its performance degrades significantly when deployed in new target domains with substantial distribution shifts. While existing self-training methods based on fixed teacher-student architectures have shown improvements, they struggle to ensure that the teacher network consistently outperforms the student under severe domain shifts. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Collaborative Mutual Learning Framework for source-free SAM adaptation, leveraging dual-networks in a dynamic and cooperative manner. Unlike fixed teacher-student paradigms, our method dynamically assigns the teacher and student roles by evaluating the reliability of each collaborative network in each training iteration. Our framework incorporates a dynamic mutual learning mechanism with three key components: a direct alignment loss for knowledge transfer, a reverse distillation loss to encourage diversity, and a triplet relationship loss to refine feature representations. These components enhance the adaptation capabilities of the collaborative networks, enabling them to generalize effectively to target domains while preserving their pre-trained knowledge. Extensive experiments on diverse target domains demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art adaptation performance.

paragraphs: The Segment Anything Model can segment unfamiliar images, but substantial changes in the target domain can degrade its performance. Adaptation methods often use a fixed teacher to supervise a student. This paper identifies a weakness in that arrangement: under severe distribution shifts, the designated teacher may not remain the more reliable network.

The proposed source-free framework uses two collaborating networks and reassesses their teacher and student roles at every training iteration. Reliability determines which network provides guidance. Three losses support this exchange: direct alignment transfers knowledge, reverse distillation encourages diversity, and a triplet relationship loss improves feature representations. The design combines learning from a stronger partner with maintaining useful differences between the networks.

Experiments across diverse target domains report state-of-the-art adaptation performance. The authors describe the framework as improving target-domain generalization while preserving pretrained knowledge. Its central contribution is making the direction of supervision responsive to changing network reliability, so collaboration does not depend on one network retaining a fixed advantage throughout adaptation.
summary.tldr: Two SAM networks dynamically exchange teacher and student roles based on reliability, improving source-free adaptation across the evaluated target domains.

title: Mutual Learning for SAM Adaptation: A Dual Collaborative Network Framework for Source-Free Domain Transfer

abstract: We address the problem of predicting the next states of a dynamical system governed by unknown temporal partial differential equations (PDEs) using only a short trajectory. While standard transformers provide a natural black-box solution to this task, the presence of a well-structured evolution operator in the data suggests a more tailored and efficient approach. Specifically, when the PDE is fully known, classical numerical solvers can evolve the state accurately with only a few parameters. Building on this observation, we introduce DISCO, a model that uses a large hypernetwork to process a short trajectory and generate the parameters of a much smaller operator network, which then predicts the next states through time integration. Our framework decouples dynamics estimation – i.e., DISCovering an evolution Operator from a short trajectory – from state prediction – i.e., evolving this operator. Experiments show that pretraining our model on diverse physics datasets achieves state-of-the-art performance while requiring significantly fewer epochs. Moreover, it generalizes well to unseen initial conditions and remains competitive when fine-tuned on downstream tasks.

paragraphs: DISCO predicts how a dynamical system will evolve from a short observed trajectory, without knowing the temporal partial differential equations governing it. The paper draws on a useful property of numerical simulation: when the governing evolution rule is known, a relatively compact solver can advance the system through time.

The architecture separates discovering that rule from using it. A large hypernetwork reads the short trajectory and generates parameters for a much smaller operator network. The operator network then predicts subsequent states through time integration. This division gives the large model responsibility for estimating dynamics and the smaller model responsibility for repeatedly evolving the state.

Experiments show that pretraining across diverse physics datasets produces state-of-the-art performance while requiring significantly fewer training epochs. The model also generalizes well to unseen initial conditions and remains competitive after fine-tuning on downstream tasks. These findings support separating dynamics estimation from state prediction as a useful architectural choice for learning across physical systems whose governing equations are unavailable.
summary.tldr: DISCO uses a large hypernetwork to infer a compact evolution operator from a short trajectory, enabling efficient prediction of unknown physical dynamics.

title: DISCO: learning to DISCover an evolution Operator for multi-physics-agnostic prediction

abstract: Tasks that involve complex interactions between objects with unknown dynamics make planning before execution difficult. These tasks require agents to iteratively improve their actions after actively exploring causes and effects in the environment. For these type of tasks, we propose Causal-PIK, a method that leverages Bayesian optimization to reason about causal interactions via a Physics-Informed Kernel to help guide efficient search for the best next action. Experimental results on Virtual Tools and PHYRE physical reasoning benchmarks show that Causal-PIK outperforms state-of-the-art results, requiring fewer actions to reach the goal. We also compare Causal-PIK to human studies, including results from a new user study we conducted on the PHYRE benchmark. We find that Causal-PIK remains competitive on tasks that are very challenging, even for human problem-solvers.

paragraphs: Physical reasoning becomes difficult when objects interact in ways an agent does not already understand. Planning an entire solution in advance may be impractical because the consequences of an action are uncertain. This paper addresses tasks where an agent actively explores the environment and improves its choices through observed causes and effects.

Causal-PIK uses Bayesian optimization to guide the search for the next action. Its central component is a physics-informed kernel, which brings information about physical interactions into that search. The method connects reasoning about how actions affect objects with the optimization process used to choose subsequent attempts.

On the Virtual Tools and PHYRE benchmarks, the authors report better results than the state of the art, with fewer actions needed to reach the goal. They also compare the method with human studies, including a new study on PHYRE. Causal-PIK remains competitive on tasks that are difficult even for human participants. These findings support the value of incorporating physical structure into action search when interaction dynamics are unknown.
summary.tldr: Causal-PIK combines Bayesian optimization with a physics-informed kernel to solve physical reasoning tasks using fewer actions.

title: Causal-PIK: Causality-based Physical Reasoning with a Physics-Informed Kernel

abstract: In-Context Reinforcement Learning (ICRL) represents a promising paradigm for developing generalist agents that learn at inference time through trial-and-error interactions, analogous to how large language models adapt contextually, but with a focus on reward maximization. However, the scalability of ICRL beyond toy tasks and single-domain settings remains an open challenge. In this work, we present the first steps toward scaling ICRL by introducing a fixed, cross-domain model capable of learning behaviors through in-context reinforcement learning. Our results demonstrate that Algorithm Distillation, a framework designed to facilitate ICRL, offers a compelling and competitive alternative to expert distillation to construct versatile action models. These findings highlight the potential of ICRL as a scalable approach for generalist decision-making systems.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning aims to let an agent learn during inference through trial-and-error interactions directed toward higher reward. The challenge is extending this behavior beyond toy problems or a single domain. Vintix takes an initial step by introducing a fixed model that can learn behaviors in context across domains.

The paper uses Algorithm Distillation, a framework designed to enable this kind of learning, to construct a versatile action model. The distinction is between the model remaining fixed and its behavior adapting through the interaction context. This places learning at inference time within the model’s use of experience, making contextual adaptation central to its decision-making role.

The reported results show Algorithm Distillation to be a competitive alternative to expert distillation for building versatile action models. The authors present this as evidence of potential for scaling in-context reinforcement learning, rather than as a completed solution to generalist decision-making. The contribution demonstrates a cross-domain direction for an approach whose scalability beyond restricted settings remains an open challenge.
summary.tldr: Vintix demonstrates a fixed cross-domain action model that learns through interaction context, supporting Algorithm Distillation as a competitive approach.

title: Vintix: Action Model via In-Context Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Industrial designers have long sought a natural and intuitive way to achieve the targeted control of prototype models—using simple natural language instructions to configure and adjust the models seamlessly according to their intentions, without relying on complex modeling commands. While Large Language Models have shown promise in this area, their potential for controlling prototype models through language remains partially underutilized. This limitation stems from gaps between designers’ languages and modeling languages, including mismatch in abstraction levels, fluctuation in semantic precision, and divergence in lexical scopes. To bridge these gaps, we propose an interface architecture that serves as a medium between the two languages. Grounded in design principles derived from a systematic investigation of fast prototyping practices, we devise the interface’s operational mechanism and develop an algorithm for its automated domain specification. Both machine-based evaluations and human studies on fast prototyping across various product design domains demonstrate the interface’s potential to function as an auxiliary module for Large Language Models, enabling precise and effective targeted control of prototype models.

paragraphs: Industrial designers want to adjust prototypes using ordinary language, but their descriptions do not map neatly onto modeling commands. The two languages differ in abstraction, precision, and vocabulary. This paper investigates an interface that can bridge those differences so that a language model can support targeted prototype changes.

The interface architecture is grounded in principles drawn from a systematic study of rapid prototyping practices. The authors specify how it operates and develop an algorithm that automatically produces its domain specification. This makes the connection between design language and modeling language an explicit component of the system, with attention to the particular product-design domain.

Machine-based evaluations and human studies across several design domains indicate that the interface can serve as a useful auxiliary module for large language models. The findings support its potential to enable precise and effective control over prototypes. The practical significance is a structured way to connect designers' intentions to model adjustments while accounting for differences in how those intentions and operations are expressed.
summary.tldr: A domain-specific interface helps language models translate designers' natural-language intentions into targeted prototype adjustments.

title: Targeted control of fast prototyping through domain-specific interface

abstract: Low-rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a powerful and efficient method for fine-tuning large-scale foundation models. Despite its popularity, the theoretical understanding of LoRA has remained underexplored. In this paper, we present a theoretical analysis of LoRA by examining its connection to the Mixture of Experts models. Under this framework, we show that a simple technique, reparameterizing LoRA matrices, can notably accelerate the low-rank matrix estimation process. In particular, we prove that reparameterization can reduce the data needed to achieve a desired estimation error from an exponential to a polynomial scale. Motivated by this insight, we propose Reparameterized Low-Rank Adaptation (RepLoRA), incorporating a lightweight MLP to reparameterize the LoRA matrices. Extensive experiments across multiple domains demonstrate that RepLoRA consistently outperforms vanilla LoRA. With limited data, RepLoRA surpasses LoRA by a substantial margin of up to 40.0% and achieves LoRA’s performance using only 30.0% of the training data, highlighting the theoretical and empirical robustness of our PEFT method.

This paper studies LoRA through a connection to mixture-of-experts models. That perspective reveals how changing the parameterization of its matrices can affect the data needed for estimation.

summary.tldr: RepLoRA reparameterizes low-rank adaptation matrices with a lightweight network, translating a theoretical sample-efficiency insight into empirical gains.

title: RepLoRA: Reparameterizing Low-rank Adaptation via the Perspective of Mixture of Experts

abstract: While state-of-the-art language models achieve impressive results through next-token prediction, they have inherent limitations such as the inability to revise already generated tokens. This has prompted exploration of alternative approaches such as discrete diffusion. However, masked diffusion, which has emerged as a popular choice due to its simplicity and effectiveness, reintroduces this inability to revise words. To overcome this, we generalize masked diffusion, deriving a new family of general interpolating discrete diffusion (GIDD) which offers greater flexibility in the design of the noising processes. Leveraging a novel diffusion ELBO, we achieve compute-matched state-of-the-art performance in diffusion language modeling. Exploiting GIDD’s flexibility, we explore a hybrid approach combining masking and uniform noise, leading to improved sample quality and unlocking the ability for the model to correct its own mistakes, an area where autoregressive models notoriously have struggled. paragraphs: Next-token language generation cannot revise tokens it has already produced. Discrete diffusion offers an alternative, but the popular masked version reintroduces this restriction. This paper generalizes masked diffusion to make the underlying noising process more flexible, creating a family called general interpolating discrete diffusion, or GIDD.

The authors derive a new diffusion evidence lower bound, a training objective that supports this broader family. With this objective, they report compute-matched state-of-the-art performance in diffusion language modeling. Matching computation matters to the stated comparison because the reported result concerns performance at a comparable computational budget.

The paper then uses GIDD’s flexibility to combine masking with uniform noise. This hybrid improves generated sample quality and allows the model to correct its own mistakes. The contribution therefore connects the design of the corruption process to the behavior available during generation: changing how tokens are noised enables a generation process that can revisit earlier choices. The reported findings concern this hybrid approach and the evaluated diffusion language-modeling setting.
summary.tldr: GIDD generalizes discrete diffusion, using flexible noise processes to improve language generation and enable correction of earlier token choices.

title: Generalized Interpolating Discrete Diffusion

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) with linear transition kernels and reward functions has recently attracted growing attention due to its computational efficiency and theoretical advancements. However, prior theoretical research in RL has primarily focused on single-objective problems, resulting in limited theoretical development for multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL). To bridge this gap, we examine MORL under lexicographic reward structures, where rewards comprise $m$ hierarchically ordered objectives. In this framework, the agent the agent maximizes objectives sequentially, prioritizing the highest-priority objective before considering subsequent ones. We introduce the first MORL algorithm with provable regret guarantees. For any objective $i \in \\{1, 2, \ldots, m\\}$, our algorithm achieves a regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(\Lambda^i(\lambda) \cdot \sqrt{d^2H^4 K})$, where $\Lambda^i(\lambda) = 1 + \lambda + \cdots + \lambda^{i-1}$, $\lambda$ quantifies the trade-off between conflicting objectives, $d$ is the feature dimension, $H$ is the episode length, and $K$ is the number of episodes. Furthermore, our algorithm can be applied in the misspecified setting, where the regret bound for the $i$-th objective becomes $\widetilde{O}(\Lambda^i(\lambda)\cdot(\sqrt{d^2H^4K}+\epsilon dH^2K))$, with $\epsilon$ denoting the degree of misspecification.

Under this lexicographic structure, the agent optimizes the highest-priority objective before considering lower-priority ones. The analysis assumes linear transition kernels and reward functions, extending theoretical work that has mainly addressed single-objective problems.

An additional factor is a sum of powers of a parameter describing conflicts between objectives. This makes the role of objective priority and conflict explicit in the guarantee.

The algorithm also applies when the linear model is misspecified. In that setting, the bound gains an additional term proportional to the degree of misspecification and the number of episodes. The contribution is a theoretical account of learning under ordered priorities, including how departures from the modeling assumptions affect the guarantees for individual objectives.
summary.tldr: The paper gives per-objective regret guarantees for linear reinforcement learning with hierarchically ordered rewards, including a misspecified setting.

title: Multi-objective Linear Reinforcement Learning with Lexicographic Rewards

abstract: Statistical adversarial data detection (SADD) detects whether an upcoming batch contains adversarial examples (AEs) by measuring the distributional discrepancies between clean examples (CEs) and AEs. In this paper, we explore the strength of SADD-based methods by theoretically showing that minimizing distributional discrepancy can help reduce the expected loss on AEs. Despite these advantages, SADD-based methods have a potential limitation: they discard inputs that are detected as AEs, leading to the loss of clean information within those inputs. To address this limitation, we propose a two-pronged adversarial defense method, named Distributional-discrepancy-based Adversarial Defense (DAD). In the training phase, DAD first optimizes the test power of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to derive MMD-OPT, which is a stone that kills two birds. MMD-OPT first serves as a guiding signal to minimize the distributional discrepancy between CEs and AEs to train a denoiser. Then, it serves as a discriminator to differentiate CEs and AEs during inference. Overall, in the inference stage, DAD consists of a two-pronged process: (1) directly feeding the detected CEs into the classifier, and (2) removing noise from the detected AEs by the distributional-discrepancy-based denoiser. Extensive experiments show that DAD outperforms current state-of-the-art (SOTA) defense methods by simultaneously improving clean and robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K against adaptive white-box attacks. Codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/DAD.

title: One Stone, Two Birds: Enhancing Adversarial Defense Through the Lens of Distributional Discrepancy

abstract: Recent progress in LLM reasoning has increasingly shifted from single-pass generation to explicit search over intermediate reasoning states. Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) organizes inference to tree-structured search with branching and backtracking, but it substantially amplifies the key–value (KV) cache: retaining KV states for a frontier of partial trajectories quickly becomes a memory bottleneck that limits throughput and constrains search depth and width under fixed hardware budgets. We address this challenge by observing that KV reuse in ToT-style inference is governed by search dynamics: near-term decoding depends primarily on the active branch and its ancestors, whereas inactive subtrees have low short-term reuse probability yet must remain recoverable for backtracking. Motivated by this, we propose ArborKV, a structure-aware eviction framework that couples a lightweight value estimator with a tree-aware allocation policy, and performs purely token-extractive eviction with lazy rehydration to support revisits. Experiments on ToT-style reasoning benchmarks show that ArborKV achieves up to $\sim4\times$ peak KV-memory reduction while preserving near-full-retention accuracy, enabling larger search configurations under fixed device budgets that would otherwise run out of memory.

paragraphs: Tree-based language-model reasoning explores several possible continuations and may return to earlier branches. Keeping the attention key–value states for all these partial paths can consume substantial memory. ArborKV addresses this storage bottleneck by using the structure of the search to decide which cached information deserves immediate space.

The central observation is that upcoming generation mainly needs the current branch and its ancestors. Other subtrees are less likely to be used soon, although backtracking means they cannot simply become inaccessible. ArborKV combines a lightweight estimate of cache value with a policy that allocates memory according to the tree. It removes selected token entries and restores needed information lazily when a branch is revisited.

On the reported Tree-of-Thoughts reasoning benchmarks, ArborKV reduces peak cache memory by up to roughly fourfold while retaining accuracy close to keeping the full cache. This makes larger searches feasible within a fixed device budget, including configurations that otherwise exhaust memory. The contribution is therefore a way to support broader or deeper reasoning searches by matching cache retention to expected branch reuse.
summary.tldr: ArborKV uses reasoning-tree structure to reduce peak KV-cache memory by up to roughly fourfold while preserving near-full-retention accuracy.

title: ArborKV: Structure-Aware KV Cache Management for Scaling Tree-based LLM Reasoning

abstract: Quadratically regularization has emerged as a potential alternative to the popular entropic regularization in computational optimal transport, offering the theoretical advantage of producing sparse couplings through its hinge density structure. Despite recent progress in one-dimensional setting and general upper bounds, fundamental questions about the localization rate of QOT optimizers around the Monge coupling have remained open. In this work, we establish a general lower bound showing that the support of the QOT optimizer cannot concentrate around the Monge graph faster than order $\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{d+2}}$ in the directed Hausdorff distance, matching the conjectured optimal exponent under standard regularity assumptions in Wiesel & Xu (2025). We also show that the QOT value gap controls the mean-squared deviation $\mathbb E_{\pi_\varepsilon}||y-T(x)||^2$ by the scale of $\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{d+2}}$. As a corollary, in the affine Brenier regime, which includes Gaussian-to-Gaussian transport, we derive a sharp pointwise tube bound of order $\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{d+2}}$ by reducing the problem to self-transport and applying recent self-transport sparsity results. Finally, we validate our theoretical bound with synthetic experiment in high dimensions setting.

paragraphs: Quadratically regularized optimal transport can produce sparse couplings through its hinge-shaped density structure. This paper studies how tightly those couplings concentrate around the Monge graph, the mapping associated with the underlying transport problem, as the regularization strength ε decreases. The central question is the rate at which that concentration can occur in dimension d.

Under standard regularity assumptions, the authors establish a lower bound: the optimizer’s support cannot approach the Monge graph faster than order ε^(1/(d+2)) in directed Hausdorff distance. This matches a conjectured optimal exponent. They also show that the regularized transport value gap controls mean-squared deviation from the map at scale ε^(2/(d+2)).

The proof reduces the problem to self-transport and applies sparsity results for that setting. Synthetic high-dimensional experiments validate the theoretical bound. The general lower bound and the sharper affine-case result describe distinct aspects of how regularized couplings localize.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds how quickly quadratically regularized transport concentrates around a Monge map and obtains a sharp bound in the affine case.

title: Quadratically Regularized Optimal Transport: Localization Bounds and Affine Case Analysis

abstract: When does learning elicit existing knowledge, and when does it primarily teach new capabilities? We find that the amount of generalizable information language models learn during training predicts the origins of their emergent capabilities. Minuscule amounts of information—in many cases, a few bits in a single example—can unlock large fractions of models’ maximum performance when capabilities are elicited rather than taught. We quantify these learning regimes using excess description length (EDL), an information-theoretic measure of generalizable information learned during training. We find that elicitation and teaching exhibit distinct EDL signatures that characterize the predominant learning mechanism as information scales: elicitation requires orders of magnitude less information than teaching to comparable performance. We demonstrate that EDL provides a practical tool for quantitatively estimating the maximum amount of predictive information models can compress from data into trainable parameters during learning. These capacity limits describe optimal tradeoffs between data and parameter count that robustly predict when parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (e.g., LoRA) will underperform full fine-tuning.

paragraphs: An improvement after training can mean that a language model learned a new capability or became better at using knowledge it already possessed. This paper investigates that distinction by measuring how much generalizable information training adds. Its central finding is that eliciting an existing capability can require dramatically less information than teaching a capability to a comparable performance level.

The authors use excess description length, or EDL, to quantify that information. They find different EDL patterns for elicitation and teaching as the information supplied during learning increases. In many elicitation cases, just a few bits contained in one example unlock a large fraction of the model’s maximum performance. This is a reported pattern across cases, rather than a claim that every capability can be unlocked so cheaply.

The authors show that these tradeoffs robustly predict when parameter-efficient approaches such as LoRA underperform full fine-tuning, connecting learning mechanisms to practical adaptation choices.
summary.tldr: An information measure distinguishes eliciting existing capabilities from teaching new ones and predicts when parameter-efficient fine-tuning falls short.

title: Bits That Count: Quantifying and Predicting Capabilities of Language Models

abstract: We propose a gradient preconditioning method that makes reward-guided generation with one-step generative models both efficient and reliable. Test-time noise optimization can unlock substantially better reward-guided generations from pretrained generative models, but it is prone to reward hacking that degrades quality and is often too slow for practical use. We precondition reward gradients by projecting them onto a carefully designed white Gaussian noise feasible set, a compact spectral set with blockwise norm constraints that tightly captures the statistics and spatial uncorrelatedness of white Gaussian noise. This preconditioning reshapes each gradient update into a noise-aligned direction, driving faster and more effective reward ascent while preventing reward hacking. The projection is closed-form and matches the $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ complexity of FFT, adding negligible overhead in practice. In experiments on FLUX with four reward models, our approach reaches a comparable Aesthetic Score using only 30% of the wall-clock time required by the state-of-the-art regularization-based method.

paragraphs: Optimizing a generative model's input noise at test time can improve the reward assigned to its outputs. However, the process can be slow and can exploit the reward model in ways that degrade output quality. This paper addresses both problems for reward-guided generation with one-step models.

The method reshapes reward gradients by projecting them onto a feasible set designed around white Gaussian noise. This set uses spectral structure and blockwise norm constraints to capture noise statistics and spatial uncorrelatedness. Each update is therefore directed toward improving reward while remaining aligned with the noise structure expected by the generator.

The projection has a closed-form solution with the same O(N log N) complexity as a fast Fourier transform and adds negligible overhead in practice. The authors describe it as enabling faster reward ascent while preventing reward hacking. On FLUX with four reward models, it reaches a comparable Aesthetic Score using 30% of the wall-clock time of the state-of-the-art regularization-based comparison method.
summary.tldr: Projecting reward gradients into noise-aligned directions speeds one-step reward-guided generation while addressing reward hacking.

title: Gradient Preconditioning for Efficient and Reliable Reward-Guided Generation

abstract: Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) trains predictors to improve downstream decision quality, but computing regret gradients typically requires differentiating through solvers or relying on surrogate losses, which can be computationally expensive or deviate from the true objective. We show that, under standard regularity with locally stable active constraints, the regret gradient admits a closed-form geometric characterization, equivalent to the prediction error projected onto the tangent space of active constraints, scaled by local curvature. This reveals that regret gradients can be obtained by filtering decision-irrelevant components from the MSE gradient, providing a simpler and more direct alternative to existing approaches. We propose PEAR (Projected Error As Regret-gradient), which computes regret gradients via a reduced linear system over active constraints, avoiding differentiation through solver iterations or additional optimization solves. Experiments on LP benchmarks and a real-world QP task show that PEAR achieves the best decision quality among all baselines while being the most computationally efficient, with gains that persist under constraint shifts.

paragraphs: Decision-focused learning trains predictions according to the decisions they produce. A prediction error matters most when it changes the quality of a downstream optimization result. Computing the corresponding training gradient often requires differentiating through an optimization solver or using a substitute loss, introducing computational expense or a mismatch with the actual decision objective.

The paper gives a geometric characterization under regularity conditions and locally stable active constraints. The regret gradient equals prediction error projected onto the tangent space of those constraints and scaled by local curvature. In plain terms, the calculation filters out error components that do not affect the decision locally, retaining the directions relevant to improving it.

PEAR implements this characterization through a reduced linear system over active constraints. It avoids differentiating through solver iterations and avoids additional optimization solves. On linear-programming benchmarks and a real-world quadratic-programming task, it achieves the best decision quality and computational efficiency among the evaluated baselines. The reported gains also persist under constraint shifts, extending the empirical usefulness of the geometric approach.
summary.tldr: PEAR uses a conditional geometric formula for regret gradients to train decision-focused predictors efficiently.

title: Decision-Focused Learning via Tangent-Space Projection of Prediction Error

abstract: Cross-architecture migration of high-performance libraries dictates ecosystem readiness on emerging hardware. The challenge is twofold: disentangling library-scale dependencies and performance-critical kernels with ISA-specific SIMD intrinsics, often trading migration speed for peak performance. While LLM-based agents offer a promising approach, are confined to function-level tasks or scalar code, failing to assess agents’ capabilities and limitations in realistic, library-scale migration. We present QM-LibBench, a benchmark for cross-architecture library-scale code migration, featuring 85 critical kernels from widely used libraries, including OpenCV, libjpeg, and NCNN. It supports comprehensive evaluations of compilability, correctness, and performance across major transitions: ARM$\rightarrow$RISC-V, x86$\rightarrow$ARM, and ARM$\rightarrow$LoongArch. Evaluation of 12 SOTA agent-LLM combinations on QM-LibBench reveals that, due to the lack of library-level navigation and hardware-aware optimization, agents regress to superficial pattern matching, yielding only 20.88% correctness and 0.83 speedup for libjpeg. Motivated by these findings, we further propose FSCM, a multi-agent framework incorporating hardware-aware global reconfiguration and performance optimization. FSCM improves OpenCV correctness to 71%. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/WisdomJoy/QM-LibBench.

paragraphs: Moving a high-performance library to another processor architecture requires understanding dependencies across the library and replacing hardware-specific operations without losing performance. Evaluations restricted to isolated functions or scalar code do not capture this combination of integration and optimization work. QM-LibBench measures agent performance at that broader scope.

The benchmark contains 85 critical kernels from libraries including OpenCV, libjpeg, and NCNN. It evaluates whether migrated code compiles, behaves correctly, and performs well across ARM-to-RISC-V, x86-to-ARM, and ARM-to-LoongArch transitions. The authors then introduce FSCM, a multi-agent framework combining hardware-aware global reconfiguration with performance optimization, raising OpenCV correctness to 71%. The findings show the importance of evaluating migration within its library and hardware context.
summary.tldr: QM-LibBench exposes agent weaknesses in library-scale hardware migration, and FSCM improves results through hardware-aware coordination and optimization.

title: QiMeng-LibBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Library-Scale Cross-Architecture Migration

abstract: ANN-to-SNN conversion offers energy-efficient inference but faces a fidelity-latency trade-off due to open-loop error accumulation. While conversion-aware training mitigates this, it sacrifices the generality of using off-the-shelf ANNs. We propose a closed-loop fine-tuning framework that calibrates these errors without altering the source model. Our approach employs a Dual Alignment Mechanism, utilizing global Kullback-Leibler divergence for output distillation and introducing an adaptive local Centered Kernel Alignment constraint, weighted by initial conversion loss, for feature alignment. We uncover a critical time-dependent dynamic: local constraints are essential for stabilizing representations in low-latency regimes (e.g., $T=8$) where global gradients are unstable, whereas global alignment drives fidelity at higher time steps. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that our method achieves over 99% of source ANN accuracy at $T=32$ (e.g., ResNet-18: 96.38% vs. 96.39%). Furthermore, this fine-tuning acts as a regularizer, yielding SNNs with input noise robustness that matches or exceeds the source ANN.

This paper introduces a closed-loop fine-tuning framework that corrects these errors while leaving the source network unchanged. It therefore retains the ability to start with an off-the-shelf artificial neural network.

The method aligns both outputs and internal features. Global Kullback-Leibler divergence transfers output behavior, while a local Centered Kernel Alignment constraint matches representations and is weighted using initial conversion loss. The authors find that these components matter differently across time budgets: local constraints stabilize low-latency representations, whereas global alignment drives fidelity at higher numbers of time steps.

Fine-tuning also acts as a regularizer, producing input-noise robustness that matches or exceeds the source model. The results connect representation alignment to accurate, robust conversion.
summary.tldr: Closed-loop output and feature distillation preserves source-network accuracy in converted spiking networks while improving robustness to input noise.

title: High-Fidelity ANN-to-SNN Conversion via Closed-Loop CKA Distillation

abstract: Scientific problem solving poses unique challenges for LLMs, requiring both deep domain knowledge and the ability to apply such knowledge through complex reasoning. While automated scientific reasoners hold great promise for assisting human scientists, there is currently no widely adopted holistic benchmark for evaluating scientific reasoning, and few approaches systematically disentangle the distinct roles of knowledge and reasoning in these tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce SciReas, a diverse suite of existing benchmarks for scientific reasoning tasks, and SciReas-Pro, a selective subset that requires more complex reasoning. Our holistic evaluation surfaces insights about scientific reasoning performance that remain hidden when relying on individual benchmarks alone. We then propose KRUX, a probing framework for studying the distinct roles of reasoning and knowledge in scientific tasks. Combining the two, we conduct an in-depth analysis that yields several key findings: (1) Retrieving task-relevant knowledge from model parameters is a critical bottleneck for LLMs in scientific reasoning; (2) Reasoning models consistently benefit from external knowledge added in-context on top of the reasoning enhancement; (3) Enhancing verbalized reasoning improves LLMs’ ability to surface task-relevant knowledge.

Our holistic evaluation surfaces insights about scientific reasoning performance that remain hidden when relying on individual benchmarks alone. We then propose KRUX, a probing framework for studying the distinct roles of reasoning and knowledge in scientific tasks. Combining the two, we conduct an in-depth analysis that yields several key findings: (1) Retrieving task-relevant knowledge from model parameters is a critical bottleneck for LLMs in scientific reasoning; (2) Reasoning models consistently benefit from external knowledge added in-context on top of the reasoning enhancement; (3) Enhancing verbalized reasoning improves LLMs’ ability to surface task-relevant knowledge.

paragraphs: Scientific problem solving requires both relevant knowledge and the ability to apply it through reasoning. A single benchmark can obscure which of these capabilities explains a model’s success or failure. This paper introduces SciReas, a collection of existing scientific reasoning benchmarks, and SciReas-Pro, a selected subset requiring more complex reasoning.

The authors pair these evaluations with KRUX, a probing framework intended to separate the roles of knowledge and reasoning. Their analysis identifies retrieving relevant knowledge from a model’s own parameters as a critical bottleneck. This points to a distinction between having learned information and successfully bringing the right information into a particular solution.

Two further findings connect the capabilities. Reasoning models consistently benefit when relevant external knowledge is supplied in context, even alongside their reasoning enhancements. Improving verbalized reasoning also helps models surface relevant knowledge. Together, the results suggest that scientific performance depends on the interaction between knowledge access and reasoning, and that evaluating these components jointly reveals patterns hidden by individual benchmarks.
summary.tldr: SciReas and KRUX show that accessing relevant knowledge is a key bottleneck in scientific reasoning and interacts with reasoning improvements.

title: Demystifying Scientific Problem-Solving in LLMs by Probing Knowledge and Reasoning

abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is a critical step for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to specialized domains, often serving as an initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning (RL). However, SFT can overfit a small set of expert data, harming generalization and eroding prior knowledge. This can limit downstream RL, which benefits from a strong, generalizable initialization for exploration. Here, we demonstrate that prior knowledge degradation primarily results from tokens in the expert data to which the base model assigns low probability. Specifically, these low-probability tokens represent a significant deviation from the model’s current prior knowledge. Due to the nature of the log-likelihood objective, they produce larger gradient magnitudes, which speed up adaptation to the new data but degrade generalization. In this paper, we study the token-wise clipping strategy, a commonly used trust-region method for bounding per-token updates. We find that it reshapes token-level learning priorities, promoting more progressive adaptation that fits the new data while preserving general abilities. Compared with standard SFT, clipping low-probability tokens reduces out-of-distribution forgetting by 11.54% and improves final RL performance by 7.09% across the agentic benchmarks. Moreover, latent-space analysis shows smaller representational drift under clipping, indicating that it provides a generalizable initialization.

title: Clipping Low-Probability Tokens in SFT Yields a Generalizable Initialization for RL

abstract: Hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain a critical challenge, where models often generate tokens that fail to align with visual evidence. To address this issue, we propose AFS: Anchor-Final Self-Supervision, a novel framework for hallucination-aware optimization in LVLMs. By leveraging discrepancies between intermediate and final layer predictions, AFS selectively applies self-supervision to visually descriptive tokens, incorporates hallucination-aware token classification, and encourages consistency between intermediate and final layer distributions. Unlike traditional methods that rely on explicit supervision or post-hoc interventions, AFS optimizes the model via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using token-specific rewards derived from internal model signals. Experiments demonstrate that AFS significantly reduces hallucinations without compromising recall in caption generation. Beyond captioning, AFS excels in discriminative tasks, improving the reliability of object existence predictions and multimodal reasoning. Furthermore, AFS demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization, transferring effectively across diverse visual domains. Code is available at https://github.com/guavayew/AFS.

paragraphs: AFS targets visual hallucinations: generated words that do not match the image evidence. It builds a training signal from differences between predictions made at intermediate model layers and those made at the final layer. This gives the model an internal basis for focusing its optimization on potentially unreliable visual descriptions.

The framework selectively supervises visually descriptive tokens, incorporates token classification that accounts for hallucination, and encourages agreement between intermediate and final prediction distributions. It uses Group Relative Policy Optimization with rewards specific to individual tokens. These rewards come from internal model signals, making the approach an optimization method rather than a correction applied only after an answer has been generated.

The experiments report significantly fewer hallucinations in image captions without reducing recall. That combination matters because fewer unsupported descriptions need not come at the cost of overlooking supported content. The paper also reports improved object-existence judgments and multimodal reasoning, together with transfer across visual datasets. The findings suggest that the internal signals used by AFS can support reliability beyond the caption-generation setting.
summary.tldr: AFS uses disagreements between model layers to create token-level training rewards that reduce visual hallucinations while preserving caption recall.

title: Anchor-Final Self-Supervision Drives Hallucination-Aware Optimization in Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models are typically benchmarked by evaluating every model on every test query. For practitioners seeking the best model to deploy, this is often wasteful: if a model clearly performs worse than others, there is no need to precisely estimate its performance. Best-arm identification algorithms can be naturally applied to drastically reduce costs by adaptively allocating evaluation budget. Further, language models often respond similarly to the same prompt—a property previous work has tried to leverage with mixed success in different use cases. We propose Synchronized Successive Rejects (SySRs), augmenting the classical Successive Reject algorithm with paired comparisons. Unlike prior attempts to leverage model similarity in best-model identification, our approach is hyperparameter-free and enjoys performance guarantees that improve with the degree of similarity between evaluated models. Empirically, our method outperforms all baselines in terms of average error rate across 15 standard benchmarks, and in terms of worst-case budget for reliably identifying the best model.

paragraphs: Choosing the best language model does not always require measuring every candidate equally precisely. Once a model looks clearly inferior, further testing may contribute little to the deployment decision. This paper uses best-arm identification, a framework for allocating tests adaptively, to reduce the expense of finding the strongest model.

Synchronized Successive Rejects, or SySRs, augments the classical Successive Reject algorithm with paired comparisons. It uses the fact that different models often respond similarly to the same prompt. Comparing paired outcomes makes that similarity useful to the selection process. The method requires no hyperparameter tuning, and its performance guarantees improve as the evaluated models become more similar.

Across 15 standard benchmarks, SySRs achieves a lower average error rate than all evaluated baselines. It also performs better on the worst-case evaluation budget required to identify the best model reliably. These findings connect the theoretical benefit of model similarity to practical savings: evaluation effort can be concentrated on comparisons that still matter for the final selection.
summary.tldr: SySRs reduces model-selection evaluation costs through adaptive paired comparisons, with guarantees that improve when models behave more similarly.

title: Cutting LLM Evaluation Costs with SySRs: A Bandit Algorithm That Provably Exploits Model Similarity

abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) in graph neural networks (GNNs) is crucial in high-stakes domains but remains a significant challenge. In graph settings, message passing often relies on strong assumptions such as exchangeability, which are rarely satisfied in practice. Moreover, achieving reliable UQ typically requires costly resampling or post-hoc calibration. To address these issues, we introduce Quantile-free Prediction Interval GNN (QpiGNN), a framework that builds on quantile regression (QR) to enable GNN-based UQ by directly optimizing coverage and interval width without requiring quantile inputs or post-processing. QpiGNN employs a dual-head architecture that decouples prediction and uncertainty, and is trained with label-only supervision through a quantile-free joint loss. This design allows efficient training and yields robust prediction intervals, with theoretical guarantees of asymptotic coverage and near-optimal width under mild assumptions. Experiments on 19 synthetic and real-world benchmarks show QpiGNN achieves average 22% higher coverage and 50% narrower intervals than baselines, while ensuring efficiency and robustness to noise and structural shifts.

paragraphs: Useful prediction intervals must balance two goals: include the true value often enough and remain narrow enough to be informative. QpiGNN addresses this tradeoff for graph neural networks, where dependencies in graph data complicate uncertainty estimation and reliable intervals can require expensive resampling or calibration.

Building on quantile regression, the method directly optimizes interval coverage and width without requiring quantile inputs or post-processing. A dual-head architecture separates prediction from uncertainty, and a joint loss trains both using label-only supervision. This makes interval quality an explicit training objective instead of leaving uncertainty entirely to a later calibration stage.

summary.tldr: QpiGNN directly learns graph prediction intervals, reporting improved coverage and narrower widths without quantile inputs or post-processing.

title: Quantile-Free Uncertainty Quantification in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The synthesis of inductive loop invariants remains a critical bottleneck in automated program verification. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in mitigating this issue, they often fail on complex programs, producing invariants that are invalid or computationally ineffective. Although fine-tuning is a natural strategy to address these limitations, obtaining high-quality training data remains an open challenge. We first formalize the properties required for a high-quality training invariant, and then present Wonda, a rigorous data curation pipeline that extracts such invariants from raw verifier output via AST-based normalization followed by LLM-driven semantic rewriting and augmentation with provable quality guarantees. Fine-tuning Small Language Models (SLMs) on Wonda-curated data yields consistent gains across the Qwen3, Llama-3.1, and Mistral families: the 4B and 8B Qwen3 models nearly double invariant correctness and double speedup rates, while Llama-3.1-8B triples both. On the challenging InvBench suite, the same 4B model outperforms an off-the-shelf model 20$\times$ its size and matches the end-to-end verification time of GPT-OSS-120B, while a 14B Qwen3 model matches that of the frontier model GPT-5.2, all without test-time compute overhead. Our code is publicly available on https://github.com/idopinto/wonda.

paragraphs: Automated program verification often needs loop invariants: properties that remain valid as a loop executes and help establish program correctness. Language models can propose them, but their suggestions may be invalid or computationally unhelpful. This paper focuses on improving the training examples used to teach smaller models this task.

Their Wonda pipeline extracts invariants from raw verifier output, normalizes them using abstract syntax trees, then applies language-model-driven semantic rewriting and augmentation with provable quality guarantees. The goal is to curate examples that improve both correctness and verification efficiency.

Fine-tuning on this data yields gains across Qwen3, Llama-3.1, and Mistral models. The reported Qwen3 4B and 8B results nearly double invariant correctness and double speedup rates, while Llama-3.1-8B triples both. On InvBench, smaller tuned models match the verification times of much larger systems in the stated comparisons. These gains require no additional test-time computation, emphasizing training-data quality as a route to faster verification.
summary.tldr: Wonda curates provably qualified invariant training data that helps smaller language models improve and accelerate program verification.

title: Not All Invariants Are Equal: Curating Training Data to Accelerate Program Verification with SLMs

abstract: Diffusion language models are a promising alternative to autoregressive models due to their potential for faster generation. Among discrete diffusion approaches, Masked diffusion currently dominates, largely driven by strong perplexity on language modeling benchmarks. In this work, we present the first scaling law study of uniform-state and interpolating discrete diffusion methods. We also show that Masked diffusion models can be made approximately 12% more FLOPs-efficient when trained with a simple cross-entropy objective. We find that perplexity is informative within a diffusion family but can be misleading across families, where models with worse likelihood scaling may be preferable due to faster and more practical sampling, as reflected by the speed-quality Pareto frontier. These results challenge the view that Masked diffusion is categorically the future of diffusion language modeling and that perplexity alone suffices for cross-algorithm comparison. Scaling all methods to 1.7B parameters, we show that uniform-state diffusion remains competitive on likelihood-based benchmarks and outperforms autoregressive and Masked diffusion models on GSM8K, despite worse validation perplexity.

This paper broadens the comparison with the first reported scaling-law study of uniform-state and interpolating discrete diffusion methods. It also finds that a simple cross-entropy training objective makes masked diffusion approximately 12% more efficient in floating-point computation.

summary.tldr: Scaling comparisons show that uniform-state diffusion can remain competitive and outperform masked diffusion on GSM8K despite worse validation perplexity.

title: Scaling Beyond Masked Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Pre-trained vision language models do not have good intuitions about the physical world. Recent work has shown that supervised fine-tuning can improve model performance on simple physical tasks. However, fine-tuned models do not appear to learn robust physical rules that can generalize to new contexts. Based on research in cognitive science, we hypothesize that models need to interact with an environment to properly learn its physical dynamics. We train models that learn through interaction with a simulated environment using reinforcement learning. While learning from interaction allows models to improve their within-task performance, it fails to produce models with generalizable physical intuitions. We find that models trained on one task do not reliably generalize to related tasks, even if the tasks share visual statistics and physical principles, and regardless of whether the models are trained through interaction.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can improve at a physical task without learning rules that transfer to another situation. This paper investigates that distinction by asking whether interaction supplies something missing from supervised fine-tuning. Inspired by cognitive science, the authors hypothesize that acting within an environment could help models learn its physical dynamics more robustly.

They train models through reinforcement learning in a simulated environment, allowing learning to occur through interaction. The central question is whether this experience produces transferable physical understanding. The evaluation therefore considers both improvement on the trained task and generalization to related tasks that share visual statistics and physical principles.

Interaction improves performance within a task, but the trained models do not reliably transfer their abilities to related tasks. This failure occurs regardless of whether training involves interaction. The findings show that the tested form of interactive learning does not establish generalizable physical intuitions, even when tasks have substantial common ground. They distinguish successful task adaptation from evidence that a model has acquired reusable physical rules.
summary.tldr: Learning through simulated interaction improves trained-task performance but does not reliably produce transferable physical intuitions in the tested vision-language models.

title: Can Vision Language Models Learn Intuitive Physics from Interaction?

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized research in software engineering, and among various tasks, LLM-based code synthesis is promising. A recent line of benchmarks aims to evaluate LLM-generated codes in time efficiency, beyond their correctness. However, space, another vital aspect of code efficiency, is rarely evaluated in prior benchmarks. To fill in the gap, this paper introduces BEST, the first benchmark for evaluating the efficiency of LLM-generated codes in both time and space. It comprises $440$ coding tasks that are rigorously constructed by experts. In addition, we propose a fine-grained subtask-based evaluation scheme by dividing each task into multiple subtasks, with different input scales and difficulties. Each subtask is then accompanied by an expert-crafted standard implementation as the efficiency baseline, which achieves the Pareto optimum. Building on BEST, we introduce a unified and novel dual-indicator (time and space) metric, named dual@${k}$, generalizing the notion of the standard pass@${k}$ metric and building on a careful and novel construction of a weight matrix of subtasks. Through extensive experiments with dual@${k}$ across $50$ LLMs on BEST, our evaluation demonstrates that while LLMs exhibit weak capabilities in generating time-efficient code, their capabilities in space-efficient code generation are even worse. The benchmark is provided at https://github.com/kmsgk0/BEST.

paragraphs: Correct code can still consume too much time or memory. BEST evaluates both dimensions of efficiency in code generated by language models, addressing the limited attention paid to memory use in earlier benchmarks. It contains 440 expert-constructed coding tasks, making resource efficiency an explicit part of the evaluation rather than treating correctness as the whole outcome.

Each task is divided into subtasks with different input sizes and difficulties. Experts provide a reference implementation for every subtask, described as Pareto-optimal: its time and space trade-off cannot be improved in one dimension without sacrificing the other. This finer evaluation distinguishes performance across input conditions instead of assigning one undifferentiated efficiency judgment to an entire task.

The authors also introduce dual@k, a metric that extends pass@k to account for both time and space through a weighting scheme over subtasks. Their evaluation of 50 language models finds weak time-efficient code generation and still weaker space-efficient generation. The findings show why evaluating both resources can expose shortcomings that correctness or runtime alone would leave unmeasured.
summary.tldr: BEST evaluates generated code on runtime and memory use, finding that 50 tested language models struggle especially with space efficiency.

title: BEST: Benchmarking Efficiency in Space and Time for LLM-Generated Code

abstract: We study the estimation of repeatedly nested expectations (RNEs) with a constant horizon (number of nestings) using quantum computing. We propose a quantum algorithm that achieves $\varepsilon$-error with cost $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-1})$, up to logarithmic factors. Standard lower bounds show this scaling is essentially optimal, yielding an almost quadratic speedup over the best classical algorithm. Our results extend prior quantum speedups for single nested expectations to repeated nesting, and therefore cover a broader range of applications, including optimal stopping. This extension requires a new derandomized variant of the classical randomized Multilevel Monte Carlo (rMLMC) algorithm. Careful de-randomization is key to overcoming a variable-time issue that typically increases quantized versions of classical randomized algorithms.

Our results extend prior quantum speedups for single nested expectations to repeated nesting, and therefore cover a broader range of applications, including optimal stopping. paragraphs: The paper studies expectations nested inside other expectations, with repeated levels of averaging. Such problems arise in applications including optimal stopping. Its goal is to estimate the final quantity accurately using quantum computation, extending earlier speedups that covered only a single nesting.

For a constant number of nesting levels, the proposed algorithm achieves error ε at a cost scaling as 1/ε, apart from logarithmic factors. Standard lower bounds establish that this dependence is essentially optimal. Compared with the best classical algorithm, the result provides an almost quadratic speedup. The constant-horizon assumption is part of this claim: the stated scaling concerns a fixed number of nestings.

The technical advance is a new derandomized version of randomized Multilevel Monte Carlo. Classical randomization can create variable execution times that complicate a quantum version and increase its cost. Carefully removing that randomization overcomes this issue. The work therefore contributes both a repeated-nesting estimation result and an algorithmic construction that makes the quantum speedup possible.
summary.tldr: For a constant nesting depth, a quantum estimator achieves essentially optimal error scaling and an almost quadratic classical speedup.

title: Optimal Quantum Speedups for Repeatedly Nested Expectation Estimation

abstract: Single-cell foundation models trained on millions of cells can learn gene expression patterns across diverse contexts. However, for predicting genetic perturbation effects they often underperform simple regression models. We hypothesize two potential limitations: targets defined on dropout-prone absolute expression, and pretraining objectives that reconstruct static co-expression rather than encoding how genes co-regulate under expression changes. We introduce $\textbf{scDEBART}$, a perturbation-specific pretraining framework that predicts log fold-changes (logFC) conditioned on basal expression, thereby learning how gene sets co-vary across expression-change contexts at scale. To obtain reliable estimates of expression change under technical sparsity, we compute logFC from scVI-denoised expression and restrict pretraining to genes with robust detection. Pretrained on 6.28 million expression-change profiles from 66.6 million human cells and fine-tuned on five Perturb-seq datasets, scDEBART achieves mean enrichment factor (EF) of 11.96, 4-7$\times$ higher than scGPT and GEARS (mean EF 1.74-2.99), and 71.4% top-1 accuracy for reverse perturbation identification compared to near-zero accuracy for prior models. In cross-modal transfer to drug perturbations (SCIPLEX), the model shows dose-dependent improvement in directional alignment (cosine similarity 0.04$\rightarrow$0.30) with above-random DEG enrichment (EF 2.91-4.32), suggesting partial transfer of learned regulatory patterns across modalities. Overall, these results indicate that large-scale pretraining on scVI-denoised expression-change profiles provides a useful inductive bias for perturbation prediction.

The authors hypothesize that existing single-cell foundation models are held back by noisy absolute-expression targets and objectives centered on static co-expression. Their alternative predicts logarithmic fold-changes conditioned on baseline expression, emphasizing how genes change together across different contexts.

To reduce the effects of technical sparsity, the framework computes changes from scVI-denoised expression and restricts pretraining to reliably detected genes. Training uses 6.28 million expression-change profiles derived from 66.6 million human cells, followed by fine-tuning on five Perturb-seq datasets. This aligns large-scale pretraining with the downstream task of predicting responses to intervention.

The model achieves a mean enrichment factor of 11.96, reported as 4–7 times that of scGPT and GEARS, and 71.4% top-1 accuracy for reverse perturbation identification. Transfer to drug perturbations shows dose-dependent improvements in directional alignment and above-random enrichment of differentially expressed genes. Those transfer results suggest partial reuse of learned regulatory patterns across modalities, supporting expression-change pretraining as a useful inductive bias.
summary.tldr: scDEBART learns denoised gene-expression changes at scale to improve perturbation prediction, with evidence of partial transfer to drug responses.

title: scDEBART: Predicting in silico Single-Cell Perturbation Responses via Large-Scale Differential Expression Learning

abstract: Real-world perception and decision making are inherently multimodal, integrating complementary signals across modalities. However, training multimodal models faces two main obstacles. First, collecting large-scale, well-aligned paired multimodal datasets is often impractical, making end-to-end multimodal training difficult. Second, existing multimodal representations frequently entangle information shared across modalities with modality-specific information, hindering interpretability and control. We introduce MultiLoReFT, an efficient and scalable low-rank representation fine-tuning framework for multimodal learning with pretrained unimodal models. MultiLoReFT extends low-rank adaptation to the multimodal setting and learns interpretable projection subspaces that decouple shared and modality-specific information. Across simulated and real-world benchmarks, it produces representations that support multimodal prediction while explicitly revealing how shared and modality-specific information is distributed across modalities.

paragraphs: Multimodal models must combine information that different inputs share while preserving information unique to each input type. Two obstacles complicate that goal: large, well-aligned paired datasets can be difficult to collect, and learned representations often mix shared and modality-specific information together. MultiLoReFT addresses these challenges using pretrained models for individual modalities.

The framework applies low-rank representation fine-tuning to the multimodal setting. It learns projection subspaces that separate information common across modalities from information specific to one modality. This organization makes the representation more interpretable and controllable because it explicitly distinguishes the two roles. Reusing pretrained unimodal models provides the starting point for its efficient and scalable adaptation approach.

Across simulated and real-world benchmarks, the resulting representations support multimodal prediction and reveal how shared and modality-specific information is distributed across modalities. The stated benefit therefore includes both predictive use and visibility into the representation’s structure. The work presents a way to combine existing unimodal capabilities while making the information contributing to multimodal predictions easier to examine.
summary.tldr: MultiLoReFT adapts pretrained unimodal models into multimodal representations that explicitly separate shared and modality-specific information.

title: MultiLoReFT: Decoupling Shared and Modality-Specific Subspaces in Multimodal Learning via Low-Rank Representation Fine-Tuning

abstract: Multi-target domain adaptation (MTDA) trains a model using a labeled source domain and several unlabeled target domains, aiming to enhance performance across all targets. However, existing methods lack a principled causal formulation and often rely on empirical domain-invariance enforcement, which can bias adaptation across targets. To fill this gap, we propose the Unbiased, Unconfounding, and Unified Causal Framework (U$^3$CF) for MTDA. To unify the alignment of multiple domains, we propose a prototype-driven alignment strategy that progressively updates prototypes by high-confidence target predictions, while the contrastive optimization objective jointly aligns target samples to semantic prototypes and preserves class discrimination. By formulating a structural causal model, we reveal that domain-invariant causal factors and domain-specific factors shape representations and labels, while the latter induce spurious label correlations across targets. Accordingly, U$^3$CF achieves unbiased prediction by disentangling representations into invariant causal components and domain-specific confounders and applying conditional intervention to block confounding effects while preserving invariant semantics. To ensure precise disentanglement, we leverage mutual information theory to derive a principled criterion for feature separation. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that U$^3$CF consistently outperforms leading methods.
