paragraphs: Multi-target domain adaptation learns from one labeled domain and several unlabeled target domains. U³CF argues that simply encouraging domain-invariant representations can bias adaptation across targets. It introduces a structural causal formulation that distinguishes invariant causal factors from domain-specific factors, with the latter producing spurious relationships with labels across target domains.

The framework aligns domains through semantic prototypes, updating them progressively using high-confidence target predictions. A contrastive objective brings target samples toward the appropriate prototypes while preserving class distinctions. It also separates representations into invariant causal components and domain-specific confounders. Conditional intervention blocks the confounding effects while retaining invariant semantics, and a criterion derived from mutual information guides feature separation.

Across four benchmarks, U³CF consistently outperforms leading methods in the reported experiments. Its contribution connects multi-domain alignment with an explicit account of which information should be preserved and which effects should be blocked. The causal formulation and prototype alignment work together to support predictions across multiple unlabeled targets.
summary.tldr: U³CF combines semantic-prototype alignment with causal feature separation and conditional intervention to improve adaptation across multiple target domains.

title: U$^3$CF: Unbiased, Unconfounding, and Unified Causal Framework for Multi-Target Domain Adaptation

abstract: As high-quality public text approaches exhaustion, a phenomenon known as the Data Wall—LLM pre-training is shifting from more tokens to better tokens. However, existing methods either rely on heuristic static filters that ignore training dynamics, or use dynamic yet optimizer-agnostic criteria based on raw gradients. We propose OPUS (Optimizer-induced Projected Utility Selection), a dynamic framework that defines utility in the optimizer-induced update space. OPUS scores candidates by projecting their effective updates, shaped by modern optimizers, onto a target direction derived from a stable, in-distribution proxy. To ensure scalability, we employ Ghost technique with CountSketch for computational efficiency, and Boltzmann sampling for data diversity, incurring only 4.7% additional compute overhead. OPUS achieves remarkable results across diverse corpora, quality tiers, optimizers, and model scales. It also outperforms previous data selection methods across different stages of training, including from-scratch pre-training and also mid-training. Beyond online selection, the OPUS utility score also demonstrates potential as a static filter for flagging and removing toxic documents from contaminated training corpora prior to training.

paragraphs: Choosing useful training text becomes increasingly important as high-quality public data becomes scarce. Static filters cannot respond to a model’s changing training needs, while some dynamic methods judge examples using raw gradients without accounting for the optimizer. OPUS evaluates candidate data according to the parameter updates the optimizer would actually produce.

It projects these effective updates onto a target direction derived from a stable, in-distribution proxy. This makes utility depend on both the current training state and the optimizer’s transformation of gradients. Ghost techniques and CountSketch support computational efficiency, while Boltzmann sampling maintains diversity in the selected data. The reported additional compute overhead is 4.7%.

They also find potential for using the utility score as a static filter to remove toxic documents before training. That filtering result is presented as a possible additional use of the score.
summary.tldr: OPUS selects training data using optimizer-shaped update utility, improving selection across training settings with 4.7% additional compute.

title: OPUS: Towards Efficient and Principled Data Selection in Large Language Model Pre-training in Every Iteration

abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated significant progress in perceiving and reasoning over multimodal inquiries, ushering in a new research era for foundation models. However, vision-language misalignment in MLLMs has emerged as a critical challenge, where the textual responses generated by these models are not factually aligned with the given text-image inputs. Existing efforts to address vision-language misalignment have focused on developing specialized vision-language connectors or leveraging visual instruction tuning from diverse domains. In this paper, we tackle this issue from a fundamental yet unexplored perspective by revisiting the core architecture of MLLMs. Most MLLMs are typically built on decoder-only LLMs consisting of a causal attention mechanism, which limits the ability of the earlier modalities (e.g., images) to incorporate information from the latter modalities (e.g., text). To address this problem a MLLM that unlocks causal attention into our proposed modality-mutual attention (MMA) to enable image tokens to attend to text tokens. This simple yet effective design allows MMA to achieve state-of-the-art performance in 12 multimodal understanding benchmarks (+6.2% on average across 3 LLMs backbones) without introducing additional parameters. Our MMA design is intended to be generic, allowing for applications across various modalities, and scalable to accommodate diverse multimodal scenarios.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can produce text that does not match the image and text they receive. This paper examines an architectural contributor: causal attention in decoder-only models prevents earlier tokens from incorporating information from later ones. When image tokens precede text tokens, the image representation cannot attend to that later text.

Modality-mutual attention changes this access pattern so image tokens can attend to text tokens. This allows visual processing within the model to incorporate information from the accompanying language. The modification addresses communication between modalities inside the attention mechanism, without adding model parameters. It therefore targets a different part of the system from specialized connectors or additional visual instruction tuning.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on 12 multimodal understanding benchmarks, with an average improvement of 6.2% across three language-model backbones. These results support the usefulness of changing cross-modal attention access. The design is intended to extend to other modalities and multimodal settings; that broader applicability is presented as a design aim beyond the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Modality-mutual attention lets image tokens attend to text tokens, improving multimodal understanding without adding parameters.

title: Seeing is Understanding: Unlocking Causal Attention into Modality-Mutual Attention for Multimodal LLMs

abstract: Nonlinear conservation laws are at the heart of many of the most important dynamical systems in science and engineering. In practical applications, such systems are often subject to various sources of uncertainty, e.g. due to sparse or noisy measurements. Inferring physical quantities and fields of interest then becomes an ill-posed problem which both classical numerical methods and modern deep learning-based methods struggle to treat appropriately. Recent work has framed classical numerical methods as Bayesian inference under Gaussian process priors, resulting in a physics-aware treatment of uncertainties. Following this line of work, we develop a novel numerically conservative method for uncertainty-aware simulations of nonlinear conservation laws. We use recent sparse approximation techniques to scale up to large-scale forward and inverse problems. For forward simulation, we inherit the accuracy of classical solvers while providing structured uncertainty quantification. On inverse problems, we recover posteriors over nonparametric source fields in seconds — outperforming neural baselines that take minutes to produce a less accurate point estimate.

paragraphs: Nonlinear conservation laws describe many physical systems, but sparse or noisy measurements can make their unknown quantities difficult to infer reliably. Several explanations of the same observations may remain plausible. The paper addresses this uncertainty through a Bayesian numerical method that preserves the conservation structure of the equations.

The approach builds on interpreting classical numerical methods as inference under Gaussian-process priors. It adds a numerically conservative method for nonlinear conservation laws and uses sparse approximations to make larger problems manageable. This connects physical structure with a probabilistic description of uncertainty, covering both forward simulation and inference of unknown source fields.

For forward problems, the authors report the accuracy of classical solvers together with structured uncertainty estimates. For inverse problems, they recover posterior distributions over nonparametric source fields in seconds, outperforming neural baselines that require minutes for less accurate point estimates. The distinction matters because a posterior represents uncertainty across possible fields, giving the inference result more information than a single estimated field in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: A conservative Bayesian solver combines classical simulation accuracy with scalable uncertainty estimates and fast inference of unknown source fields.

title: Scalable Bayesian Inference for Nonlinear Conservation Laws

abstract: With the rapid emergence of multi-behavior learning in recommender systems, leveraging auxiliary user behaviors has proven effective for mitigating target-behavior data sparsity. Yet auxiliary behavior graphs frequently contain noisy or irrelevant interactions that do not align with the target task, impeding the learning of accurate user and item embeddings. Moreover, the scarcity of direct supervised from the target behavior complicates the extraction of informative collaborative signals. In this paper, we introduce GCIB Graph Contrastive Information Bottleneck, a novel framework that denoises auxiliary behavior information and enriches target behavior representations at both the structural and feature levels. At the structural level, GCIB employs a Graph Information Bottleneck (GIB) objective to maximize mutual information between the denoised auxiliary graph and the target-behavior graph while minimizing mutual information with the original auxiliary graph. This formulation preserves task-relevant structural patterns and suppresses spurious interactions. At the feature level, we propose a cross-behavior Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) scheme in which denoised auxiliary features and target-behavior features serve as complementary views for both users and items. By contrasting these views, GCIB enriches sparse target-behavior representations with semantics distilled from auxiliary behaviors. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that GCIB outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its ability to learn noise-resilient and target-aware representations for multi-behavior recommendation.

paragraphs: A recommender may have little data about the behavior it ultimately wants to predict, while observing more auxiliary user behaviors. Those extra interactions can help, but some are irrelevant or noisy. GCIB aims to extract the useful parts of auxiliary behavior graphs and use them to strengthen sparse representations of the target behavior.

At the structural level, an information-bottleneck objective encourages the denoised auxiliary graph to retain information about the target graph while reducing information retained from the original auxiliary graph. This combination favors task-relevant patterns and suppresses spurious interactions. At the feature level, a contrastive learning scheme connects denoised auxiliary features with target-behavior features for both users and items.

These two mechanisms address different parts of the problem: which relationships to retain and how to transfer useful information into representations. Across multiple real-world datasets, the authors report better performance than leading baselines. The findings support combining structural denoising with cross-behavior representation learning when direct supervision for the target behavior is scarce.
summary.tldr: GCIB filters auxiliary interaction graphs and contrasts behavior-specific features to improve recommendation when target-behavior data is sparse.

title: GCIB: Graph Contrastive Information Bottleneck for Multi-Behavior Recommendation

abstract: The limited transferability of adversarial attacks on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) stems from their failure to navigate model-specific safety alignments, where superficial perturbations exploit surrogate-specific artifacts rather than shared safety-critical features. We reveal through linear probing that safety-related representations are concentrated within specific intermediate neuronal circuits, which act as localized defense bottlenecks that can be disentangled from transferable features. To overcome this barrier, we propose the Safety Circuit Intervention Attack (SCIA), a framework that surgically steers internal representations to bypass these localized safety mechanisms. SCIA employs a dual-objective steering strategy that suppresses the defensive circuit encoding safety features while amplifying the transferable circuit capturing model-agnostic representations, effectively decoupling adversarial patterns from surrogate-specific safety behaviors. Furthermore, we incorporate contrastive semantic steering and spectral smoothness regularization to guide optimization toward compliant semantic regions while producing visually coherent perturbations. Experimental results demonstrate that SCIA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in bypassing unseen black-box VLMs.

paragraphs: Adversarial inputs developed against one vision-language model often transfer poorly to another. This paper attributes that difficulty to differences in models’ safety alignment: an attack may exploit peculiarities of its development model instead of features shared across models. summary.tldr: SCIA links localized safety representations to attack transferability and reports stronger attacks against unseen vision-language models.

title: Dissecting the Safety Circuit: Neuronal Intervention for Transferable Adversarial Attacks on VLMs

abstract: Visual prostheses hold great promise for restoring vision in blind individuals. While researchers have successfully utilized M/EEG signals to evoke visual perceptions during the brain decoding stage of visual prostheses, the complementary process of converting images into M/EEG signals in the brain encoding stage remains largely unexplored, hindering the formation of a complete functional pipeline. In this work, we present a novel image-to-brain signal framework that generates M/EEG from images by leveraging the diffusion transformer architecture enhanced with cross-attention mechanisms. Specifically, we employ a diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture based on denoising diffusion implicit models (DDIM) to achieve brain signal generation. To realize the goal of image-to-brain signal conversion, we use cross-attention mechanisms to align brain signal embeddings with CLIP image embeddings. Moreover, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to generate image captions, and concatenate the resulting CLIP text embeddings with CLIP image embeddings to form unified embeddings for cross-attention alignment, enabling our model to capture core semantic information. Furthermore, we introduce a learnable spatio-temporal position encoding that combines brain region embeddings with temporal embeddings to capture both spatial and temporal characteristics of brain signals. We evaluate the framework on two multimodal benchmark datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG) and demonstrate that it generates biologically plausible brain signals.

paragraphs: This paper addresses an encoding problem relevant to visual prostheses: generating M/EEG brain signals from images. It complements work on decoding visual information from brain signals by studying the conversion in the other direction. The proposed framework uses a diffusion transformer to generate signals conditioned on image information.

The demonstrated contribution is therefore an image-conditioned brain-signal generator that combines semantic guidance with spatial and temporal structure, addressing an encoding component of the broader visual-prosthesis pipeline.
summary.tldr: A diffusion transformer combines CLIP image and caption representations with spatial and temporal encoding to generate plausible M/EEG signals.

title: Image-to-Brain Signal Generation for Visual Prosthesis with CLIP Guided Multimodal Diffusion Models

abstract: In this work, we address the critical yet underexplored challenge of symmetric multimodal-to-multimodal (MM2MM) retrieval, where queries and contexts are interchangeable. Existing universal multimodal retrieval works struggle with this task, as they are constrained by the labeled asymmetric datasets used. We produce SOLAR (Self-supervised jOint LeArning for symmetric multimodal Retrieval), a novel two-stage self-supervised framework that leverages readily available unlabeled web-scale image-text pairs. Based on the observation that both semantic alignment and discrepancies exist between two modalities, in the first stage, we learn the intersection mask of image-text pair, allowing us to align intersection while preserving semantic of difference. In the second stage, the learned mask is further utilized to construct positive and hardnegative samples via masking different parts of image/text, which enable us to conduct self-supervised multimodal embedding learning. Complementing this framework, we present a new benchmark featuring high-quality human-verified positive and hard-negative pairs to evaluate symmetric MM2MM retrieval under realistic conditions, as well as the corresponding pipeline. Extensive experiments against ten SOTA methods show SOLAR surpasses the strongest supervised VLM by 7.08 points on this benchmark, with over 50x fewer model parameters and a 5x smaller embedding dimension. Code, model and benchmark are available at https://github.com/codefuse-ai/SOLAR.

paragraphs: Symmetric multimodal retrieval searches between items containing both images and text, with either side able to serve as the query. Existing universal retrieval methods struggle because their labeled training datasets impose asymmetric roles. SOLAR addresses this using a two-stage self-supervised framework trained from readily available, unlabeled image-text pairs.

The first stage learns a mask representing the semantic intersection between an image and its text. It aligns shared meaning while preserving information that appears in only one modality. The second stage uses that mask to hide different portions of images or text, constructing positive examples and difficult negatives for learning multimodal embeddings.

The authors also introduce a benchmark with human-verified positive and hard-negative pairs. Against ten state-of-the-art methods, SOLAR exceeds the strongest supervised vision-language model by 7.08 points on that benchmark, while using over 50 times fewer parameters and embeddings five times smaller. These results support learning from both shared and differing image-text content for this symmetric retrieval setting.
summary.tldr: SOLAR learns symmetric multimodal retrieval from unlabeled image-text pairs by modeling both shared and modality-specific meaning.

title: SOLAR: Self-supervised Joint Learning for Symmetric Multimodal Retrieval

abstract: This paper presents UniFast-HGR, a scalable surrogate for Hirschfeld–Gebelein–Rényi (HGR) maximal correlation in high-dimensional multimodal learning. The method replaces explicit covariance whitening with centered and $\ell_2$-normalized cosine alignment, uses the covariance-to-Gram trace identity to construct a local-batch structural surrogate, and removes invariant diagonal self-correlation through Trivial Spectrum Suppression (TSS). The resulting objective retains paired dependence maximization and the covariance-control role of Soft-HGR while replacing its finite-sample covariance estimator with a differentiable local-batch objective whose dominant structural cost is $O(m^2K)$ for local batch size $m$ and feature dimension $K$. OptFast-HGR further reduces the practical memory burden by estimating the off-diagonal structural term through stochastic projection. Experiments across retrieval, image classification, remote sensing segmentation, and multimodal emotion recognition show consistent gains over covariance-based HGR/CCA variants and contrastive or neural MI-estimator objectives on strong multimodal backbones, while microbenchmarks confirm stable behavior at extreme feature dimensions.

paragraphs: UniFast-HGR targets the computational burden of learning dependence between high-dimensional modalities using maximal correlation. It is a scalable surrogate for the Hirschfeld–Gebelein–Rényi objective. The design retains paired dependence maximization and the covariance-control role of Soft-HGR while changing how the necessary relationships are estimated within a training batch.

The method replaces explicit covariance whitening with centered, length-normalized cosine alignment. It uses an identity linking covariance and Gram-matrix traces to form a local-batch structural objective, then removes invariant diagonal self-correlations through Trivial Spectrum Suppression. Its dominant structural cost is O(m²K), where m is local batch size and K is feature dimension. An additional variant uses stochastic projection to reduce practical memory requirements.

Experiments cover retrieval, image classification, remote sensing segmentation, and multimodal emotion recognition. The authors report consistent gains over covariance-based HGR/CCA variants and contrastive or neural mutual-information objectives on strong backbones. Microbenchmarks also show stable behavior at extreme feature dimensions, supporting the approach as a practical dependence-learning objective for large multimodal representations.
summary.tldr: UniFast-HGR reformulates maximal-correlation learning around local-batch operations to improve scalability and multimodal task performance.

title: UniFast-HGR: Scalable and Efficient Maximal Correlation for Multimodal Models

abstract: We propose Block Adaptive Signum (BAS), which bridges Adam and SignSGD via block-wise scaling of sign updates. By discarding element-wise second moments, BAS reduces memory overhead relative to AdamW without sacrificing performance in our tested settings. Crucially, BAS mimics Adam’s dynamics closely enough to directly inherit its hyperparameters, matching the performance of AdamW without the need for re-tuning, a common fragility of prior low-memory optimizers. This structural alignment makes it particularly suitable for tuning Adam-pretrained models. Furthermore, we exploit the inherent robustness of sign-based updates to store the first moment in FP8 without performance degradation. This shrinks the optimizer-state footprint to 12.5% of AdamW’s. We theoretically prove convergence under standard assumptions and introduce a communication-efficient variant enabled by the sign-based update. Across extensive evaluations, including pre-training a 1.5B model on 100B tokens and supervised fine-tuning of models up to 32B parameters, we demonstrate that BAS achieves performance on par with AdamW.

paragraphs: Training large language models requires memory for the optimizer’s running statistics as well as model weights. Block Adaptive Signum, or BAS, reduces this overhead by combining sign-based updates with scaling shared across blocks of parameters. It discards the element-wise second-moment statistics used by Adam-style optimizers while retaining update behavior intended to resemble Adam closely.

That similarity matters because changing optimizers can otherwise require substantial hyperparameter retuning. In the tested settings, BAS directly inherits Adam’s hyperparameters and matches AdamW’s performance. This makes the method particularly relevant for adapting models already pretrained with Adam. The authors also exploit the robustness of sign updates to store the first-moment statistics in FP8 without observed performance degradation.

Together, these changes reduce optimizer-state memory to 12.5% of AdamW’s footprint. Evaluations include pretraining a 1.5-billion-parameter model on 100 billion tokens and supervised fine-tuning of models up to 32 billion parameters, with performance on par with AdamW. The paper additionally proves convergence under standard assumptions and introduces a communication-efficient variant based on sign updates.
summary.tldr: BAS matches AdamW in tested training settings while reusing Adam hyperparameters and reducing optimizer-state memory to 12.5%.

abstract: We propose a novel ensemble learning algorithm called Triskel, which has two interesting features. First, Triskel learns an ensemble of classifiers, each biased to have high precision on instances from a single class (as opposed to, for example, boosting, where the ensemble members are biased to maximise accuracy over a subset of instances from all classes). Second, the ensemble members’ voting weights are assigned so that certain pairs of biased classifiers outweigh the rest of the ensemble, if their predictions agree. Our experiments demonstrate that Triskel often outperforms boosting, in terms of both accuracy and training time. We also present an ROC analysis, which shows that Triskel’s iterative structure corresponds to a sequence of nested ROC spaces. The analysis predicts that Triskel works best when there are concavities in the ROC curves; this prediction agrees with our empirical results.

paragraphs: Triskel is an ensemble algorithm whose members specialize in making high-precision predictions for individual classes. Each classifier is deliberately biased toward one class. This differs from the boosting strategy described in the paper, where members aim for accuracy on selected examples drawn from across the classes.

The ensemble also uses a distinctive voting rule. Weights are assigned so that certain pairs of specialized classifiers outweigh all remaining members when those two agree. Agreement between designated specialists can therefore determine the ensemble's decision. Both the specialization and the voting weights are central parts of how Triskel combines its members.

Experiments show that Triskel often beats boosting in accuracy and training time. An ROC analysis connects its iterative construction to a sequence of nested ROC spaces and predicts that it works best when ROC curves contain concavities. The empirical findings agree with that prediction. This gives the reported gains a structural interpretation while preserving their qualified scope: the paper reports frequent advantages, not uniform superiority.
summary.tldr: Triskel combines class-specialized classifiers with decisive pairwise voting and often outperforms boosting in accuracy and training time.

title: Ensembles of biased classifiers

abstract: Subgroup discovery is the task of identifying the top k patterns in a database with most significant deviation in the distribution of a target attribute Y . Subgroup discovery is a popular approach for identifying interesting patterns in data, because it effectively combines statistical significance with an understandable representation of patterns as a logical formula. However, it is often a problem that some subgroups, even if they are statistically highly significant, are not interesting to the user for some reason. In this paper, we present an approach based on the work on ranking Support Vector Machines that ranks subgroups with respect to the user's concept of interestingness, and finds subgroups that are interesting to the user. It will be shown that this approach can significantly increase the quality of the subgroups.

paragraphs: Subgroup discovery searches a database for patterns whose target attribute has an unusually different distribution. These patterns can be expressed as logical formulas, giving users an understandable description of the groups being identified. A highly significant deviation, however, does not by itself establish that a group is interesting to the person using the system.

This paper introduces an approach based on ranking support vector machines to order subgroups according to a user's notion of interestingness. The ranking objective brings the user's preferences into the discovery process. This changes what counts as a useful result: the method aims to find subgroups aligned with the user's interests alongside the statistical motivation for subgroup discovery.

The authors report that this approach can significantly improve subgroup quality. The significance of that finding is the connection between understandable statistical patterns and their relevance to a particular user. The result supports adapting subgroup ranking to user interests, while retaining the distinction between a statistically unusual group and one the user actually values.
summary.tldr: A ranking-SVM approach personalizes subgroup discovery to the user's interests and can significantly improve the quality of discovered groups.

title: Ranking interesting subgroups

abstract: We present a novel approach for structure prediction that addresses the difficulty of obtaining labeled structures for training. We observe that structured output problems often have a companion learning problem of determining whether a given input possesses a good structure. For example, the companion problem for the part-of-speech (POS) tagging task asks whether a given sequence of words has a corresponding sequence of POS tags that is ``legitimate''. While obtaining direct supervision for structures is difficult and expensive, it is often very easy to obtain indirect supervision from the companion binary decision problem.In this paper, we develop a large margin framework that jointly learns from both direct and indirect forms of supervision. Our experiments exhibit the significant contribution of the easy-to-get indirect binary supervision on three important NLP structure learning problems.

For example, the companion problem for the part-of-speech (POS) tagging task asks whether a given sequence of words has a corresponding sequence of POS tags that is ``legitimate''. While obtaining direct supervision for structures is difficult and expensive, it is often very easy to obtain indirect supervision from the companion binary decision problem.In this paper, we develop a large margin framework that jointly learns from both direct and indirect forms of supervision. Our experiments exhibit the significant contribution of the easy-to-get indirect binary supervision on three important NLP structure learning problems.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires outputs with internal organization, which can make complete training annotations expensive to obtain. This paper observes that many such tasks have a simpler companion question: does an input possess a good structure? Answering that binary question can be much easier than supplying the full structured output itself.

For part-of-speech tagging, the companion question asks whether a word sequence has a legitimate corresponding sequence of tags. This supplies indirect supervision about the existence of an acceptable structure. The authors develop a large-margin framework that jointly learns from these binary judgments and from direct annotations of structures, combining the two sources of training information.

Experiments on three natural-language structure learning problems show a significant contribution from the easier-to-obtain indirect supervision. The result supports using companion decision tasks to supplement structured labels. The paper's central contribution is a learning framework that connects inexpensive judgments about structural acceptability with the more detailed prediction task, allowing both forms of evidence to inform training.
summary.tldr: A large-margin framework improves structured learning by combining direct annotations with easier binary judgments about whether inputs admit good structures.

title: Structured Output Learning with Indirect Supervision

abstract: When equipped with kernel functions, online learning algorithms are susceptible to the �curse of kernelization� that causes unbounded growth in the model size. To address this issue, we present a family of budgeted online learning algorithms for multi-class classification which have constant space and time complexity per update. Our approach is based on the multi-class version of the popular Pegasos algorithm. It keeps the number of support vectors bounded during learning through budget maintenance. By treating the budget maintenance as a source of the gradient error, we prove that the gap between the budgeted Pegasos and the optimal solution directly depends on the average model degradation due to budget maintenance. To minimize the model degradation, we study greedy multi-class budget maintenance methods based on removal, projection, and merging of support vectors. Empirical results show that the proposed budgeted online algorithms achieve accuracy comparable to non-budget multi-class kernelized Pegasos while being extremely computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Kernel-based online learners can accumulate more support vectors as training continues, allowing their models to grow without bound. This paper develops budgeted versions of multiclass Pegasos that cap the number of support vectors. For a fixed budget, the algorithms have constant space and time complexity per update.

Enforcing that cap can change the model and reduce its quality. The authors treat this budget-maintenance effect as an error in the gradient used for learning. Their analysis connects the gap from the optimal solution directly to the average model degradation introduced by maintenance. This gives a theoretical reason to focus on how the budget is enforced, rather than considering only its size.

The paper studies greedy maintenance methods that remove, project, or merge support vectors to reduce that degradation. Empirically, the resulting algorithms achieve accuracy comparable to unrestricted multiclass kernelized Pegasos while being highly computationally efficient. The contribution combines bounded resource use with an account of the optimization cost of maintaining that bound.
summary.tldr: Budgeted multiclass Pegasos bounds model growth and links its optimization gap to the degradation caused by maintaining the budget.

title: Multi-Class Pegasos on a Budget

abstract: Learning from electronic medical records (EMR) is challenging due to their relational nature and the need to capture the uncertain dependence between a patient's past and future health status. Statistical relational learning (SRL), which combines relational and probabilistic representations, is a natural fit for analyzing EMRs. SRL is less adept at handling the inherent latent structure, such as connections between related medications or diseases, in EMRs. One solution is to capture the latent structure via a relational clustering of objects. We propose a novel approach that, instead of pre-clustering the objects, performs a demand-driven clustering during the learning process. We evaluate our algorithm on three real-world tasks where the goal is to use EMRs to predict whether a patient will have an adverse reaction to a medication. We find that the proposed approach is more accurate than performing no clustering, pre-clustering and using expert-constructed medical heterarchies.

paragraphs: Electronic medical records contain relationships among patients, medications, diseases, and health events. Predicting a future adverse drug reaction requires handling both these connections and uncertainty about how past health relates to future outcomes. Statistical relational learning combines relational and probabilistic representations, making it a natural approach to this kind of prediction.

The difficulty addressed here is latent structure: related medications or diseases may share useful patterns that are not directly represented. Clustering can expose those groupings, but choosing groups before learning separates that decision from the prediction task. The proposed method instead builds clusters as they are needed during learning, allowing the learning process to guide which groupings become useful.

The authors evaluate the approach on three real-world tasks that predict adverse medication reactions from medical records. It achieves higher accuracy than learning without clustering, clustering in advance, and using expert-built medical heterarchies. These findings support task-guided clustering as a useful way to represent hidden relationships in the evaluated medical prediction settings.
summary.tldr: Clustering medications and diseases during learning improves adverse-drug-reaction prediction across three evaluated medical-record tasks.

title: Demand-Driven Clustering in Relational Domains for Predicting Adverse Drug Events

abstract: This manuscript develops the theory of agglomerative clustering with Bregman divergences. Geometric smoothing techniques are developed to deal with degenerate clusters. To allow for cluster models based on exponential families with overcomplete representations, Bregman divergences are developed for nondifferentiable convex functions.
originalAbstract: This manuscript develops the theory of agglomerative clustering with Bregman divergences. Geometric smoothing techniques are developed to deal with degenerate clusters. To allow for cluster models based on exponential families with overcomplete representations, Bregman divergences are developed for nondifferentiable convex functions.

paragraphs: This paper develops the theory of agglomerative clustering using Bregman divergences. The clustering process builds groups through successive merges, with the divergence providing the mathematical basis for comparing them. The contribution concerns how to formulate this process in settings where the geometry or representation of a cluster makes the analysis more difficult.

One part of the work develops geometric smoothing techniques for degenerate clusters. These are cases that require special treatment within the clustering formulation. Smoothing gives the theory a way to handle such clusters, making their treatment an explicit part of the mathematical framework rather than leaving them outside its scope.

A second part develops Bregman divergences for convex functions that are not differentiable. The stated motivation is to accommodate cluster models based on exponential families with overcomplete representations. Together, these developments extend the mathematical tools available for agglomerative clustering: one addresses degenerate clusters, and the other supports a broader form of cluster representation. The paper's stated contribution is this theoretical development.
summary.tldr: The paper extends Bregman-based agglomerative clustering theory to handle degenerate clusters and exponential-family models with overcomplete representations.
